The Jets now turn to a familiar face in Geno Smith, who is coming off one of the worst seasons of his 13-year career. Not only did the 35-year-old go 2-13 as the Raiders' starter, but he also led the league in sacks taken (55) and interceptions (17). It was a disaster, but I would argue that Smith is upgrading his situation, going from Sin City to New York.
The Jets definitely have a better offensive line than the Raiders did in 2025, with Olu Fashanu, Dylan Parham , Josh Myers , Joe Tippmann and Armand Membou . The Jets also have legit weaponry with Breece Hall , Garrett Wilson , Omar Cooper Jr . and Kenyon Sadiq . I certainly don't view Smith as one of the best quarterbacks in the NFL, but I do view him as an obvious upgrade from what the Jets had last year. He had two 4,200-yard passing seasons in three years with the Seahawks. If Smith can just rely on his playmakers and take care of the football, the Jets will average more than 263 yards of total offense in 2026.
CBS Sports' fantasy projected statline : 3,460 passing yards, 24 TDs, 10 INTs
There is a quarterback battle going on in Atlanta, but Michael Penix Jr. is coming off a third ACL tear, while the Falcons quickly pursued and signed Tua Tagovailoa . The CBS Sports fantasy team believes Tagovailoa is going to see extensive action in 2026 compared to Penix.
When paired with Mike McDaniel, Tagovailoa looked like an efficient point guard for a high-powered passing attack. Most of the time. His 44 wins were the most by a Dolphins quarterback since Dan Marino retired, and he led the NFL in passer rating in 2022, passing yards in 2023 and completion percentage in 2024. Then, last season happened. Tagovailoa threw a career-high 15 interceptions and averaged 6.9 yards per attempt, which was his worst mark with McDaniel.
Tagovailoa went 4-14 vs. teams with a winning record under McDaniel, and has clearly regressed since that big 2023 season. That's why it was a bit curious that the Falcons immediately pursued Tagovailoa as soon as the Dolphins swallowed an NFL-record $99 million dead cap hit just to cut him. With that said, all Kevin Stefanski wants is an effective point guard to run his offense, because it's full of talented playmakers such as Bijan Robinson , Drake London and Kyle Pitts . Can Tagovailoa play that role? We'll find out.
CBS Sports' fantasy projected statline for Kirk Cousins : 674 passing yards, 5 TDs, 4 INTs Fernando Mendoza's fantasy projected statline : 2,630 passing yards, 19 TDs, 16 INTs
The Raiders had one of their worst seasons in franchise history last year, finishing 3-14 under Pete Carroll, ranking dead last in scoring offense (14.2 points per game) and total offense (245.2 yards per game). Carroll's gamble to bring in Geno Smith did not work, as he threw more interceptions (17) than any quarterback in the NFL.
As we enter 2026, it's fair to hypothesize that the Raiders upgraded their quarterback room in a major way. Vegas signed veteran Kirk Cousins in free agency and drafted former Indiana star and college football legend Fernando Mendoza with the No. 1 overall pick. The Raiders are expected to start Cousins to begin the season -- and perhaps their best-case scenario is if Cousins starts the entire year. If Cousins plays out the year, you can assume that means the Raiders were competitive and their quarterback was playing well enough to keep Mendoza on the bench. However, some believe Mendoza should start right away. Doug Pederson made an interesting case .
Cousins is coming off an overall disappointing two seasons with the Falcons, in which he went 12-10 as the starter, but he did step in for Michael Penix Jr . last season and help Atlanta end the year on a four-game win streak. Cousins averaged 219 passing yards per game and threw seven touchdowns compared to two interceptions during that stretch. He's about to turn 38-years-old, but Cousins showed he can still run an offense.
As for Mendoza, I'm not sure he was viewed as a generational, can't-miss prospect. But he was just the fourth player in the Common Draft Era to be selected No. 1 overall after winning the Heisman Trophy and a National Championship, joining Joe Burrow , Jameis Winston and Cam Newton . Mendoza led Indiana to a perfect 16-0 record. Pretty remarkable.
Our fantasy football projections indicate that Cousins will not be playing many games before…

title: No 2026 International games? The Cardinals originated this
summary: In May, when the NFL schedule was revealed, several things jumped off the map. For one, the Arizona Cardinals didn’t have any prime-time games. Secondly, with nine international contests, the Cardinals were omitted from this series as well. And then, Las Vegas made Arizona the underdog in every regular-season game this year. Ouch. RELATED: CARDINALS […]
full_text: In May, when the NFL schedule was revealed, several things jumped off the map. For one, the Arizona Cardinals didn’t have any prime-time games. Secondly, with nine international contests, the Cardinals were omitted from this series as well. And then, Las Vegas made Arizona the underdog in every regular-season game this year. Ouch. RELATED: CARDINALS NAMED AFTER THE COLOR – NOT THE BIRD The Cardinals should have at least had a game in Germany or maybe Spain. The league is playing in Australia and in France for the first time, and yet the Cardinals weren’t even mentioned as participating in either contest. The Cardinals invented having the NFL play in stadiums not located in North America. It would have been symbolic for Arizona to go to one of these countries and bring the NFL game to a new fanbase. But the original club was not invited, nor was it even in the conversation. Apparently, losing 14 games in the prior season will do that. The year was 1976. The date was August 16. The St. Louis Cardinals played the San Diego Chargers in a forgotten Week 3 preseason matchup in Japan. It was the first-ever NFL contest of any kind that was played outside of the confines of North America. Expanding the game Outside of the United States and Canada, in the 1970s, the game of American Football was like Americans watching cricket. People across the globe had no idea how the game was played: the rules were confusing, players wore huge padded uniforms, helmets obstructed each player’s face, plus the game was full of violence and collisions. The NFL got the bright idea that the league should attempt to take its game to the world, considering that the entire globe was considered an untapped resource. The NFL has always been aggressive towards seeking out new money trails. But the rest of the world was considered a super highway instead of a trail. It just needed some recognition and exposure, and that would involve hosting live games. So, the owners discussed it. They threw out ideas. There was some positivity involved, but also many doubts. After all, football, known as soccer to fans in the United States and Canada, was a worldwide sport. It didn’t have to be introduced to any other country on this planet. Fans already knew the game’s rules, and everyone played the game as a kid. But not American Football. While soccer didn’t require a size metric, American Football players were big. They were viewed as gladiators going into battle instead of playing a sport. The NFL liked the idea of playing in other countries, but the concept needed to be tested before the league would go all in. Where should they start? The short distance to Mexico? Maybe South America? This game needed to be regionally close so that airfare for two complete teams, coaches, support staff, front office personnel, cheerleaders, and medical staff would be cheaper. And then, all of that equipment had to be shipped, which wasn’t going to be inexpensive either. Not to mention the most obvious: Initially having to worry about a language barrier. This made an English-speaking country a priority. Yeah, none of that happened. The first game was all the way in Tokyo, Japan. This meant none of the conditions the owners suggested were going to be followed. Asia? Exactly how did this go about? The Mainichi Star Bowl The United States was entering a bicentennial year in 1976. Numerous activities and events occurred nationally to celebrate 200 years since becoming a new country. It just so happened that the City of St. Louis had a relationship with a city situated in central Japan called Suwa, located just over two hours from Tokyo. A Japanese-American named Frank Takahashi was a produce farmer from the Los Angeles area. He had just seen the NFL start two new franchises in two new cities. He knew at some point the league would offer another round of expansion. Seattle and Tampa Bay cost $16 million each. Takahashi thought an NFL team would do well in Japan, most likely to settle in Tokyo. And he wanted to own it. The idea was submitted to the NFL owners. They liked the idea of expanding the league’s reach and popularity. An exhibition game was suggested and financed by Takahashi through efforts with the NFL. The Rams were located in Los Angeles Rams while just south was the San Diego Chargers. It was decided that the Chargers would become one team, and after looking at their 1976 preseason schedule, their game against the St. Louis Cardinals was the best option, especially since St. Louis had a relationship with Suwa. For three preseason games, the Cardinals wore a Suwa, Japan, patch on their jerseys. Takahashi figured if the game was a complete sell-out, he would break even. But the experience and exposure would provide him with the inside edge if a team was ever considered in Japan. He believed that once the league got over there for the preseason game, the topic would be discussed. And so would he. Back then, playing an NFL regular-season game was out of the question for anywhere other than their own stadiums. In fact, that suggestion would have been laughable. But a preseason game? Teams played in non-NFL cities all the time back in the day, such as Columbus, Akron, Norfolk, Jacksonville, Sacramento, Tulsa, San Antonio, Birmingham, Hartford, and Orlando, just to name a few. An exhibition game that did not count in the standings? Keep that conversation going while the room grabs some Cokes and mixes another cold one. The Cardinals were coached by Don Coryell, while Tommy Prothro was the head coach of the Chargers, with team owners Bill Bidwill and Gene Klein. Takahashi was able to secure sponsors, the Mainichi Daily News and the Sports Nippon Newspaper Company . So, the game was dubbed “The Mainichi Star Bowl,” even though it was an NFL game instead of college, and was strictly an exhibition. The Japanese did not care, plus it was something they had never seen before. After all, American football players were huge compared to the people of Japan. LINK: KORAKUEN STADIUM Korakuen Stadium in Tokyo was built in 1937 as a baseball stadium and home field to the Nippon Ham Fighters of the Pacific League. Michael Jackson and Madonna would later hold performances there. It held 45,000 for concerts and 38,000 for football, but decades later was demolished to make room for a high-rise, the Tokyo Dome Hotel. The Chargers flew out of San Diego, and the Cardinals left from San Francisco after a four-hour flight from St. Louis. Both planes refueled in Alaska. After all, it was a 13-hour flight. The Cardinals’ players, coaches, trainers, cheerleaders, and front office personnel all stayed at the “New Otani Hotel” with plenty of time to go sightseeing. The Chargers stayed at the “Grand Palace Hotel.” Players who didn’t want the local food ended up at a McDonald’s just down the street. Today, when an NFL game is played in an international city, the media is everywhere, and the locals and the hometown media photograph everything the players do. Back then, both rosters of players were just an oddity in the streets—very large men who obviously didn’t fit the surroundings. Players gave their hosts some impromptu football camps, which were interesting to see Japanese players in shoulder pads and helmets. Keep in mind, this was right in the middle of training camp, so the two teams practiced every day in full pads in the morning during their 8-day stay, then had free time to explore the city. The Cardinals had to get into their uniforms in their hotel rooms, parade through the hotel lobby, and then were shuttled on a bus. American Football players in full pads were an unusual sight, like Roman gladiators walking towards the arena – without the bus, that is. The playing field was Astro-Turf. Because it was a baseball stadium being used for only one football game, the lines used for football were lined with flour. It was played in humid, misty rain, and the cooking agent would cake and sometimes start to rise, which would clog up…

full_text: Arizona Cardinals defensive lineman Walter Nolen III takes photos with fans during training camp at State Farm Stadium in Glendale on July 26, 2026. | Joe Rondone/The Republic / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. title: Cardinals DC Nick Rallis up next: His presser
summary: The Arizona Cardinals are in full swing training camp mode. With a new head coach, a new OC, and a new special teams coordinator, most of the main coaching jobs came from somewhere else. Except for DC Nick Rallis. Head coach Mike LaFleur liked his style and defensive scheme, and he has been with the […]
full_text: Arizona Cardinals defensive coordinator Nick Rallis speaks with the media during training camp at State Farm Stadium in Glendale, on July 25, 2026. | Joe Rondone/The Republic / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images The Arizona Cardinals are in full swing training camp mode. With a new head coach, a new OC, and a new special teams coordinator, most of the main coaching jobs came from somewhere else. Except for DC Nick Rallis. Head coach Mike LaFleur liked his style and defensive scheme, and he has been with the club for three seasons. Usually, a new head man will bring in guys he has worked with in the past along the trail somewhere, but LaFleur and Rallis have never crossed paths. RELATED: OC NATHANIEL HACKETT OPENS UP Now that officially training camp has begun, Rallis is able to see the new guys a bit more and try to get a feel for where each player is at. There will be quite a few positions up for grabs, but thankfully, most positions will carry over the starter from last year. While the new offense is the talk of camp, Rallis’ group will need to step up this year. They were ranked the #27 defense overall last year. That breakdown is being ranked #24 in pass defense with 31 passing TDs and an average of 230.8 passing yards a game. They were #25 against the run, with an average of 126.9 rushing yards a game and allowed 19 rushing touchdowns. Rallis had his first training camp press conference. Here is what he said: ————————————————————————————- Q: How’s it been so far? How’s the start been? Rallis: It’s been good. Like you’d expect things to correct. I love the things that we can control, which is our attitude, our energy, our effort, and our focus levels. Those have been on point, and they’ve got to maintain that way, right? That’s easy to do for the first couple of days. You’ve got to be consistent with that. But I’ve been pleased. Q: We heard from BJ (Ojulari) yesterday, and just kind of his journey throughout his NFL career has been pretty tumultuous. What do you make of his resilience and where he’s at, his growth and what you expect from him this year? Rallis: People in this game, when you suffer an injury, you have to be resilient. And it’s hard. You just name it what it is. Like it’s really hard. Sometimes it can be depressing even during that time when you’re not able to be out on the field because you work so hard for those moments. You’ve got to look at this as growth to say that I can overcome adversity. And what’s exciting about BJ is he looks really good right now. He looks like a guy that’s put in a lot of work to get back to the player that he is. Things to continue to get better at, obviously. But it’s good to have him back out there full go and letting it loose. Q: And now that he’s fully healthy, what parts of his game are you seeing that’s reminding you, oh yeah, I remember this is who he was? Rallis: He’s got so much elusiveness off the edge. The thing I’m excited about when we get into pads is him setting those edges cuz I thought he’s done a really good job of that. He’s picked right back up from when he was feeling his best. That’s the BJ you see out there right now. Q: Coming back from an injury as well, he looked pretty explosive just in drills. What have you seen? Rallis: I saw the same thing. Obviously, as we get going, there’ll be things that he’s got an improvement plan that he can correct certain things. I know he’s got it on his mind cuz he was talking to me about it yesterday. Take it day by day. I know he’s a really good player, and so excited to have him back out there. Q: Max (Melton) had a nice pass breakup yesterday, and you guys have so many corners battling for time and spots on the depth chart. He has a lot of expectations because of where he was drafted. Where is he mentally? Like what is your kind of outlook on where he is? Rallis: He’s in a great spot. I think he took even a step from Day 1 to Day 2, going back to the offseason program, certain things that he needed to improve on. You saw him make some huge strides. I think he’s continuing to just develop his knowledge of the game and have some accelerated thinking based on what the offense is presenting before the snap. He’s in a phenomenal spot. And as you said, the whole room, it’s a great problem to have cuz you got so many guys that can go out there and play winning NFL football. It’s very competitive right now, which is what you want for that cornerback competition opposite Will (Johnson). What can make those guys stand out, because as you said, it’s a deep group. What can make those guys stand out in that competition? Everyone’s in competition right now across the whole roster. From the cornerback specifically number one to the cover guys. To me, like a premier guy at that spot can take away the best; there’s always going to be schematic things that, when you play a really good receiver. You’ll be dedicating numbers to him, but at the end of the day, there’s going to be one-on-ones throughout the game. And there’s going to be stressful downs for those guys. Can they go and win those downs? They’re not going to win all of them. To me, it’s the hardest position in football besides quarterback. Just because there are so many good receivers across this league, and you can be on an island out there with space. If you can deny the ball when you’re in a one-on-one matchup, to me, that’s everything. From there, like no matter what position, are you executing at a consistent level? Do you have a playing style, and can you take the ball away? Q: How is Starling (Thomas) looking and how does he fit into that conversation? Rallis: He’s right in there. He’s looked really good. He has worked very hard to get back to Himself, and there’s probably some rust he still needs to knock off. We’re only two days in, but you could just see he made a play yesterday, and the response from his teammates. I think says a lot about who he is to this team. Q; Another guy, Elijah Jones, had a couple of those plays yesterday. What kind of growth have you seen out of him? Rallis: Major growth. I think that the biggest growth I saw was in the offseason program. You just saw a comfort level. What I love about his game right now is he doesn’t get sped up. So, what I mean by that is, off of his releases or whether he’s playing off, just those first five yards are pivotal for a corner to be in good position throughout the down. And he has multiple ways that he can get up there and press right now that he’s very comfortable with. And he just never finds himself sped up later in the down. And then from there, like if you’re in a good position, he’s got length, he’s got speed, he’s got ability to disrupt the football, and let it loose. Excited where he’s trending. Q: How has Sean (Murphy-Bunting) adjusted? Rallis: He needed that time in the offseason program. Because he hadn’t been at a nickel, besides back when he was in Tampa and that was, selectively. You can just see like a comfort level right now, and we ask our nickels to do a lot, and so I’m not just even talking about playing that nickel spot. He’s playing deep zones and doing everything, and he’s taken a huge step. And he knows that. He’s made some big plays so far in two days. Q: When you have him wrap it and then whenever Garrett (Williams) comes back, how do you kind of decide? What are you looking for between those three in terms of just nickel? Rallis: We’ll assess that day by day. In terms of the nickel spot, it can depend on the situation and the package we’re in. If those guys can all help us win, they’re all going to play for us this year. Everybody in that back end. Q: How much of a physicality jump is that to go from outside to inside? Rallis: Situationally. It depends on how you match nickel. If you’re matching it versus bigger groups, a lot of times they do get down there in the box, and that’s where you’re going to see a little bit more physicality happening. Even in 11 personnel, if they are on the slot depends on…

The Steelers defeated the Browns 17-7. (Photo by George Gojkovich/Getty Images) | Getty Images Baltimore Beatdown is all about Almost Ravens this week! In addition to our reader-driven bracket narrowing down the biggest near-acquisitions in team history, our staff will also be providing their opinions on their favorite moves the Ravens almost pulled off. Today, we’re focusing on the coaches that were nearly hired by the team: Art Modell firing Bill Belichick when the Browns moved to Baltimore is, by far, the biggest and coolest ‘what if?’ in Ravens history. But would Belichick have still become one of the greatest coaches of all-time? Better yet, would he have still drafted a certain unheralded quarterback out of Michigan in 2000? These are, of course, unanswerable questions, but one reason to think it would have worked: Belichick was always better at coaching than he was managing team personnel. But if he was paired with Ozzie Newsome, the Ravens could have built a dynasty. What could have been… – Nikhil Mehta My favorite coach the Ravens almost hired in Kyle Shanahan. Instead of Shanahan, the Ravens hired Gary Kubiak for their offensive coordinator role in 2014. Kubiak led the team’s offense to notable success that year and was poached by the Denver Broncos for a head coaching job. Shanahan might have had the same trajectory in Baltimore as well, or maybe things work out differently and he’d be around for a longer time. Either way, Shanahan has established himself as one of the league’s top offensive masterminds and head coaches in recent years, and having him in Baltimore early on would have been a positive. – Frank Platko It has to be Bill Belichick for me. A Maryland raised guy who learned football from his dad in Annapolis coaching at the Naval Academy, he’s arguably the smartest football mind the football world has seen. When Art Modell moved his football franchise to Baltimore from Cleveland, Belichick was informed he’d be sticking on to coach for the team. Instead he was fired after the move was made official. Belichick is giving a lot of credit for laying the groundwork for what the Baltimore Ravens would become as an organization. Belichick would obviously move on from the Cleveland/Baltimore debacle and end up piloting one of the greatest dynasty’s in any sport with Tom Brady in New England. Who knows, maybe without Brady it wouldn’t have led to anything. But I sure think about what could have been if Belichick had been handed the keys the Ravens organization, paired with Ozzie Newsome as the General Manager. The Ravens have two Super Bowls. How many could they have if arguably the greatest coach in NFL history was there? – Zach Canter t would feel wrong to choose someone other than perhaps the greatest coach of all time here. While Bill Belichick’s track record without Tom Brady at quarterback isn’t great, you still have to imagine he would have success in Baltimore with the absurd level of talent on the defensive side of the ball in the 2000s. Rather he would have survived the early years of the franchise finding its footing is another question, but picturing one of the NFL’s greatest defensive minds with Ray Lewis, Ed Reed, Terrell Suggs, and Haloti Ngata on the field together in their prime is certainly an exciting scenario. – Dustin Cox Who is the biggest Almost-Raven in franchise history? | Baltimore Beatdown

title: The Buffalo Bills and the NFL uniform and helmet rules explained: Primary, alternates, and throwbacks
summary: If it feels like you’re seeing more alternate uniforms and helmet combinations around the NFL than ever before, you’re not imagining things. Over the last several seasons and after their renewed partnership with Nike, the league has gradually relaxed its uniform restrictions, giving teams more opportunities to showcase alternate looks while still maintaining each franchise’s […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - OCTOBER 5: Curtis Samuel #1 of the Buffalo Bills runs with the ball for a touchdown during the third quarter against the New England Patriots at Highmark Stadium on October 5, 2025 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images If it feels like you’re seeing more alternate uniforms and helmet combinations around the NFL than ever before, you’re not imagining things. Over the last several seasons and after their renewed partnership with Nike, the league has gradually relaxed its uniform restrictions, giving teams more opportunities to showcase alternate looks while still maintaining each franchise’s identity. With the Buffalo Bills recently unveiling a new alternate uniform and the NFL’s new Rivalries program arriving last season , many fans have been asking the same question: What exactly are the NFL’s uniform rules? NFL home and away uniforms Despite what many fans believe, the home team gets to decide whether it wants to wear its official colored jersey or white jersey. Once the home team makes its selection, the visiting team simply wears the contrasting option. NFL alternate uniforms and throwbacks The NFL allows teams to wear alternate uniforms, throwbacks, or classic jerseys up to four times during the regular season. That four-game total includes all alternate jersey designs, regardless of whether they’re modern alternates, throwbacks, or “Color Rush” inspired uniforms. NFL helmet rules One of the biggest changes in recent years came when the NFL eliminated the long-standing one helmet rule. Today, teams can carry up to three different helmet designs during a season. That could include: Primary helmet Alternate helmet Throwback or legacy helmet For the Bills this means our primary white, the alternate blue, and then they could still use the 90s red. The standing buffalo and the cold front white rivalries helmet are both base-white helmets with different stickers, and since they match the primary white, it’s not considered another helmet. NFL/Nike Rivalries program Just when fans thought they understood the rules, the NFL introduced something entirely new last year. Beginning last season, a number of teams started receiving a specially designed NFL x Nike Rivalries uniform. The concept of these uniforms is intended to celebrate divisional rivalries while highlighting each franchise’s history, culture, and local identity. For AFC East teams like Buffalo, that meant for one designated home game last season against a division opponent the NFL required the featured “Rivalries” look. Why the Rivalries uniform is different Unlike traditional alternate uniforms, the Rivalries collection does not count against the NFL’s four-game alternate uniform limit or 3 helmets. Instead: Each Rivalries uniform remains active for three seasons after its debut. Teams are required to wear it during one designated home divisional game each year. The program exists in addition to a team’s normal alternate uniform schedule. One important uniform restriction for the playoffs If you’re hoping to see your favorite alternate look during a playoff run, that won’t happen as the NFL does not permit alternate, rivals, or throwback uniforms in the postseason. During the playoffs, teams must wear their standard/primary approved home or road uniforms. That includes the Super Bowl. What the uniform and helmet rules mean for the Buffalo Bills The Bills can now rotate between multiple uniforms and helmets throughout the regular season while also participating in the NFL’s new Rivalries program. The Bills could essentially wear their “Nickel City” alternates with the blue helmet, color rush with the primary helmet, 90s throwbacks with the red helmet, AND the “Rivalries” uniforms with the rivalries helmet this season without violating NFL rules. Whether you loved or hated the newly revealed alternate uniform, one thing is clear: the days of every Sunday looking exactly the same are over. The NFL has fully embraced uniform variety, and with additional alternates and “Rivalries” designs scheduled to debut across the league, fans should expect even more debates every time they are released.

title: Buffalo Bills’ new helmets may have borrowed heavily from one fan’s idea
summary: If you’re reading this version of my Buffalo Bills Mandalorian helmet reveal it’s because of one thing and one thing only. The team copied my homework. The original intent was that I got people hooked on the project with the helmet being the tantalizing final reveal. I was going to show off each piece, bit […]
full_text: If you’re reading this version of my Buffalo Bills Mandalorian helmet reveal it’s because of one thing and one thing only. The team copied my homework. The original intent was that I got people hooked on the project with the helmet being the tantalizing final reveal. I was going to show off each piece, bit by bit, until I was able to showcase the full set of Mando gear with the helmet as the cherry on top. But then the Bills released an alternate uniform combination to the world. And their helmet looks like a ripoff of mine. So here you go! An early release of my work to show that the Bills not only are reading my work, but actively copying it. What did the Bills steal exactly? Way back on April 14, I revealed the concept for my Mandalorian helmet, found here . It included the following graphic intended to show a side-by-side of the helmet’s original Sabine Wren design with my intended one. As you can clearly see, the charge stripe on a blue background was my idea. Sure it’s a **** illustration, but the idea is quite clear. I even discussed the base color to replicate my beskar steel was going to be a coat of pewter-colored paint. Yes, the Bills are rolling with “nickel” to go with the city’s nickname, but us Buffalo Rumblings faithful know the score. They were copying my homework all along. The real question isn’t the headline. It’s obvious they owe me a design credit. The real question is; can I spray paint better than I draw? AT LONG LAST! I won’t go into too many details on the process here, you’ve seen some of how I made stencils using the Frog Tape, and you’ll see some more when we get to my shoulder armor. I will say that I agonized on how to get the lines straight. I really needed to nail that. I lost actual sleep. Then it hit me. You know what has some really straight lines already? The tape, you dummy. Me. I was the dummy. The second that realization hit, I couldn’t wait to finish the final paint. You’re not here for stories though. So here’s some more of the final paint to check out, starting with my reveal video as I gleefully take off the tape to see how I did. Hopefully that was enjoyable and not for Rex Ryan reasons if you catch my drift. Wanna see some still shots of it? Of course you do! Here you go. In all its Mando glory. I tried to get the rangefinder to match the look when down and that turned out to be a pretty simple affair. Even better, this lights up when down and I managed to get the electronics back together so it still works the way it should. I rolled the dice on the pewter paint holding the texture to look like pitted and aged steel and that worked out beautifully. It’s not a flawless job, but I’m very happy with the result. This project wouldn’t have been possible without support. My friend who had the idea to buy and Bills up the helmets. You can see our respective work side by side right here. My family. My youngest in particular has helped brainstorm design ideas. The white stripe with red ombre effect on the back of the helmet was her idea. The fans of this site that have encouraged me to make this bigger and better with every step. Anyway, here’s a video with I think just about perfect lighting to show off the full thing. I’ll close on a final thought for those of you who might hold me accountable for promises made. Back in the second chapter in this odyssey, I said I was going to do something on the left side of the helmet. Specifically, you might recall that I was going to paint a hybrid bison/mythosaur symbol on the side. Here’s a very basic mockup of the plan. Well here’s the thing. I got the stripe on the helmet and decided I liked it without anything else on it. I consulted my friend and daughter and they both agreed. The only thing that went on after the charge stripe was the white and red ombre on the back. That said, I haven’t abandoned the bison/mythosaur sigil. In fact, it’s just about ready to go onto its final placement. It won’t be on the helmet. And while I think I’m finding out I’m pretty good with stencils and spray paint, there’s one thing I know I’m even better at. In other words, you might have seen the helmet, but you might want to stay tuned. There’s plenty of Buffalo Bills and other elements to go in this project. I might be biased but I think you’re going to love a lot of them. Let’s see the Bills try to copy what’s coming next…

title: Buffalo Bills new alternate uniforms unveiled
summary: A new season and a new stadium deserves a new look. The Bills have unveiled a new alternate uniform, giving fans another look to add to their […]
full_text: A new season and a new stadium deserves a new look. As the Buffalo Bills prepare to kick off the inaugural season at the new Highmark Stadium, one of the worst-kept secrets of the offseason has officially become reality. The Bills have unveiled a new alternate uniform, giving fans another look to add to their collection of jerseys. For most NFL fanbases, the release of a new uniform sparks a debate that can last for weeks. Some are instant home runs, with fans lining up outside team stores or crashing online shops to grab one before they sell out. Others… well, not every alternate jersey is destined to become a classic. Resilient. Gritty. Blue Collar. #BillsMafia | https://t.co/dSv2Kf4qfF pic.twitter.com/sSEbyEEyPt — Buffalo Bills (@BuffaloBills) July 27, 2026 Earlier this month, it was confirmed that Buffalo would debut a new alternate uniform for the inaugural season in the new stadium. But long before the official release there were reports that the alternate would feature a gray design inspired by Buffalo’s “Nickel City” nickname. That report matched earlier leaks that had circulated online months ago, adding even more credibility to what many fans were already expecting. The leaks also speculated a blue helmet, giving fans plenty to clamor on about. NFL rules allow teams to carry up to three alternate helmets and alternates or throwbacks uniforms can each be worn as many as four times during the regular season . This means the Bills would have their primary helmet, this new alternate helmet, and a throwback. The throwback could be either the standing buffalo helmet or their beloved 90s red helmets. The Bills have not announced what date(s) they will wear the uniform. Whether you love it, hate it, or fall somewhere in the middle, one thing is certain, fans are going to be talking about this uniform combination for quite a while. What’s your first impression of the new alternate uniform? Do you love it? If not, do you think it’ll grow on you after seeing it on the field? Or do you hate it as much as I do? I’ll be honest, I think it’s awful. I genuinely don’t understand who sat in a room and decided this was the winning design. I would have loved to be a fly on the wall throughout the entire process, from the first concept to the final mock-up and approval. I can’t help but wonder if anyone raised their hand and said, “Maybe we should go back to the drawing board.” I’m genuinely curious how this ended up being the look that represents the beginning of a new era at Highmark Stadium. Maybe seeing it on the field will change some minds, but right now I just don’t see it. For a franchise opening a brand-new stadium, this feels like a huge swing and a miss. But that’s just one opinion. Where do you stand? Is this a jersey you’ll proudly wear on Sundays, or one you’ll pretend never existed? And be honest… are you still buying one anyway because, well, that’s what Bills Mafia does? Because if history tells us anything, Bills Mafia probably already has one sitting in the shopping cart . title: Buffalo Bills 2026 scouting report: defensive tackle T.J. Sanders
summary: The Buffalo Bills aren’t known for playing their defensive linemen in multiple positions like they are their offensive linemen. Usually, if a player is drafted as a defensive end, that’s where he’s playing. The same goes for defensive tackle, although there is some nuance to that given the former defense’s need for one-tech and three-tech […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NY - SEPTEMBER 18: T.J. Sanders #98 of the Buffalo Bills lines up before the snap during an NFL football game against the Miami Dolphins at Highmark Stadium on September 18, 2025 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills aren’t known for playing their defensive linemen in multiple positions like they are their offensive linemen. Usually, if a player is drafted as a defensive end, that’s where he’s playing. The same goes for defensive tackle, although there is some nuance to that given the former defense’s need for one-tech and three-tech players. Sometimes, though, there are players who can fill multiple roles up front. Rare are the players who can go both inside and outside along the defensive line, but last year, the Bills ended up playing a rookie in a more versatile role. Was that sheerly out of necessity, or were the Bills forecasting that player’s future? Perhaps it’s a self-fulfilling prophecy, but in today’s edition of “91 players in 91 days,” we discuss a young player who will likely see time at multiple spots along Buffalo’s new-look defensive line. _____________________________________________________________________________ Name: T.J. Sanders Number: 98 Position: DT Height/Weight: 6’4” 297 lbs. Age: 23 (24 on 7/30/2027) Experience/Draft: 2; selected by Buffalo in the second round (No. 41 overall) of the 2025 NFL Draft) College: South Carolina Acquired: Second-round draft choice Financial situation (per Spotrac): Sanders enters the second year of his four-year rookie contract. For the 2026 seaosn, his cap hit is $2,419,411. If he’s released, Buffalo will carry a dead cap charge of $8,136,967. 2025 Recap: In the early going, Sanders played more than perhaps Buffalo thought he would thanks to an injury to Ed Oliver. Sanders was pushed around in those early matchups, as he was consistently beaten at the point of attack, and he looked especially weak in his anchor against the run. He totaled just two tackles in his first four games. However, a knee injury suffered before Buffalo played the New England Patriots led the team to place him on injured reserve. When he returned, he looked like a far better player. Sanders was activated from IR ahead of Buffalo’s Week Eleven matchup with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, and he had three tackles in that game alone. He finished the regular season strong, and he even made his first career starts in Buffalo’s last two regular season games. He played a mix of defensive tackle and defensive end, proving to be quite versatile in addition to showing his overall improvement. He had 16 tackles, one sack, and one pass knockdown during the regular season. Although he played 35 total snaps in the playoffs, he did not register on the stat sheet. Positional outlook: Sanders is one of eight defensive tackles listed on the current roster. Tommy Akingbesote, DeWayne Carter, Deone Walker, Ed Oliver, Zion Logue, Zane Durant, and Phidarian Mathis are the others. Landon Jackson and Kody Huisman are listed at defensive end, which is another spot where Sanders may see time this season. 2026 Offseason: Sanders is healthy and participating in offseason work to date. 2026 Season outlook: As strange as it seems, Sanders’ experience at multiple spots last season will likely give him a leg up this year in new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard’s scheme. It wasn’t exactly ideal to watch Sanders, who we assumed would be a three-tech defensive tackle in former head coach Sean McDermott’s scheme, play defensive end, but in Leonhard’s new odd-man front, it’s not only possible that Sanders will line up at DE, it’s likely. Arguably, Sanders played better at defensive end last season than he did at defensive tackle, so perhaps McDermott was on to something when he was playing Sanders there out of necessity. Sanders is a roster lock this season, but his role is what we’ll have to see as the Bills move through camp. Ideally, he sees significant time as a starting down lineman in a 4i or 5-tech role. He’ll need to be better in his anchor, and hopefully a year in a professional strength and conditioning program will help in that regard. Can Sanders find the gear that he showed while a member of the Gamecocks, where he totaled 17.5 tackles for loss and 9.5 sacks across three seasons? That would certainly be nice, but Buffalo can’t necessarily count on that, either. We don’t know how often Leonhard will rotate his defensive linemen, so it’s possible that Sanders could be in line for a greater percentage of snaps than he had under McDermott, who was notorious for rotating his defensive line constantly within games. Either way, the Bills would like to see Sanders take a great leap forward in his second season. Shifting to a more attack-oriented defense could be just what the doctor ordered, and Sanders has the ability to play multiple spots on the defensive line. He’ll be a big part of the rotation this year provided that he stays healthy.

full_text: CHARLOTTE, NC - DECEMBER 04: Michael Vick #7 of the Atlanta Falcons evades a tackle by Will Witherspoon #54 of the Carolina Panthers during a game on December 4, 2005 at the Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Sporting News via Getty Images via Getty Images) | Sporting News via Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #47. Will Witherspoon Among the litany of great Panthers linebackers in their relatively short existence, Will Witherspoon was often overlooked. The Panthers selected Witherspoon in the third round of the 2002 NFL Draft. That particular draft had a handful of major Panthers players who helped the team reach the Super Bowl the following season including Julius Peppers and Deshaun Foster in the first two rounds. Witherspoon was originally a middle linebacker and backed up 2001 first round pick and current Panthers GM Dan Morgan. Morgan suffered some injuries in the 2002 season, allowing Witherspoon to rack up 15 appearances and eight starts in the middle of the defense. Witherspoon showed so much promise that he was moved to the weak side linebacker position the following year so he and Morgan could be on the field together. That decision paid off both personally and for the team itself as Witherspoon and Morgan were monsters in the second level of the Panthers defense that helped take them to the Super Bowl. Witherspoon’s third season was arguably his best. He logged 103 tackles, three sacks, four interceptions, and 14 passes defended. With Dan Morgan battling injury after injury year after year, Witherspoon was a consistent force on the defense for his entire four year stint with the Panthers. Unfortunately for the Panthers, that meant Witherspoon became a highly coveted free agent after his rookie contract expired. Witherspoon ultimately signed a massive six year, $33 million contract with the St Louis Rams (the equivalent of about $16 million per year in today’s NFL). The Panthers could not match that offer, so Witherspoon played middle linebacker for the Rams until the middle of the 2009 season when he was traded to the Philadelphia Eagles for a wide receiver and a fifth round pick. After spending three seasons with the Tennessee Titans, he followed coach Jeff Fisher to St Louis for a second tenure with the Rams. That ended up being his final season in the NFL. While his time in Charlotte was relatively short, his production and impact during one of the best stretches of Panthers football ever earned him this spot on our countdown of the Top 100 Panthers.

full_text: CHARLOTTE, NC - OCTOBER 26: Carolina Panthers offensive lineman Brady Christensen (70) during an NFL football game between the Buffalo Bills and the Carolina Panthers on October 26, 2025 at Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte, N.C. (Photo by John Byrum/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Brady Christensen has long been a piece of the Carolina Panthers’ offensive line equation. The 70th overall pick from the 2021 NFL Draft has a handful of starts at almost every OL position and has flashed the potential to crack the starting five. Unfortunately for him, his contract year was marred by a torn Achilles midseason. Now he’s back with the Carolina Panthers and with a much less certain future. Between his inability to seize a starting spot when he was younger and the often brutal toll an Achilles injury can take on lineman’s athleticism, it is no surprise that most fans don’t expect him to step into a starting spot. That’s even accounting for Taylor Moton missing an unknown amount of the season with blood clots. It is a testament to the quality of the work Christensen has done in his four years with the Panthers, however, that about a third of fans think he has the potential to start right away this season. (David T. Foster III/Charlotte Observer/Tribune News Service via Getty Images) Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #48. Charles Godfrey Panthers stats: 82 games, 3 74 tackles, 11 interceptions Career stats: 95 games, 386 tackles, 11 interceptions If there was a Carolina Panthers “Hall of the Very Good”, Charles Godfrey would be among the first players inducted. While he was a very good free safety for six-plus years for the Panthers, he never got Pro Bowl recognition nor was he fawned over by the national media. But over 82 games in Carolina, Godfrey was a consistently impactful presence in the secondary. He was drafted by the Panthers in the third round of the 2008 NFL Draft. The Iowa product defied the odds for most third rounders by winning a starting safety spot Week 1 of his rookie season. He started all 16 games with 61 tackles, one interception, and five passes defended. Carolina went 12-4 that season and Panthers fans knew the team had found its long-term solution at the back end of the secondary. Over his first five seasons from 2008 through 2012 Godfrey managed to stay relatively healthy, missing seven games over that stretch. Over his first five seasons he averaged nearly 54 tackles per season, 2.2 interceptions, and 6.2 passes defended. Many Panthers fans will also remember him for his flowing hair that trailed him like a kite’s tail as he sprinted across the field. Then in 2013 his season was cut short to just two games due to an Achilles injury In 2014 he returned from injury but was moved from free safety to slot corner, and he struggled in his new role. He played seven up-and-down games with 19 tackles before being released with the season still in full swing. He was replaced at free safety by Thomas DeCoud as the Panthers pulled the most NFC South feat possible by winning the division with a 7-8-1 record that year. After his mid-season release in 2015 he remained in the NFC South by signing with the Atlanta Falcons – Eww! – and played sparingly over five games with all of his snaps coming on special teams. He returned to the Falcons in 2016 and appeared in eight games with 12 tackles before calling it a career.

full_text: The latest Chicago Bears player to be unveiled in the NFL’s Top 100 countdown might not be a surprise to fans, but amazingly it’s his first time making the cut. Left guard Joe Thuney comes in at #49 on this year’s list following a 2025 campaign that saw the future Hall of Famer win the inaugural NFL Protector of the Year award. Thuney has been named to the Pro Bowl 4-times, has been a 3-time first-team All-Pro, and a 2-time second-team All-Pro. He’s also won four Super Bowls. Yet Thuney has somehow never made the player-voted Top 100 list. In the Top 100 reveal video, Packers edge rusher Micah Parsons calls Thuney “Mr. Consistent” and a “mastermind at the line.” The video also features comments from Creed Humphrey, Thuney’s former teammate in Kansas City, as well as Tampa Bay’s Tristan Wirfs, who makes a point to talk about Thuney’s ability to move out to left tackle on the offensive line and still have success there as well. Check out the NFL’s video revealing Thuney as #49 on the list below. No. 49 on the NFL Top 100 Players of 2026… @ChicagoBears OL Joe Thuney! @NFLFilms pic.twitter.com/nujG7vXg6Z — NFL (@NFL) July 27, 2026 Thuney is the third player on the Bears’ 2026 roster to be named to the list, following Caleb Williams (#51) and Montez Sweat (#91). Kevin Byard also made the list (#61) for his 2025 campaign with the Bears. Do you think #49 is too low on the list? Or just right? Let us know in the comments section below!

title: Chicago Bears 2026 Training Camp Position Breakdown: Running back
summary: Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johnson gets the offensive genius and offensive innovator label dropped on him from time to time, and yes, he is those things, but he’s also an old-school smash-mouth football guy. His Lions teams were always near the top of the league rankings in running the ball, so it’s no surprise […]
full_text: Jun 9, 2026; Lake Forest, IL, USA; Chicago Bears running back Roschon Johnson (23) warms up during Chicago Bears Minicamp at Halas Hall. Mandatory Credit: Kamil Krzaczynski-Imagn Images | Kamil Krzaczynski-Imagn Images Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johnson gets the offensive genius and offensive innovator label dropped on him from time to time, and yes, he is those things, but he’s also an old-school smash-mouth football guy. His Lions teams were always near the top of the league rankings in running the ball, so it’s no surprise he improved that aspect of the Bears in year one. In year two, the Bears lost running backs coach Eric Bieniemy to the Chiefs, but they hired Eric Studesville, who is not only a well-respected teacher of the position but also had just spent the previous four years working for Mike McDaniel in Miami. McDaniel’s running game was one of the most innovative in the NFL, and Ben Johnson is ready to add some new wrinkles to his run game. “He’s [Studesville] got a wealth of experience from a number of different places,” Johnson said about his assistant coach in June. “I can’t wait to dive into his cutups that he’s got for Miami. They did some unique things, particularly in the run game, over the last few years.” Roster Locks The Bears had a better scheme, a revamped offensive line, and a commitment to multiple tight end sets in 2025, and all of that helped D’Andre Swift’s average yards per carry increase by over a yard from 2024. Swift also matured as a runner, taking what the defense gave him and lowering his shoulder when he had to. Swift, who turned 27 earlier this year, still plays with quickness and speed, and I expect another outstanding season from him. Kyle Monangai was a nice complement to Swift last year, but his second season should bring a bigger impact. “There are a lot of things I can improve on for sure,” Monangai said via the team site after the season. “I was just coming into this thing, just trying to gain the trust of the organization, gain the trust of my teammates, make them feel like they made the right decision in bringing me here, and then trying to help us win games at the end of the day.” While I believe Swift will remain the starter, I wouldn’t be surprised if their snap counts were closer to split in 2026. A Good Bet To Make It I think it’s wide open behind Swift and Monangai. Roster Bubble/Practice Squad With Travis Homer gone, Roschon Johnson will try to become the Bears’ top special teams running back, but injuries have hit him each of his first three seasons. Brittain Brown spent most of last year on the Bears’ practice squad, but in his one game, he had more rushing yards (37) than Homer and Johnson had combined the entire year (15). Salvon Ahmed spent 2020 to 2023 in Miami with Studesville, but the last two years he was on the Broncos, then the Colts’ practice squad. Rookie UDFA Coleman Bennett was a physical runner at Kennesaw State, but that might not translate to the NFL due to his size (5’11”, 185). The Bears might have their eye on the waiver wire on cut-down day. Besides the top two tailbacks, who do you think make the team?

title: Chicago Bears Question of the Day: Will Tyson Bagent stay QB2 all season?
summary: Entering his 4th season with the Bears, Tyson Bagent remains a steadfast presence. Ever since arriving from Shepard University in 2023, he’s been nothing but business, support, and hard work. To this point in his career, Bagent has earned everything that has come his way, most notably the two-year $10 million deal he signed in […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - JANUARY 18: Tyson Bagent #17 of the Chicago Bears warms up prior to an NFL divisional playoff game against the Los Angeles Rams at Soldier Field on January 18, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Entering his 4th season with the Bears, Tyson Bagent remains a steadfast presence. Ever since arriving from Shepard University in 2023, he’s been nothing but business, support, and hard work. To this point in his career, Bagent has earned everything that has come his way, most notably the two-year $10 million deal he signed in 2025. Still, with Caleb Williams being positioned as the long-term starter in Chicago, you can’t help but imagine that Bagent’s time with the Bears has an eventual expiration date. In fact, with the current trend of former backups earning starting jobs (and big contracts) you have to imagine Bagent’s competitive spirit will lead him elsewhere sooner rather than later. Which leads me to my question…. Will Tyson Bagent be the Bears QB2 for the entirety of the 2026 season? The implication of this question is not about if Bagent is supplanted by Keenum or another QB as the primary backup for the Bears, but whether another team goes shopping for QB help midseason. There are two primary scenarios where Bagent could plausibly be traded mid-season. A starting QB gets injured, and Bagent is brought in to keep the ship afloat. A team moves on from their starter and view Bagent as a potential long term option. A midseason trade for a backup quarterback more often leans towards the first scenario, but there are some teams that may want a jump on bringing Bagent into their building before the season is over. But first, let’s look at Bagent’s career so far. Bagent is the all-time passing leader in NCAA Division II history, posting 13,658 yards on a 69% completion percentage, and 123 TDs to 38 INTs. In the NFL he has started 4 games, going 2-2. He has passed for 917 yards on 66.4% completion, with 3 TDs to 6 INTs. All 6 of those INTs happened in his rookie year when filling in for the injured Justin Fields However, his best performance was in the 2025 preseason where he threw for 401 yards, 5 TDs, and 1 INT in three starts. This is where the chatter around his potential grew. Beyond his statistics, Bagent is a known gym rat whose non-traditional conditioning techniques have captivated fans. So, is he a good candidate to be traded? Considering he is one of the few backups that are still ascending, I think there is a very good chance he gets traded in 2026. Let’s look at some places that make sense. Playoff Teams With Fragile QBs and Imperfect Backups This first category is for teams that need to compete, have an established (and injury prone) QB1, but a poor QB2 option. Denver Broncos Bo Nix is recovering from a bad injury in the playoffs, while the Broncos are absolutely gearing for a deep playoff run. To this point in his career, Jared Stidham has underwhelmed. He has also been in the league long enough for us to know who he is. Los Angeles Chargers Justin Herbert doesn’t have a long injury history, but he has missed enough time to make you worried. He has fractured his left hand/wrist three times and injured his throwing shoulder three times. When you look at the now journeyman Trey Lance behind him, you wonder if a better backup is needed. Tampa Bay Buccaneers While Baker Mayfield is known to be a tough guy willing to play through injuries, a report noted he played with a litany of ailments in 2025 including MCL and PCL injuries. Pair this with a below average backup in Jake Browning, and it’s very possible Bagent could be viewed as an option in Tampa. Teams Looking to Improve QB1 Arizona Cardinals While the Cardinals appear to be preparing themselves for a #1 overall pick, it’s possible that a talented core of Jeremiyah Love, Marvin Harrison Jr., and Trey McBride keep them from being at the top. In that scenario, it may be worth taking on a flyer with Bagent midseason to give them time to evaluate ahead of the draft. New York Jets The Jets have found their way back to Geno Smith, who looks like he might be near the end of an interesting career. While a player like Cade Klubnik is interesting, they may not want to throw him into the first if Smith proves to be done. Bringing in a vet, that still possesses a ceiling like Bagent could be a savvy move for the Jets. Bagent has been a great teammate and backup for the Bears so far in his career, and I firmly believe a bigger opportunity exists right around the corner for him. I suspect the Bears will get enough calls this year to trade Bagent for a nice draft package. Now it’s your turn! Do you think Tyson Bagent will remain QB2 for the entire 2026 season? Sound off in the comments!

title: Bengals Tuesday Trenches: The start of training camp
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals are back to work this week as training camp officially gets underway. Their first practice is scheduled for Wednesday (7/29), kicking off the process of trimming the roster from roughly 90 players down to the final 53. It also marks the end of the NFL’s annual summer lull. After weeks of almost […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OH - JANUARY 04: Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow (9) looks at the scorebord during the game against the Cleveland Browns and the Cincinnati Bengals on January 4, 2026, at Paycor Stadium in Cincinnati, OH. (Photo by Ian Johnson/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Cincinnati Bengals are back to work this week as training camp officially gets underway. Their first practice is scheduled for Wednesday (7/29), kicking off the process of trimming the roster from roughly 90 players down to the final 53. It also marks the end of the NFL’s annual summer lull. After weeks of almost nothing happening throughout June and July, football is finally back. Thank the football gods. Here are a few storylines to watch as camp opens. Defensive line depth The Bengals completely rebuilt their defensive front this offseason, adding Dexter Lawrence, Boye Mafe and Jonathan Allen, while also drafting Landon Robinson and Cashius Howell. Even with B.J. Hill expected to begin camp on the PUP list, there’s little reason to panic because of how much depth Cincinnati added. The biggest question may not be who starts—it may be who gets cut. There are only so many roster spots available, and at least one talented defensive lineman is likely to be left looking for work elsewhere. Late free-agent additions Last August, the Bengals signed Dalton Risner late in the preseason. He eventually took over the starting right guard job, earned a new contract and helped give Joe Burrow the same starting offensive line in consecutive seasons for the first time in his career. Could lightning strike twice? The Bengals largely bypassed linebacker in both free agency and the draft, and there are still veterans on the market who could help. Cornerback is another position worth watching. Cincinnati signed Ja’Sir Taylor and drafted Tacario Davis, but is that enough? If the Bengals make another veteran addition before Week 1, linebacker or cornerback seems like the most likely destination. Running back is also a possibility, although it feels like more of a long shot. An evolving training camp philosophy One of the defining characteristics of the Zac Taylor era has been slow starts. The Bengals have tried to address that by changing their approach to training camp, including playing starters during the preseason. Even so, the only time they’ve been better than 2-2 through the first four weeks came during their Super Bowl run in 2021. This roster is far too talented to spend another season digging itself out of an early hole. Will the coaching staff continue tweaking its training camp approach in hopes of finally getting off to a fast start? We’ll find out soon enough. Who’s next for an extension? Several key contributors are entering the final year of their contracts in 2026. Dax Hill, DJ Turner II, Andrei Iosivas, Jordan Battle, Chase Brown and others are all scheduled to become free agents after the season. The Bengals will undoubtedly extend some of them—but certainly not all. Who will be wearing Bengals stripes for the final time? The battle for WR3 Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins have WR1 and WR1A locked down, but who claims the third receiver role? The Bengals have rotated players such as Andrei Iosivas and Charlie Jones into that spot, while Mike Gesicki has also absorbed plenty of receiving opportunities from the tight end position. Still, no one has firmly established themselves as the clear third option behind one of the NFL’s best receiving duos. Training camp could change that. The tight end rotation This position group is especially intriguing because of Erick All Jr.’s return from the knee injury that has sidelined him since Week 9 of the 2024 season. Gesicki is essentially a wide receiver playing tight end, while Drew Sample is one of the league’s better blocking tight ends. All has the potential to provide the best of both worlds. If he can stay healthy, could he completely change the dynamic of Cincinnati’s offense? More storylines will emerge as training camp unfolds, but these are a few of the biggest heading into Week 1. Which one are you watching most closely? Sound off! Relevant Song Lyrics: Guess who just got back today? title: Duke Tobin does not anticipate DJ Turner or Dax Hill skipping practice amidst ongoing contract talks
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals have a good problem most teams would take. They have two young corners worthy of re-signing for a second contract. DJ Turner (a second-round pick in the 2023 draft) and Dax Hill (a first-round selection from the 2022 draft) are both quality starters. Especially Turner, who has received the underrated tag pretty […]
full_text: Cincinnati cornerback DJ Turner (0) takes the field during minicamp, Tuesday, June 16, 2026, at Kettering Health Practice Fields in downtown Cincinnati. | Frank Bowen IV/The Enquirer / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images The Cincinnati Bengals have a good problem most teams would take. They have two young corners worthy of re-signing for a second contract. DJ Turner (a second-round pick in the 2023 draft) and Dax Hill (a first-round selection from the 2022 draft) are both quality starters. Especially Turner, who has received the underrated tag pretty frequently this offseason. However, it is still a problem when you need to re-sign them. The Bengals have been spending quite a bit, and while they could re-sign both players. The team would be left without the wiggle room it usually would like to have. We’ve seen players like Trey Hendrickson, Jessie Bates, and Ja’Marr Chase all skip out on portions of training camp while entering the last years of their respective contracts. The Bengals aren’t expecting that this time around. “When you draft guys like that that come in and find roles and elevate their game and elevate the people around them. Those are guys you want to be around,” Director of Player Personnel Duke Tobin said of the cornerback duo . “And I’m not going to make any predictions about future contracts. We have everyone signed up right now, which is really good. It’s a good feeling. I think everyone is locked in on the season, and we’ll see what the future holds. But right now, our focus is winning and winning now.” “I’m not going to give any potential contract details or anything like that. Everyone’s under contract, and we want the good players to stay here long term. That’s always the way we’ve been.” Tobin’s last line is certainly one most fans will scoff at considering the team’s track record. It also seems like this is mostly from the team’s perspective that they do not expect any hold-ins or hold-outs. They would probably have a good idea, though, given they are negotiating with these players’ agents, but hold-ins and trade requests remain the only leverage a player looking for a new deal has without sacrificing (potentially) tons of money in the process. We did see Tee Higgins practice during training camp the year that he would eventually play on the franchise tag. However, that has been more of the exception than the rule around the NFL. Ultimately, it is up to each player to do what they think is best for their situation. You could argue that playing out the contract and performing well would let you hit the market with some momentum. But you could just as easily suffer a major injury and then need to prove yourself all over again if you are even able to play at that level again. We will see how Turner and Hill decide to handle their business. "We want the good players to stay here long term." "I'm not going to make any predictions about future contracts. We have everyone signed up right now, which is really good." Duke Tobin on contract seasons for DJ Turner, Dax Hill, Chase Brown. pic.twitter.com/OMAs5hKuki — Joe Danneman (@FOX19Joe) July 27, 2026

title: Bengals express excitement for Dax Hill as he enters a contract year
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals currently have both of their starting cornerbacks set to play out the final years of their contracts this fall. While DJ Turner rightfully gets more of the attention as one of the NFL’s best young corners, don’t sleep on what his running mate can do in what could be a breakout campaign […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals cornerback Dax Hill (23) intercepts a pass intended for Jacksonville Jaguars wide receiver Travis Hunter (12) in the first quarter of the NFL Week 2 game between the Cincinnati Bengals and the Jacksonville Jaguars at Paycor Stadium in downtown Cincinnati on Sunday, Sept. 14, 2025. The Jaguars led 17-10 at halftime. | Sam Greene/The Enquirer / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images The Cincinnati Bengals currently have both of their starting cornerbacks set to play out the final years of their contracts this fall. While DJ Turner rightfully gets more of the attention as one of the NFL’s best young corners, don’t sleep on what his running mate can do in what could be a breakout campaign for Dax Hill. It’s been quite the journey for Hill, a 2022 first-round pick out of Michigan who began his career at safety for two seasons, then bounced between slot and boundary corner for the past two years before finally settling in on the boundary for the second half of the 2025 season. He also suffered a torn ACL five games into the 2024 season that slowed his development. But after getting his bearings while moving to the boundary full time in Week 11 last year, Hill ended the season on a strong note that’s generated a lot of excitement for what he can do over a full season. Bengals moved Dax Hill to Outside CB in Week 11. From that point on: – Allowed just 15 Rec on 30 targets (50% Rec % Ranked 9th/61st) – Allowed just 22.6 Yards Per Game – 6 PBUs to 0 TDs Allowed – PFFs 10th Rated CB – Just 2 Missed Tackles (6.3% Ranked 11th/61 CBs) — Marcus Whitman (@TFG_Football) March 2, 2026 Now, Hill will enter the 2026 season as a full-time starter on the boundary, head coach Zac Taylor confirmed on Monday. “Outside is absolutely where we want him to play. Outside is absolutely where he will play,” Taylor told reporters when asked about Hill’s position status. Defensive coordinator Al Golden, now in his second season leading the Bengals defense, sees a bright future ahead for the 25-year-old Hill. “I think clearly when we made that move (moving Hill to the boundary full time), we made great strides as a team, and I think a lot of that also has to do with his personal improvement over that time for Dax and the healing,” Golden told reporters on Monday. “He played with so much confidence down the stretch for us. “And he brings a physical presence at corner. I would say he’s one of the best tackling corners that there is. He brings length, experience. I see him starting at a whole different level than he was a year ago, fighting through what he had to fight through a year ago.” It remains to be seen if the Bengals will extend Hill or let him play out what is the fifth-year option of his rookie contract, but one thing is for sure: There’s a lot of hope in the building that he can become a star that helps take this rebuilt defense to the next level. Dax Hill returns as the starting outside corner opposite of DJ Turner. Both guys will be in contract years, and looking to have their best seasons to date. pic.twitter.com/xPRMZBwDiu — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) July 23, 2026

title: Bengals News: Training camp week arrives
summary: It is finally that time of year when NFL teams return to the practice fields for training camp. New schemes will be installed, new players and coaches will get their shot to show they belong, and football fans get to scratch the itch of the game returning. The Cincinnati Bengals are no different. There is […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow (9) warms up before a preseason training camp practice in downtown Cincinnati on Thursday, July 31, 2025. | Sam Greene/The Enquirer / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images It is finally that time of year when NFL teams return to the practice fields for training camp. New schemes will be installed, new players and coaches will get their shot to show they belong, and football fans get to scratch the itch of the game returning. The Cincinnati Bengals are no different. There is an air of excitement around the team and its fanbase. We will see defensive players like Dexter Lawrence and Bryan Cook take the field and get an idea of how they will fit. The much more boring side of things is the injury list and the players who will be on it. B.J. Hill is the only notable player so far, and he is just on the Active/Physically Unable to Perform list. Rookie center Connor Lew avoids any injury list after suffering a torn ACL. It is a good sign Lew will be able to practice. He is worth monitoring, as Ted Karras is 33 years old, and while he will always be welcome as a Bengal, Father Time remains undefeated. We may be getting a good look at the next center for Cincinnati depending on how slowly the team brings him along. Let us know down below who you are most excited to see in training camp this year. Cincinnati Bengals place two players on injury lists, but the omission of notable rookie is the real story ahead of training camp The injury is the reason Lew lasted until the fourth round of the 2026 NFL Draft. Had he been healthy, he would have likely been off the board within the first 100 picks. The Bengals were praised for selecting him at that point, getting a quality center prospect on an injury discount. Bengals Announce 2026 Training Camp Schedule Bengals Training Camp presented by Kettering Health will kick off on Wednesday, July 29 with the first of six practices open to the public, including a special Friday night practice in Paycor Stadium on Aug. 7. Four additional practices will be open exclusively to Season Ticket Members and Waitlist Members. Ja’Marr Chase puts the NFL on alert before Bengals training camp “Alright, right now we in Miami, man. Literally last workout before we report, bro. Man, I ain’t gonna lie, it’s been a good offseason…Honestly, can’t complain about nothing. S’s going on. Haters gonna hate, but the one thing that ain’t stopping is that money. That s is always gonna flow, you know why? ‘Cause we working. If y’all ain’t working, wake the f*** up.” Cincinnati Bengals an Underrated NFL Contender Entering 2026 Season The defense should be way better with all the additions. Still, three consecutive years of declining defensive play means Cincinnati has to prove they are better early on, or that goodwill could completely disappear.
