summary: With training camp just days away, it’s time to start our Bubble Watch series. For those new to the site, every week during training camp and the preseason, our staff of 11 voters will make their predictions for every player we believe is currently on the roster bubble. We’ll both list out a chart of […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OH - OCTOBER 05: Detroit Lions offensive lineman Giovanni Manu (59) walks off the field after the game against the Detroit Lions and the Cincinnati Bengals on October 5, 2025, at Paycor Stadium in Cincinnati, OH. (Photo by Ian Johnson/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images With training camp just days away, it’s time to start our Bubble Watch series. For those new to the site, every week during training camp and the preseason, our staff of 11 voters will make their predictions for every player we believe is currently on the roster bubble. We’ll both list out a chart of all of our votes, and break down all of the training camp battles and trends for each player. We kick off the series by predicting the fate of 15 different players who I picked as entering training camp on the roster bubble. Below are our predictions, and under that is a more detailed breakdown of each position battle. View Link Quarterback: Assumed in: Jared Goff, Teddy Bridgewater Luke Altmyer: 1 “IN” vote For now, I believe Detroit’s top two quarterback positions are set. That could certainly change if Teddy Bridgewater struggles this preseason, but I think the Lions value his mentorship abilities too much to put him on the bubble. That leaves the conversation as to whether undrafted rookie Luke Altmyer can justify a spot on Detroit’s 53-man roster as QB3. Entering camp, only one staffer—Brett Whitefield—has him in. Running back: Assumed in: Jahmyr Gibbs, Isiah Pacheco, Sione Vaki Jacob Saylors: 9 “IN” votes Again, some may take issue with Sione Vaki being an assumed in, but he’s arguably Detroit’s best special team player, and I don’t see the team departing with him. As of now, it really feels like only Jacob Saylors could justify keeping a fourth running back after a strong special teams outing in 2025. But if Kye Robichaux or Jabari Small show out in the preseason, they could work their way onto the bubble. Wide receiver: Assumed in: Amon-Ra St. Brown, Jameson Williams, Isaac TeSlaa, Greg Dortch Cedrick Wilson Jr.: 8 “IN” votes Dominic Lovett: 8 votes Tom Kennedy: 1 vote Jackson Meeks: 0 votes Detroit’s 1-4 receivers feel pretty set for the time being, and most of our staff has the Lions keeping two others: veteran Cedrick Wilson Jr. and second-year wideout Dominic Lovett. But a few staffers had Detroit only keeping five receivers, and Tom Kennedy snuck in a vote after some surprise special team contributions last year. I found it mildly surprising that Jackson Meeks didn’t receive a vote, but he also still feels like a bit of a project as he continues to work at both tight end and wideout. Tight end: Assumed in: Sam LaPorta, Brock Wright Tyler Conklin: 11 “IN” votes Miles Kitselman: 1 vote Zach Horton: 0 votes It should be noted that most Pride of Detroit staffers made their predictions before Conklin was placed on the Physically Unable to Perform list to start training cam p . However, we still don’t know the severity of the injury he suffered during spring practices, so it’s still very possible he wins the TE3 spot. That said, undrafted rookie Miles Kitselman—one of Detroit’s most praised UDFA signings—also managed to get in a vote. And if Conklin sits for an extended amount of practices, don’t be surprised if Kitselman, Meeks, or Horton start to get some hype. Offensive tackle: Assumed in: Penei Sewell, Blake Miller, Larry Borom Giovanni Manu: 3 votes Colby Sorsdal: 0 votes Is this the end of the line for Giovanni Manu? Just about three-fourths of our staff believe so. With the addition of Larry Borom as the clear preferred OT3, Manu will have to show enough growth to justify keeping a fourth offensive tackle. As of right now, the staff isn’t buying it. Interior offensive line: Assumed in: Tate Ratledge, Cade Mays, Christian Mahogany, Miles Frazier Ben Bartch: 11 votes Juice Scruggs: 11 votes Seth McLaughlin: 0 votes Michael Niese: 0 votes Even though the starting left guard position is up for grabs, and there’s a lot of new competition among Detroit’s interior offensive line depth, the entire staff is in unanimous agreement about the roster spots filled by this group. Ben Bartch will challenge for the starting left guard position—and should, at worst, be an upgrade over Michael Niese. Meanwhile, Juice Scruggs enters camp as the heavy favorite to win the backup center job.
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: Discussion: Who is the Lions’ most important positional coach?
summary: Head coaches and coordinators are among the first people praised for a good season or blamed for a poor one. However, a team’s success runs deeper than those spots on the coaching staff. Positional coaches are often underappreciated and overlooked, given that their successes or failures are typically not obvious to the untrained eye. If […]
full_text: Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff (16) talks to quarterbacks coach Mark Brunell during warm up ahead of the Cleveland Browns game at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Sept. 28, 2025. | Junfu Han / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images Head coaches and coordinators are among the first people praised for a good season or blamed for a poor one. However, a team’s success runs deeper than those spots on the coaching staff. Positional coaches are often underappreciated and overlooked, given that their successes or failures are typically not obvious to the untrained eye. If a receiver runs a great route, the offensive coordinator often gets praised for the play call, not the receivers coach that taught it. If a defensive back makes a great read and breaks up a pass, the defensive backs coach does not always get credit for helping with a week’s worth of film review and play recognition. When a backup linebacker steps into the game and plays well, our first thought is not about how good of a job the linebackers coach did preparing that group ahead of time. The Detroit Lions have an ample number of position coaches that play a key role in their success (and failure at times). Of these names, who is the most important? Today’s Question of the Day is: Who is the Lions’ most important positional coach? My answer: Hank Fraley. There are no shortage of important coaches on the Lions staff. The relationship between quarterback and quarterback coach is critical to growth and success, and the Lions seemingly have a good duo with Jared Goff and Mark Brunell. Scottie Montgomery (wide receivers) and Jim O’Neil (safeties) have the subtitle of associate and assistant head coach, respectively, highlighting their importance to Dan Campbell’s crew. Elsewhere, Kacy Rodgers’ role as defensive line coach and run game coordinator, coupled with his extensive resume, make him an excellent pairing with a young defensive coordinator in Kelvin Sheppard. However, the Lions live and die by their offensive line, and the man at the center of it is himself a former center, Hank Fraley. When the Lions were thriving in 2023 and 2024, it was Fraley’s offensive line that was paving the way. From protecting Goff and allowing plays to develop downfield to creating massive running lanes for Jahmyr Gibbs to sprint through, the blocking up front made the Lions a successful team. Last season was the first time that the Lions took a step back since Campbell took over in 2021, and it is no coincidence that the Lions also underwent a significant reshuffle on the offensive line that same year. Losing Frank Ragnow and Kevin Zeitler was a difficult task, and while rookie Tate Ratledge performed admirably, cohesion across the line faltered. Fraley has proven himself to be a brilliant mind when it comes to blocking schemes, hence his recent title of run game coordinator. However, a coach can only do so much when his starting lineup is changing every week. In 2026, the Lions took some significant actions towards establishing a consistent offensive line going forward. Penei Sewell shifts to left tackle, replacing the veteran Taylor Decker. The team signed Cade Mays to firm up the interior. In the draft, they selected Blake Miller to man the right side of the line. Ratledge returns at right guard, while Christian Mahogany is the frontrunner for an open competition at left guard. Aside from the uncertainty at left guard—a battle that will play out in training camp—the Lions have put forth a lot of answers in response to a subpar 2025 campaign. Now that the team has restocked their talent pool, the onus is now on Fraley to get the best out of this offensive line group. If that happens, the Lions could be looking at a quick rebound.

Yassmin’s initial signing cost dwarfs more than half of Green Bay’s 2026 UDFA signings. OL Gus Hartwig Gus Hartwig is a OC prospect in the 2025 draft class. He scored a 6.33 #RAS out of a possible 10.00. This ranked 231 out of 627 OC from 1987 to 2025. https://t.co/5ZzK14aBPu pic.twitter.com/o2OfjKsd1f — RAS.football (@MathBomb) March 14, 2025 Hartwig played five years at Purdue and was a high school All-American coming into college. He was signed as an undrafted free agent by the New York Jets in 2025, where he was injured in the summer (unspecified leg injury) and spent the year on the injured reserve. He was waived by the team in May. He was ranked as the 12th center in the 2025 class per The Beast and was an East-West Shrine Bowl participant during his draft cycle. Hartwig also dealt with some knee issues in college. K Lenny Krieg Like Yassmin, Krieg is eligible for an international exemption, as he is a German national. As we wrote yesterday when we received word that Krieg would be worked out , he went a perfect 14 of 14 at the NFL Scouting Combine in 2025 before earning a spot on the Atlanta Falcons’ practice squad. After the season, he signed a reserve-futures deal with the New York Jets, who waived him on June 1st, two days before the team signed veteran kicker Jason Sanders.

title: Packers to honor Bob Harlan on Lambeau Field facade in 2026
summary: No single person is more responsible for the current state of the Green Bay Packers as an organization than Bob Harlan. The former team president and CEO oversaw two decades of dramatic change in Green Bay as the franchise transformed from a backwater, bottom-feeding franchise back into one of the most successful and desirable franchises […]
full_text: UNITED STATES - MARCH 04: Bob Harlan, former chief executive officer of the Green Bay Packers, speaks during a news conference regarding the retirement of quarterback Brett Favre at Lambeau Field in Green Bay, Wisconsin, U.S., on Tuesday, March 4, 2008. Favre, 38, said today he would finish his career after 17 NFL seasons, 16 of them with Green Bay, where he won an unprecedented three NFL most-valuable player awards and a league championship after the 1996 season. (Photo by Matt Ludtke/Bloomberg via Getty Images) | Bloomberg via Getty Images No single person is more responsible for the current state of the Green Bay Packers as an organization than Bob Harlan. The former team president and CEO oversaw two decades of dramatic change in Green Bay as the franchise transformed from a backwater, bottom-feeding franchise back into one of the most successful and desirable franchises in all of North American pro sports. This fall, the Packers will bestow one of the franchise’s greatest honors on Harlan. At Monday’s 2026 Shareholders Meeting, current CEO Ed Policy announced that the Packers will place Harlan’s name on the Lambeau Field facade this season, with the revealing to take place during a ceremony at halftime of the Packers’ week 9 game against the Carolina Panthers. Harlan’s biggest change after taking charge of the franchise was to hire Ron Wolf as general manager and give him complete control over all football-related decisions, removing the Packers’ board from having any input. While Harlan handled the financials and the overall health of the organization, leading to renovations of Lambeau Field and the construction of many of the team’s current facilities, Wolf was charged with making the football team itself competitive. Under Harlan’s stewardship, the Packers returned to glory with a win in Super Bowl XXXI less than a decade after he took over. The team would win another Super Bowl with a new general manager, Ted Thompson, whom Harlan hired into the job in 2004. Mark Murphy succeeded Harlan as CEO in 2008 before himself retiring last summer and handing the reins over to Policy. Harlan, who passed away in March at the age of 89, will be the second non-player to have his name added to the facade inside the stadium. Thompson was the first, with the team honoring him as a special contributor during the 2021 season after he passed away in January of that year.

title: Packers’ pass rush needs another late-game threat to help Micah Parsons
summary: There has been much discussion of the Green Bay Packers’ need to get more out of their pass rush in 2026. With Micah Parsons likely out for at least four games, the team certainly needs to find a way to generate more pressure on the quarterback while their superstar gets back towards full health. Parsons’ […]
full_text: Green Bay Packers defensive end Lukas Van Ness (90) celebrates his sack of Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Flacco (16) during the third quarter of their game Sunday, October 12, 2025 at Lambeau Field in Green Bay, Wisconsin. | Mark Hoffman/Milwaukee Journal Sentinel / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images There has been much discussion of the Green Bay Packers’ need to get more out of their pass rush in 2026. With Micah Parsons likely out for at least four games, the team certainly needs to find a way to generate more pressure on the quarterback while their superstar gets back towards full health. Parsons’ 12.5 sacks represented just over one-third of the team’s total, underscoring the need to find more sources of pressure. However, a look at when sacks took place shows just how much of a one-man show the Packers’ pass rush was late in games and how badly the team needs help for Parsons when games are on the line. A whopping 8 of Parsons’ 12.5 sacks came in the last 15 minutes of regulation or in overtime, the most for any player in the NFL last season. Unfortunately for the Packers, that number was half of the entire team’s total, as the rest of the defense was especially inept at bringing quarterbacks to the ground with the game on the line. Here are the sack totals for the Packers in the 4th quarter and overtime last season: Micah Parsons: 8 Rashan Gary: 2 Devonte Wyatt: 2 Brenton Cox: 1 Kingsley Enagbare: 1 Lukas Van Ness: 1 Karl Brooks: 0.5 Barryn Sorrell: 0.5 As noted above, Parsons recorded almost two-thirds of his sacks late in games. Gary, on the other hand, had 7.5 sacks in total last season, but only had two after the fourth quarter began. That only bolsters the argument that his conditioning was abysmal in 2025, and it surely helps to explain why the Packers were content to deal him away this offseason. To make matters worse, a few of these sacks are barely meaningful at all. One of Gary’s two sacks came on the very first play of the fourth quarter in week one, just barely fitting inside the criteria. Meanwhile, Cox’s sack came in the week 18 game against the Minnesota Vikings, when he blew up Max Brosmer — it happened in an entirely meaningless game against the worst quarterback to start an NFL game last season. (Well, probably the second-worst, behind his counterpart in week 18, Clayton Tune.) If this isn’t illustration enough of the team’s need to find someone to help Parsons close out games on the defensive side of the ball, let’s look at the team’s splits when they did or did not record a late-game sack. When getting at least one sack after the start of the 4th quarter last season, the Packers were 7-2-1. But when they failed to sack the quarterback in that time frame, they had just a 2-6 record. There’s a bit of a chicken-and-egg situation here, of course. Teams with a lead are more likely to be able to pin their pass rushers’ ears back and get after the quarterback, giving them more sack opportunities. In many ways, it’s similar to the old cliché about getting a certain number of carries or yards in the run game and the correlation (not necessarily causation) those numbers have with winning games. Still, even if the sacks aren’t always directly responsible for wins, they certainly did correlate closely with the Packers’ results in 2025. Look at what happened to the team when Parsons got injured. The team’s five-game losing streak to end the season coincided with his injury, and in that time frame they had just two late-game sacks: the one from Cox mentioned earlier and one from Lukas Van Ness early in the fourth quarter of the Wild Card loss in Chicago (which also came very early in the 4th quarter). Their pass rush completely fell apart without Parsons, but it was most evident late in games when they absolutely needed someone on defense to make a play and they just couldn’t get it. Maybe Van Ness takes that step and can help Parsons close the door on wins this season. Maybe Devonte Wyatt stays healthy and contributes a bigger interior rush to help get some big stops. Maybe a younger player like Sorrell or Dani Dennis-Sutton can step up. If Parsons is going to be the Packers’ closer once again, it sure would be nice if he had a couple of setup men to help him out.

title: Packers CEO Ed Policy says Lambeau Field will not be renamed
summary: The Green Bay Packers might be exploring new revenue streams to keep up with the rest of the NFL, but one thing will not be changing any time soon: the name of Lambeau Field. One of the biggest questions raised by CEO Ed Policy’s recent comments to the press was about the status of the […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - SEPTEMBER 11: A general view of the stadium is seen prior to the game between the Washington Commanders and the Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field on September 11, 2025 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers might be exploring new revenue streams to keep up with the rest of the NFL, but one thing will not be changing any time soon: the name of Lambeau Field. One of the biggest questions raised by CEO Ed Policy’s recent comments to the press was about the status of the legendary stadium’s name. With Policy recently acknowledging that the Packers’ ownership structure limits certain avenues for raising funds, one potential option that the organization could have pursued was a naming rights deal for the most iconic venue in professional football. However, Policy put any of those questions to rest quickly and firmly during Monday’s 2026 Shareholders Meeting with a single sentence: “We are not selling the naming rights to Lambeau Field.” That statement came during a section of the meeting that addressed the organization’s plan to keep the Packers in Green Bay. While the team has expressed an openness to selling naming rights to other buildings and facets of the team facilities, such as the practice facilities across the street, Lambeau Field’s name is officially hands off for the foreseeable future. Instead, the team’s focus will remain on generating additional revenue through other means, such as the Titletown District developments around the stadium and the use of Lambeau Field for other, non-Packers-related events. For example, one of those such events is coming up on the first Saturday in September when the stadium will play host to a college football game between the Wisconsin Badgers and the Notre Dame Fighting Irish. This news should not be a surprise. Lambeau Field is one of just two NFL stadiums without a naming rights deal of some kind, with Soldier Field being the other. Arrowhead Stadium, home of the Kansas City Chiefs, is an oddity; the stadium itself retains that name, but the team sold naming rights to the field inside to GEHA, an insurance company. However, both the Chicago Bears and the Chiefs are working on building new stadiums across state lines from their current homes, with the new venues sure to have some form of corporate branding involved. It is possible that the “GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium” model could be a possibility for the Packers and Lambeau Field down the line, but for now that remains off the table. Lambeau Field will simply be “Lambeau Field,” at least for the foreseeable future.

title: Packers 2025 Callsheet: Goal Line
summary: If you’re new to this series, we’re reviewing how the Green Bay Packers offense performed in 2025 by situation. We’re doing that by building out a call sheet, which I ran down in my initial post. This is the 12th (and final) article in the series, where we’re looking at the Goal Line. Generally, I look […]
full_text: If you’re new to this series, we’re reviewing how the Green Bay Packers offense performed in 2025 by situation. We’re doing that by building out a call sheet, which I ran down in my initial post . This is the 12th (and final) article in the series, where we’re looking at the Goal Line. Generally, I look at the Low Red Zone as plays between the opponent’s 1-10 yard line, but I wanted to break it down 1 step further this year and bring in a goal line section. Based on some research, I’ve decided that the goal line package should start at the 3-yard line. So today, we’re building out the goal line section of our callsheet. Once we get down to this area of the field, you probably won’t be shocked to find that there isn’t a very large sample size. And you would be correct. In 2025, the Packers averaged 1.5 goal line plays per game, tied for 12th in the league. The Rams were at the top of the league with 2.4 plays per game, and the Jets were at the bottom with 0.4 plays per game. In terms of how they performed in this area, your Green Bay Packers were at the top of the league in both success rate (80%) and TD Rate (68%). On the season, the Packers scored 17 TDs in this area, tied for 3rd in the league. The Rams – with a TD rate of 55% – are at the top with 22 TDs. If the Packers had the same number of plays the Rams did, they would have ended the season with 27 TDs. Part of that is due to the number of drives: per FTN , the Rams had 18 more drives than the Packers last year (the Rams ranked 19th in drive pace last year, while the Packers ranked 30th). But it’s also how the Packers & Rams performed in the non-goal line red zone. The Rams had a success rate of 58.7% in the low red zone last season (2nd in the league), while the Packers were at 46.8% (16th). If the Packers can pick up the pace a bit and perform a little better in the low red zone in 2026, they’ll be cooking with gas. We’ve got 2 plays to look at today, but I’m going to throw in an extra for 2 point purposes. And also because I want to. In 2025, the Packers were better passing the ball then running the ball in goal line situations. When passing, they had a success rate of 88.9% and a TD rate of 88.9%. When running, they had a success rate of 65% and a TD rate of 50%. So we’re rolling with 2 passes and 1 run. Passes Shield (1.5 YPA, 100% TD Rate) This is one of my favorite concepts in this part of the field. The Packers have had great success with it, typically as the pass tag on an RPO. They had good success this year with a variant of this, but they didn’t actually run the original play in their goal line package in 2025. They ran it as part of their low red zone package this year, so I’ll show that first. Shield is a two-man concept, with the inside man running a route up the field and the outside receiver running a Now slant off the hip. The idea is for the first receiver to create a natural rub – a “shield”, if you will – for the receiver behind him. It can be extremely hard to cover in this area of the field. In the play above, Watson is working as the Shield, Doubs is working the Now slant, and Rasheed Walker ends the play as the Savior. There’s a nice little wrinkle that the Packers used at the goal line this year. I’ve just been calling it Shout (Shield/Out). Get the defense looking for Shield, then have the outside man release to the pylon. TE Release (2.0 YPA, 100% TD Rate) In the tight confines of the goal line, there are a handful of ways to spring open a receiver. You can use misdirection by showing a look you’ve shown a thousand times and mixing it up just a tad, or you can set up a natural rub. Or you can do both. Josh Whyle goes in motion and looks to be angling to block out the EMOL (End Man On Line), but arcs around and releases to the flat. As another defender runs to cover, he runs into Christian Watson, running an in-cutting route. Runs Wide Zone (1.6 YPA, 60% TD Rate) I was all set to put Inside Zone in this spot, but, at a rate level, it was outperformed by Wide Zone in this area, which I did not anticipate. Inside Zone had a higher success rate (71.4%), but a lower TD Rate (50%). That still made Inside Zone a nice contender, but I’m giving the edge to Wide Zone here. (It’s worth noting that all 3 of the Packers TDs off Wide Zone came from a no huddle look.) Get the offense flowing to one side and the running back will follow the flow of the line while looking for cutbacks. Here is how that section looks on our callsheet: Here is where you can find the other parts in this series: An Introduction 1st & 10 2nd & Long 2nd & Medium 2nd & Short 3rd & Long 3rd & Medium 3rd & Short 4th & Short High Red Zone Low Red Zone That’s a wrap on our callsheet series! I love going through this exercise every offseason because it gives me a chance to revisit the season as a whole, while also giving me the chance to dig into what works and what doesn’t. It helps fully close the books on the previous season, while also giving me a good sense of where the offense may be heading into the next season. I hope you all enjoyed reading these half as much as I enjoyed writing them. Albums listened to: IAN SWEET – Shiverstruck ; Sister Ray Davies – Holy Island ; Pete Yorn – All the Beauty

title: Green Bay Packers News: No, the Packers aren’t on the verge of selling out
summary: On Friday, the Green Bay Packers released their annual financial report ahead of the team’s Shareholders Meeting, which will take place today. As usual, the report gives a unique look into the NFL’s financial picture as a whole, but this year’s report also seems to be the source of a new narrative: that the Packers […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WI - JULY 25: New Green Bay Packers President Ed Policy addresses the shareholders at the 2025 Green Bay Packers Shareholders meeting at Lambeau Field on July 25, 2025 in Green Bay, WI. (Photo by Larry Radloff/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images On Friday, the Green Bay Packers released their annual financial report ahead of the team’s Shareholders Meeting, which will take place today. As usual, the report gives a unique look into the NFL’s financial picture as a whole, but this year’s report also seems to be the source of a new narrative: that the Packers need to sell out and shift to a more conventional ownership structure. That’s the position of a handful of national NFL pundits who are apparently only able to think of a single way for the Packers to raise some additional money to stay competitive financially with the rest of the NFL. Yes, over the weekend, CEO Ed Policy addressed the idea that the team needs to get creative in raising money. But dissolving the team and selling to a billionaire owner just isn’t on the table — especially not, as one writer suggested, in the next few months . Other teams are able to raise money via small percentage sales of the franchise to private equity firms or other minority ownership groups. That’s fine. But having a $1 million operating loss, after back-to-back years of operating profits in excess of $60 million, isn’t some sort of giant red flag that the team can’t compete, especially when the team brought in more than $130 million in non-operating income. Policy is doing what any good CEO is doing: observing the market and his competitors and thinking of ways to make sure that his own organization can stay competitive in the future. That’s all. Frankly, it’s exactly what he should be doing. And to my fellow owners: relax and don’t let the Mike Florios of the world rile you up. Packers CEO says financial bump needed to stay competitive | ESPN Ed Policy’s comments aren’t indicative of any sort of impending sale to a single owner, and any talking head who suggests that as an option can shut up right now. Policy does say that the team will start to get creative with its revenue streams, sure, but that’s not going to result from a complete shift in ownership structure. Packers’ finances remain strong amidst changing NFL landscape | Packers.com It’s pretty wild how differently this story gets framed, depending on the news outlet. Yes, the Packers netted an operating loss of about a million bucks, but their non-operating income was more than $130 million, putting them squarely in the black and in a good financial position. 10 players we’re most excited to watch at Packers 2026 training camp | Packers Wire Unsurprisingly, MarShawn Lloyd is near the top of the list, which includes a wide range of players from the most important — quarterback Jordan Love — to a UDFA rookie in J. Michael Sturdivant. Five Most Important Storylines Entering Packers Training Camp | SI.com From the pass rush to kicker, here are the critical questions the team needs to answer over the next five weeks. Count Binface Threatens to Nationalize Sega Over a Shenmue 4 Update | VG Times If this whole headline makes sense to you immediately without having to think about it, then congratulations! You’re just like me in having a truly bizarre set of interests.

title: The Road to Paradise, or how the 2026-27 season could go right for the Houston Texans
summary: As a Houston pro sports fan, you are almost contractually obligated to look for, and expect the worst to happen, usually in a highly dramatic and painfully creative fashion. Earlier, we discussed how the 2026-27 season could go so, so wrong for the Texans. However, for all that can go wrong, you have to acknowledge […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - JUNE 09: Houston Texans gather during Houston Texans mandatory mini-camp at Houston Methodist Training Center on June 09, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Jack Gorman/Getty Images) | Getty Images As a Houston pro sports fan, you are almost contractually obligated to look for, and expect the worst to happen, usually in a highly dramatic and painfully creative fashion. Earlier, we discussed how the 2026-27 season could go so, so wrong for the Texans. However, for all that can go wrong, you have to acknowledge that things might go right. With that, a few of the ways that the 2026-27 leads to the long-sought after glory the Texans have been after since 2002 (and the Houston football fan since 1961 (the last of the AFL titles)). A beyond historic defense: Last year, Houston had a really good-to-great defense. For 2026-27, many of those players that dominated the defense return, all in prime playing condition. Additionally, the Texans only reinforced those positions that were considered a little “weak”. They added Reed Blankenship to further strengthen that secondary, giving the squad arguably the best nickel package in the game. The defensive tackle position got some major upgrades with the drafting of MacDonald, an interior wrecker from Ohio State who many felt was the best interior DL in the 2026 draft. Add that Togiai and Rankins return to further cement the interior, and this squad can start dreaming of not only picking up where they left off last season but perhaps take their place in the pantheon of elite NFL defenses. Sure, defensive performances can vary from season. Yet, what helps the Texans is that their defense was not based on any particular scheme, nor were they overly reliant on the fickle fortune of turnovers. They have great players and so long as great players stay healthy and motivated, they can blast through any turnover number variance or adaptation to a defensive scheme. Given some of the talent additions to the lineup, improvement is a reasonable expectation. So long as injuries hold off, this team could be even more dangerous on defense. The Texans get a consistently good run game going : Generally, teams with strong defenses like to have a tough, punishing ground game. If nothing else, the ground game indicates greater physicality and can reduce the time that a defense is on the field, keeping them fresher and making it harder for an opposing offense to do enough to counter the defense. Give a QB a better run game, and said QB will be a better thrower. Last season, even with the extra effort from Marks, the Texans did not have a particularly effective/efficient ground game. In theory, David Montgomery, along with a revamped offensive line, can give Houston that much more effective ground attack. That would open up play-action, keep defenses honest, and allow Stroud the time and security to make those big pass plays he is capable of delivering. This would also be a major help later in the season, when weather can limit QBs like Stroud. A running game travels in all conditions. Houston spent a lot to get that going. If it does, Houston will be very much in business. Stroud’s playoff meltdown was a blip, not a feature : Maybe Stroud is not a cold-weather QB. However, his career is better than what he showed in last season’s playoff run. Somewhat related with the run game/offensive line considerations, if that works, it takes a good bit of pressure off Stroud, thus allowing him to elevate his game. In 2024, no quarterback faced more pressure and faced more third and longs. In 2025, the sack numbers were down, but the opposing pressure win rate was such that Stroud had to get rid of a lot of passes early. Any increased degree of security, especially from the offensive interior, and any significant improvement in the efficiency of the run game, will go a long way to alleviating the pressure on Stroud. Give Stroud better security, and his harsh weather struggles will not be as big a factor. If all goes to plan, Stroud’s 2025-26 playoff struggles will only be a footnote on his path to glory. We don’t worry about the punting game : Solid special teams have been a franchise hallmark since Frank Ross took the helm. The kicking game, even with all the rule changes, has been solid for Houston. The coverage units tend to be among the stronger ones in the game. When Jon Weeks left last offseason, the long snapper position came open, and Austin Brinkman stepped in with no issues. Now, Houston will need to adjust to its 3rd punter since 2021. The main contenders are Kai Kroeger, who comes over via trade with the Saints, and Jack Stonehouse, an UDFA from Syracuse. Normally, punting doesn’t generate a ton of headlines, but with a defensively strong team like Houston, a good punting game is almost a must. Tommy Townsend was solid, but not spectacular, as Houston let him walk to the Titans this offseason. However, Kroeger ranked 31st in net punting last season and had two blocked. Is he more cost-efficient? Sure. However, there might be a reason why he was so cost-efficient. Stonehouse did well enough as Syracuse, so this might be a competition. That the winning punter will be under the Ross tutelage is encouraging. If Ross can continue his solid special teams track record, even in the punting game, things should be just fine. Multiple playoff games at Reliant : Under the Ryans regime, the Houston Texans are 2-0 in home playoff games, with an average margin of victory of 25.5. They are 1-3 in road playoff games, with an average margin of defeat of 15.0 points. Ideally, Houston could get at least a top 2 seed, so that they would either be assured of a bye or multiple home playoff game opportunities. Under Ryans, they’ve been the 4th seed twice and the 5th seed once. Easier said than done to obtain that top 2 seed, but if Houston can somehow manage to get that seeding and host multiple playoff games, those Super Bowl dreams become that much more realistic. Much can go wrong during the NFL season, and Houston fans know this all too well. However, a realist understands that positive outcomes are also part of life. If one or more of these things happen, perhaps the Texans can break through that Divisional Round barrier and advance to the glory beyond

title: Houston Texans 2026 Training Camp Primer
summary: Houston Texans training camp kicks off this Wednesday. The fresh grass at Reliant Stadium is eager to receive its 25th edition of the Houston Texans roster. Expectations could not be higher. The bar has been set at the divisional round and nothing less would satisfy the fanbase. There are plenty of reasons to believe. In […]
full_text: Houston Texans training camp kicks off this Wednesday. The fresh grass at Reliant Stadium is eager to receive its 25th edition of the Houston Texans roster. Expectations could not be higher. The bar has been set at the divisional round and nothing less would satisfy the fanbase. There are plenty of reasons to believe. In an article later this week, I’ll wax poetic on the optimism the fans should have for the team. Below, you’ll find all the information needed to prepare you for the upcoming campaign. Current 53-man roster prediction: Rosterology 2.0 Top Training Camp Battles: Center : Jake Andrews, Keylan Rutledge, Evan Brown, Febechi Nwaiwu, Jarrett Patterson Backup Nickel : Alijah Huzzie, Kamari Ramsey Wide Receiver Six : Lewis Bond and Justin Watson Defensive End Depth : Dominique Robinson, Ali Gaye, Solomon Byrd, or a possible free agent Backup Linebackers : Jake Hansen, Jake Hummel, Jamal Hill, Wade Woodaz, Aiden Fisher, Marte Mapu Analysis : This is the deepest training camp roster in Texans’ history. As you can see, few battles are for starting spots. New veterans and up-and-coming draft picks squabble for spots on the roster. All eyes will be on the offensive line competition to see which players win roles and which are granted opportunities simply because they were drafted. Top Undrafted Rookies to watch: James Neal III, OT – Iowa State Collin Wright, CB – Stanford Noah Whittington, RB – Oregon Analysis : James Neal III was a three-year starter at left tackle at Iowa State. He’ll compete directly with Blake Fisher for the backup tackle role. Neal projects to be a more natural fit at LT than Fisher, whose patience must be running dry with this coaching staff after not earning a starting role for two seasons. Collin Wright fell down draft boards due to a lack of speed, but that isn’t a concern in the Texans’ defense. Finally, Noah Whittington is a seasoned, downhill running back who has the clearest shot at breaking into a light RB room. Top free agent additions: Logan Hall, DT/DE (Tampa Bay) Dominique Robinson, DE (Chicago) Jake Hummel, LB (Baltimore) Reed Blankenship, S (Philadelphia) Wyatt Teller, OG – (Cleveland) Braden Smith, OT – (Indianapolis) Foster Moreau, TE – (New Orleans) David Montgomery, RB – (Detroit) Analysis : The veterans here bring a mixed bag of experience and injuries. As you’ll see below, many are coming off disappointing seasons, which is why they were able to make their way to Houston on team-friendly salaries. The combination of Wyatt Teller and Braden Smith hold the entire team’s fortunes in their hands. If they can return to their previous form, there’s no telling how good this team will be. Look for Logan Hall to be a surprise impact player on the defensive line as he plays every position across the front. Injury concerns heading into camp: Tank Dell, (knee, leg) Dell’s progress has been well documented via social media. Nick Caserio voiced his expectation of the fourth-year WR to be ready by training camp. Braden Smith (neck surgery) Smith’s lingering neck surgery has cast doubt on his availability at the start of camp. The Texans may err on the side of caution with this injury due to the presence of veteran Trent Brown. Houston simply needs 17 healthy games out of the two tackles. Marlin Klein (hamstring) ‘Sideline Klein’ appears to have recovered from a hamstring injury suffered in early June. He should be back and healthy in time for the start of training camp. No rookie needs a more public and positive camp as much as Klein. Brevin Jordan (ACL) A one-year deal extends Jordan’s chance to bring his dynamic playmaking to the Texans offense. Back-to-back knee injuries hopefully won’t stymie his athleticism. Logan Hall (groin and knee) A minor groin injury and knee tendonitis as reported by Aaron Wilson kept Hall out of OTAs and minicamp. He too is “expected to be ready for training camp” and should have a major role on the defense. Underdogs to root for Alijah Huzzie, Nickel Last year’s UDFA started the last game of the season. A special teams ace and personal favorite. Swarm mentality 101. Jaylin Smith, CB Last year’s third-round pick struggled with injuries in between spurts of good play. Word from OTAs is he’s impressed and ready to roll. If he can break into the rotation, it would unlock an entire trove of different schemes and formations for the defense. Jamal Hill, LB 2024 sixth-rounder is well-liked by the staff. He’s an athletic former safety who wins on special teams. A hand injury forced him to wear a cast over the summer. He’s a fun watch when he gets on the field and is good in pass coverage. British Brooks, FB/RB After losing 17 pounds this offseason , Brooks is making a bid for the final running back role. He’s up against Jawhar Jordan and rookie Noah Whittington, but Brooks’ role as a fullback should still be in place. The question is whether the offense keeps him over a true running back or veteran tight end. Kyonte Hamilton, DT Another former draft pick (2025 seventh round) who was derailed due to injury. He fractured his ankle during last year’s training camp. Now healthy, there is opportunity for Hamilton to climb up the depth chart and steal a roster spot in a thinner DT room than last year. Potential roster snubs Cade Stover, TE The numbers don’t work in Stover’s favor after the Texans signed Foster Moreau and drafted Marlin Klein. Five TEs is extremely rare for any team to keep. Stover must define his role to keep his hopes alive in a crowded position room. M.J. Stewart, CB The Texans trust Stewart in the secondary and on special teams. Similar to Stover, the team signed Reed Blankenship and drafted Kamari Ramsey. Stewart started four games in 2025 but may struggle to find a spot in a crowded defensive back room.. Blake Fisher, OT Former second-round pick has yet to show any promise or potential. His stint as a sixth lineman in jumbo packages is not a sustainable career for him. Depending on needs in the interior of the line, the performance of undrafted rookies, and the numbers game of the roster, Fisher could see himself on the outside looking in several weeks. Team outlook: The miserable and bewildering loss to the New England Patriots in the Divisional Round left a bad taste in fans’ mouths. However, that shouldn’t outweigh what was a miraculous season with plenty of high points. This season is a major inflection point in the career of C.J. Stroud. A great season could put him among the league’s highest‑paid quarterbacks. A poor season would raise difficult questions about his trajectory. A bad run of form would see him out of a job. The defense has more elite talent than ever before. They are thinner this year than last and are already down E.J. Seed, but have a dozen young and talented players waiting in the wings. A tough schedule is ahead, but this 25th season for the Houston Texans will be as exciting, demanding, and impactful as any before it.

title: Colts’ PUP list contained another notable omission
summary: On Monday, the Indianapolis Colts announced that both starting wide receiver Alec Pierce (ankle) and projected starting rookie linebacker CJ Allen (calf) would begin training camp on PUP. The former wasn’t a surprise at all, as Pierce is expected to return later on in training camp from a purported minor cleanup surgery on his injured […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - OCTOBER 05: DeForest Buckner #99 of the Indianapolis Colts looks on prior to the game against the Las Vegas Raiders at Lucas Oil Stadium on October 05, 2025 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Monday, the Indianapolis Colts announced that both starting wide receiver Alec Pierce (ankle) and projected starting rookie linebacker CJ Allen (calf) would begin training camp on PUP. The former wasn’t a surprise at all, as Pierce is expected to return later on in training camp from a purported minor cleanup surgery on his injured ankle earlier this offseason. However, Allen’s injury is a new one and came as a surprise, as he apparently aggravated his calf during a workout, although it’s not expected to be a long-term injury by any means. That being said, there’s still one notable omission from the Colts’ PUP list, as veteran defensive tackle DeForest Buckner, who is still working his way back from a season-ending neck injury, isn’t on it yet. While Buckner did not participate in earlier team organized workouts or veteran minicamp this offseason, it appears he may be physically cleared to participate in training camp—at least on a limited basis and/or pitch count early on. However, it’s possible that there may be a roster move regarding Buckner ahead, as he still may have some meaningful work left to do in his ongoing neck recovery. Last season, Buckner recorded 47 tackles (30 solo), 9 tackles for loss, 4.0 sacks, and 36 QB pressures during 10 starts before his year was cut short because of a lingering neck injury—which required surgery in early January.
author: Luke Schultheis

title: Colts place Alec Pierce and CJ Allen on PUP list to begin training camp
summary: The Colts will open training camp with two important players on the physically unable to perform list. Wide receiver Alec Pierce and rookie linebacker CJ Allen have both been placed on the PUP list as Indianapolis begins camp. The designation means both players are not ready to practice at the start of camp, although players […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - JUNE 11: Indianapolis Colts wide receiver Alec Pierce (14) watches a drill during the Indianapolis Colts Minicamp on June 11, 2026 at the Indiana Farm Bureau Football Center in Indianapolis, IN. (Photo by Zach Bolinger/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Colts will open training camp with two important players on the physically unable to perform list. Wide receiver Alec Pierce and rookie linebacker CJ Allen have both been placed on the PUP list as Indianapolis begins camp. The designation means both players are not ready to practice at the start of camp, although players on the active/PUP list can be activated at any time before the regular season. Pierce’s status is not a major surprise. He underwent an ankle cleanup procedure earlier this offseason after dealing with the issue during the 2025 season, and Colts head coach Shane Steichen previously said the team expected him back “at some point in training camp.” Pierce explained in June that the ankle worsened late last season and eventually required surgery after a PRP injection did not solve the problem. The Colts have maintained that the injury is not expected to create long-term issues. General manager Chris Ballard said in April that Pierce’s recovery timeline was around three months and that the team did not expect any long-term implications from the procedure. Still, this is worth monitoring because Pierce is expected to play a major role in the offense. He is coming off the best season of his career, crossing the 1,000-yard mark while again giving Indianapolis a true vertical presence. Missing early camp reps is not ideal, especially with Daniel Jones back as the full-time starter and needing timing with his receivers off his Achilles injury. Pierce does not need every summer rep to know his role, but this offense needs its top weapons available as soon as possible so there is less gelling needed later in the summer. Allen’s placement is a little more notable because he is a rookie and needs the practice time. The Colts drafted him to play early, and there is a clear path for him to earn a major role in the defense. Linebacker is one of the spots where Indianapolis needs quick growth, and Allen’s athleticism and college experience at Georgia made him one of the rookies most likely to contribute right away. That is why even a short absence matters. A veteran can miss a few practices and catch up quickly. A rookie linebacker needs the installation periods, the communication reps, and the live-speed adjustments that come with camp. If Allen is activated soon, this probably becomes a minor note. If it lingers, it could affect how quickly he pushes for a starting job. For now, there is no reason to panic. The active/PUP list is often used cautiously at the start of camp, and neither player is automatically at risk of missing regular-season time. However, the Colts need Pierce healthy for the passing game and Allen ready to compete in a defense that should have early snaps available for him. This is not a major setback yet. It is an early camp storyline worth watching.
author: Andrew Aziz

title: Colts’ emerging young center named among NFL.com’s 2026 ‘All-Under-25-Team’
summary: According to NFL.com’s Nick Shook, Indianapolis Colts 3rd-year center Tanor Bortolini has been named among their 2026 ‘All-Under-25-Team’: Tanor Bortolini Indianapolis Colts · Age 24 There’s something about Wisconsin linemen that tends to catch my eye in Indianapolis during the NFL Scouting Combine, and Bortolini was only the latest to do so back in the winter of […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MO - NOVEMBER 23: Indianapolis Colts center Tanor Bortolini (60) during an NFL game between the Indianapolis Colts and the Kansas City Chiefs on November 23, 2025 at GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, MO. (Photo by Jeffrey Brown/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images According to NFL.com’s Nick Shook, Indianapolis Colts 3rd-year center Tanor Bortolini has been named among their 2026 ‘All-Under-25-Team’: Tanor Bortolini Indianapolis Colts · Age 24 There’s something about Wisconsin linemen that tends to catch my eye in Indianapolis during the NFL Scouting Combine, and Bortolini was only the latest to do so back in the winter of 2024. Luckily for Indianapolis, he still flew under the radar, lasting until the fourth round of the draft and spending his first season at guard, learning alongside the player he’d eventually replace, center Ryan Kelly. Bortolini switched to the pivot in 2025, anchored one of the NFL’s best (and most expertly rebuilt) offensive lines and earned a stellar Pro Football Focus grade, ranking third among all centers. It seems general manager Chris Ballard has successfully found his long-term replacement at a crucially important position. Waiting in the wings at center as a rookie back in 2024, Bortolini didn’t miss a beat during his first time as a full-time starting center just a season later in 2025, as he more than effectively replaced longtime Pro Bowl veteran center fixture Ryan Kelly in the middle of the Colts offensive line—which was no easy feat. Per PFF (subscription), this past season Bortolini earned a +82.6 overall grade, which was the 3rd highest among all qualifying players at the center position. Specifically, he had a +88.2 run blocking grade, and a +66.2 pass blocking grade—as he allowed 0 sacks and 17 QB pressures during his 566 total pass blocking snaps. The 24-year-old Wisconsin native has already shown consistently solid fundamentals by being a sound technician in his overall blocking, with a highly cerebral approach to the game, while also flashing the well above average athleticism to get out and block in space—while climbing to the 2nd and even 3rd levels of opposing defenses. While it’s still early in the 2024 4th round pick’s pro career, the Colts appear to have found their long-term starting center for the foreseeable future.
author: Luke Schultheis

title: Daniel Jones cleared for full participation at Colts training camp
summary: Daniel Jones will be ready when the Colts open training camp. Jones confirmed Monday on The Pat McAfee Show that he will fully participate when training camp begins this week at Grand Park. The Colts quarterback said the plan is for him to return to 11-on-11 team drills, adding that he is “ready to go” […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - JUNE 11: Daniel Jones #17 of the Indianapolis Colts participates in minicamp at Indiana Farm Bureau Football Center on June 11, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Michael Hickey/Getty Images) | Getty Images Daniel Jones will be ready when the Colts open training camp. "I'm feeling really good and I'm gonna be full go to start training camp.. I'm ready to go" ~ @Daniel_Jones10 That's GREAT news 👏 #PMSLive pic.twitter.com/UcWFE1zKsl — Pat McAfee (@PatMcAfeeShow) July 27, 2026 Jones confirmed Monday on The Pat McAfee Show that he will fully participate when training camp begins this week at Grand Park. The Colts quarterback said the plan is for him to return to 11-on-11 team drills, adding that he is “ready to go” after working his way back from the Achilles injury he suffered last season in December. That is a significant step for Jones and the Colts, who needed some clarity at quarterback before camp opened. Jones had already participated in seven-on-seven drills during OTAs and continued doing extra sprint work after practice, but training camp will represent a more complete test. The speed, traffic, pocket movement and timing of 11-on-11 work are different from offseason drills, especially for a quarterback coming off an Achilles tear. Jones’ goal throughout the recovery process was to be fully ready for camp, and he appears to have reached that point. The injury happened in Week 14 against the Jaguars, meaning Jones will be returning to full participation about seven and a half months later. For Indianapolis, this removes one of the first major questions of camp. The Colts do not need Jones limited, eased in slowly or missing key reps while trying to build chemistry with the offense. They need him working with the first-team unit and proving that last season’s success before the injury can carry over. Before getting hurt, Jones had thrown for 3,101 yards and 19 touchdowns in 13 starts, while also adding five rushing touchdowns. Among qualifying quarterbacks, he ranked third in yards per attempt, sixth in QBR and seventh in passing yards, while the Colts’ offense led the league in points per game through Week 11. The bigger question still has to be answered on the field. Being cleared for training camp is good news, but it does not guarantee Jones will be the same player right away or that the offense will immediately pick up where it left off. He still has to show that the Achilles is not limiting his movement, confidence or ability to operate under pressure. Still, this is the update the Colts needed. Their season depends heavily on Jones giving them stable quarterback play.
author: Andrew Aziz

title: Colts futures watch: Which team bets are worth considering?
summary: Odds courtesy of FanDuel, please gamble responsibly The Colts are not a difficult team for sportsbooks to price right now. They have been stuck in the middle for years, and the current futures market reflects that. Indianapolis is listed at +370 to win the AFC South, +166 to make the playoffs, and -125 to go […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - JUNE 1: rIndianapolis Colts head coach Shane Steichen watches a drill during the Indianapolis Colts OTA on June 1, 2026 at the Indiana Farm Bureau Football Center in Indianapolis, IN. (Photo by Zach Bolinger/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Odds courtesy of FanDuel , please gamble responsibly The Colts are not a difficult team for sportsbooks to price right now. They have been stuck in the middle for years, and the current futures market reflects that. Indianapolis is listed at +370 to win the AFC South , +166 to make the playoffs , and -125 to go over 7.5 wins . Those numbers all point to the same general view: the Colts are not a bad team, but they are also not being priced like a team that has clearly made the jump. We won’t even look at the Super Bowl odds at +4500… The roster has talent, but the problem is that most of the team’s futures value still comes down to the same question that has followed the franchise for years: can the quarterback play be good enough? To win the AFC South: +370 The division price is interesting, but it is not screaming value. The Titans are probably not ready to fully take over the division, although they should be better and could absolutely take a game off the Colts. The Texans still look like a team in that 10-to-12 win range, especially with a defense that should remain one of the stronger units in the conference. The Jaguars are coming off a fantastic season with 13 wins and a close playoff loss, and while some regression is possible, they still have to be treated like one of the main teams to beat. That makes the math difficult for Indianapolis. With Houston and Jacksonville both reasonably expected to be around 10 wins or better, the Colts likely need 11 wins to feel good about winning the division. At 10 wins, they may have a chance, but they would need help and tiebreakers to break their way. At +370, the implied probability is about 21 percent, and that feels close to right. The Colts need to find roughly three more wins compared to last season, and it is hard to say the roster has improved enough on paper to assume that happens automatically. If Jones is fully healthy and plays like he did during the best stretch of last season, then the Colts can absolutely be competitive. If he is average, limited by the Achilles, or inconsistent against better teams, winning the division will be impossible. This is not a crazy bet. It is just not one with much clear value. To make the playoffs: +166 This is the most intriguing team future. The path to a playoff spot is much more realistic than the path to a division title. The Colts probably need 10 wins to feel good about making it, while nine wins at least keeps them in the conversation depending on the AFC wild-card picture. Finding two more wins is a lot easier to imagine than finding three or four, especially when last season had several games that slipped away. The Chiefs, Seahawks and Rams games come to mind. Those were the types of games that separate an average team from a playoff team. Indianapolis did not close enough of them, and that is why it stayed in the middle. If Shane Steichen takes a step forward as a coach, the defense performs better in bigger games, and Jones gives the offense steady quarterback play, the Colts can absolutely get to 10 wins. Taylor can still carry games, the offensive line should be strong, and the secondary has enough talent to be a legitimate strength. The question is whether the Colts can stop playing like a team that finds ways to finish around .500. At +166, making the playoffs is worth a look. It is not a lock by any means, but it gives you a better risk-reward profile than the division number because Indianapolis does not need to beat out both Houston and Jacksonville. It just needs to be good enough to get into the field. Of the team futures, this is the one I like best. Over 7.5 wins: -125 The win total feels properly priced. The Colts have lived around this number for years. They have been average, and sportsbooks are treating them like an average team again. That makes it hard to find a major edge. The over is very possible if Jones stays healthy. If he gives the Colts stable quarterback play for a full season, eight wins should be within reach, and there is a path to nine or 10 if the defense improves and the team closes games better. The roster should be good enough to avoid a complete collapse. The concern is that the number is not generous. At -125, you are paying extra juice on a line that already feels sharp. You also have to trust Jones’ health and consistency, which is not a small ask. If he misses time or regresses, the Colts could easily slide back toward seven wins or worse. This is not a bad bet because 8-9 wins is a very realistic outcome. It is just not an especially attractive one at the price. Final verdict The Colts’ team futures are mostly well priced. That makes sense because the market has figured out what this team has been for years: talented enough to stay relevant, flawed enough to miss the playoffs, and usually somewhere close to .500. The division bet at +370 is not unreasonable, but the Colts probably need 11 wins to win the AFC South, and that requires a bigger jump than I am comfortable betting on. The over 7.5 wins is also fair, although the price makes it less appealing given the quarterback health question. The best play is Colts to make the playoffs at +166 . It still depends heavily on Jones, Steichen and the defense being better in key moments, but it does not require Indianapolis to become the best team in the division. It only requires the Colts to turn a few close losses into wins and finally climb out of the middle.

title: Monday Musings: Gratitude for the Chiefs’ traditional uniforms
summary: In recent seasons, the NFL’s partnership with Nike for gameday uniforms has birthed some unique kits for teams to wear in place of the regular uniforms. On Monday, the Buffalo Bills revealed the latest case in this category with gray jerseys and gray pants. It’s days like this that personally make me grateful for the […]

(Photo by Jeffrey Brown/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images In recent seasons, the NFL’s partnership with Nike for gameday uniforms has birthed some unique kits for teams to wear in place of the regular uniforms. On Monday, the Buffalo Bills revealed the latest case in this category with gray jerseys and gray pants. Resilient. Gritty. Blue Collar. #BillsMafia | https://t.co/dSv2Kf4qfF pic.twitter.com/sSEbyEEyPt — Buffalo Bills (@BuffaloBills) July 27, 2026 It’s days like this that personally make me grateful for the Kansas City Chiefs ’ stubbornness in keeping the red-and-gold uniforms mostly the same over decades of football. In 2009, the 50th anniversary of the franchise’s start, Kansas City paid homage to the Dallas Texans by wearing uniforms that resembled the early-1960s look and helmets with the old-school Texans logo. To my knowledge, that was the only time the Chiefs have made a significant decision to wear an alternate uniform. In the era of head coach Andy Reid, the team has worn red pants with red jerseys in select home games, but that is as far as it feels Chairman and CEO Clark Hunt is willing to go. If it means avoiding the chance of an all-gray Chiefs uniform, I’m thankful for the willpower to keep tradition. According to NFL.com , the Chiefs are scheduled to wear Nike’s “Rivalries” uniforms in 2027, but it remains to be seen what that will look like if it comes to fruition. What do you think of the Chiefs holding firm on tradition with the uniforms? Would you want to see the franchise try something new? Let us know in the comments!

title: Chiefs rookie safety Xavier Nwankpa is ready to impact special teams
summary: After playing four seasons of football at the University of Iowa, few NFL Draft prospects are prepared to understand special teams like Kansas City Chiefs undrafted rookie safety Xavier Nwankpa is. The Hawkeyes’ football program is infamous for playing low-scoring, field-position games, which is why Nwankpa is uniquely prepared to make a run at the […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - JUNE 10: Xavier Nwankpa #29 of the Kansas City Chiefs participates in mandatory minicamp at The University of Kansas Hospital Arrowhead Training Complex on June 10, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Kyle Rivas/Getty Images) | Getty Images After playing four seasons of football at the University of Iowa, few NFL Draft prospects are prepared to understand special teams like Kansas City Chiefs undrafted rookie safety Xavier Nwankpa is. The Hawkeyes’ football program is infamous for playing low-scoring, field-position games, which is why Nwankpa is uniquely prepared to make a run at the Chiefs’ 53-man roster. A backup defensive back needs to play a part in the third phase of football; Nwankpa has understood that since his freshman year in Iowa City, Iowa. “That was a big part of what I did in college,” Nwankpa said in a press conference following Monday’s practice. “I was a four-phaser through my four years in college, so I just want to keep doing that, and whatever chance I can do to get on the field. [To] eventually develop some defensive reps is what I want to do.” Chiefs UDFA S Xavier Nwankpa knows special teams are vital to making the team. "That was a big part of what I did in college." No kidding, Nwankpa played 466 ST snaps over 4 seasons at Iowa, at least 75 per year (PFF) He covered 235 punts over 4 years — Ron Kopp Jr (@RonOnChiefs) July 27, 2026 According to Pro Football Focus , Nwankpa played 466 snaps on special teams over four years at Iowa. His career-high mark of 187 snaps came during his freshman season, but he played at least 75 snaps during each of his four years. He covered 235 punts, blocked for 108 punt returns and pursued a tackle on 52 kickoffs. It takes a versatile player to impact different parts of a game, but Nwankpa also points to intelligence and cohesion with teammates as strengths of his. “My physicality can stand out on some tape,” Nwankpa began. “I’m a pretty smart guy, able to communicate very well and help everyone get on the same page, clean up any mistakes on the back end to eliminate big plays.” The 22-year-old safety revealed to reporters that Chiefs safeties coach Andre Curtis called Nwankpa during the fifth round of this year’s NFL Draft to pursue him as an undrafted signing. He was committed to Kansas City quickly. “I feel like they get DBs [and] they go get them paid,” Nwankpa shared about why he chose the Chiefs. “There weren’t too many veteran safeties on this team, so I wanted to come in and have a chance, play some special teams; obviously, Coach Spags is a great defensive coordinator.” A guy who put together an outstanding day was S Xavier Nwankpa. I’m curious to see if he can continue to stack days like today together. He had multiple pass breakups, good anticipating and baited a couple of throws include an INT. #Chiefs #ChiefsCamp41 #ChiefsKingdom — Nick Jacobs (@Jacobs71) July 25, 2026 With veteran Alohi Gilman leading a safety position consisting of returning players like Chamarri Conner and Jaden Hicks, the team isn’t necessarily looking for impactful defenders at the safety position. Special teams coordinator Dave Toub, however, may be seeking players to help improve a poor performance by his unit last season. “[I’ll[ take advantage of any reps I can get,” Nwankpa expressed. “Young guy, undrafted guy, just trying to go out there so when I get my number called, go make some plays and capitalize on those opportunities. That’s all I can ask for.”

title: 10 Biggest Chiefs Questions: Can Mahomes play with fewer scrambles?
summary: There are many qualities that make Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes a special player. His arm strength is incredible. Mahomes’ ability to change his arm angle is arguably the best the NFL has ever seen. He can adjust his throw to hit any throwing window. Mahomes’ feel for space and coverage is some of […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - DECEMBER 14: Patrick Mahomes #15 of the Kansas City Chiefs runs with the ball for a touchdown during the first quarter of the NFL football game against the Los Angeles Chargers at GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium on December 14, 2025 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images There are many qualities that make Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes a special player. His arm strength is incredible. Mahomes’ ability to change his arm angle is arguably the best the NFL has ever seen. He can adjust his throw to hit any throwing window. Mahomes’ feel for space and coverage is some of the best ever. However, the first thing I think about in Mahomes’ game is all the plays outside the pocket or scrambling over his career. Mahomes has the arm strength and flexibility to make a throw from any platform, even while sprinting. He forces defenses to cover every blade of grass behind the line of scrimmage, since Mahomes is a threat to throw from any position. He also has the speed to create explosive runs with his legs. Mahomes’ feel in the pocket for small openings has bailed the Chiefs out many times. Mahomes has made countless crucial first downs with his rushing ability. As the Chiefs’ offensive infrastructure and talent have decreased in recent years, Mahomes’s ability to scramble to create throwing or rushing windows has become even more important. The Chiefs’ wide receivers have needed more time to get open downfield against man coverage, and Mahomes gives them that with his scrambles. Arguably, the Chiefs best answer on third down in recent years has been Mahomes scrambles. His ability to get just enough for a first down has kept the offense buoyant. While this has been a major weapon for the Chiefs, this need for Mahomes to create so much with his legs caught up to him. The floor fell out for the Chiefs’ offense last season. The team couldn’t run the ball at all, and the wide receivers struggled to do anything downfield. The offense was cramped and could not string together drives often. “There was so much pressure on Mahomes to carry things. … The Kansas City Chiefs must find a way to make life easier for [Patrick Mahomes].” @tthasselbeck and @minakimes on how the Chiefs should handle Mahomes' return from injury 🏈 pic.twitter.com/I2jaGDTKEu — NFL on ESPN (@ESPNNFL) July 24, 2026 In an attempt to overcome this, Mahomes had to scramble more often. By the end of the season, despite Mahomes’s best heroics, he wasn’t able to lift the offense with his playmaking. To make matters worse, Mahomes tore his ACL against the Los Angeles Chargers during the fourth quarter of Week 15. Not only was that the final conclusion of a rough season, but it affects this coming season too. Mahomes has proven over the years to be able to come back from an injury quicker than others, and he’s doing that again. Despite only tearing his ACL seven months ago, Mahomes has been a full participant in training camp. It’s remarkable that Mahomes is going to even be able to play that shortly after his injury. Just having Mahomes back, even if he’s limited, is a major boost to the offense. However, Mahomes is going to have to alter his playing style to account for his injury, mainly running less. Mahomes acknowledged this in a recent press conference about running less this season . If anyone could come back in that short amount of time and still be able to run, it is Mahomes. However, the most likely outcome is that Mahomes is going to need to scramble less after the injury. That will materially change the offense. What could that look like? Patrick Mahomes (knee) on changes to his play this season: "I think I ran a little bit too much last season… If all else fails, I'll just hand it off to K9 and let him go to work." pic.twitter.com/dLlhbMqdc2 — Underdog NFL (@UnderdogNFL) July 24, 2026 As Mahomes mentioned, having running back Kenneth Walker as a nearby weapon should help with that. Walker gives the Chiefs a credible run threat that defenses have to account for. He’s also potentially their best avenue to creating explosive plays, particularly if Mahomes is limited in his running. A byproduct of running the ball more might be going under center. Going under center can help the run game by unlocking easier angles to block and allowing extra blockers into the play. Another benefit of going under center is that the Chiefs can keep Mahomes in the pocket while giving him more protection. There can be extra bodies dedicated to protection. Having the threat of a run will make those play actions look easier, and it also helps the receivers in this offense. Using condensed formations from under center can get the receivers free releases and more space to run into. Mahomes can also manipulate zone defenders from his eyes. It would be an easy transition for Mahomes to be more of a play-action quarterback. Still, the question is about third-and-long situations. The Chiefs can’t mitigate the primary receiver issues on these snaps, as defenses aren’t going to fear the run. Teams will play man coverage without strong proof that Kansas City’s receivers strike fear in one-on-one situations. Mahomes has long helped this issue with his legs. If that’s off the table, how will the Chiefs be able to compensate for that? The offense will need receivers to step up in these situations to help Mahomes out. I’m skeptical. The Chiefs will likely struggle to move the chains on third-and-long if Mahomes has to stay within the pocket, but having a stronger run game can mitigate how many of those situations you’re put in. Another thing the Chiefs could do is throw short of the sticks on third down and be more aggressive on fourth down. If a third-and-8 can become a fourth-and-short, the play calling can rely on short-pass concepts that help the receivers. The hope is that the Chiefs are able to adapt the offense to more under-center formations early in the season as Mahomes gets comfortable. The best-case scenario is that as the season goes on, Mahomes becomes more capable and willing to scramble and run. If the offense can spend the early part of the season developing the run game, that is a formula that could be dangerous by the playoffs, when Mahomes is potentially hitting a physical stride But until Mahomes is fully comfortable with scrambling again, the Chiefs are going to need to adapt the offense, or the team could really struggle to move the ball. It’s on the staff to adapt the scheme to account for this.

Whether it was sniffing out the fake punt to further ignite a comeback from down 24-0 in the second quarter of the AFC Divisional round playoff game in the 2019 season, or stuffing running back Derrick Henry in the AFC Championship a week later, Sorensen should always be remembered fondly, even if he played himself into a role bigger than he ever should’ve held by the end of his Chiefs career. 49 yards: The length of the long-ball touchdown catch by Tyquan Thornton in Week 2 This is simple: let’s see more of these types of plays in the 2026 season. The Chiefs were unable to beat the Philadelphia Eagles in this game, but the play was a rare deep-ball highlight for quarterback Patrick Mahomes and the offense.

title: Aaron Donald isn’t only star DT who could be added to a defense
summary: While the Los Angeles Rams prepare for the potential return of Aaron Donald, he’s not the only superstar defensive tackle who could be added to a defense right before the season starts. Buccaneers defensive tackle Vita Vea, a two-time Pro Bowler who has averaged six sacks per season over the last four years, has requested […]
full_text: TAMPA, FLORIDA - JUNE 17: Vita Vea #50 of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers watches drills during mandatory minicamp the AdventHealth Training Center on June 17, 2026 in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Mike Carlson/Getty Images) | Getty Images While the Los Angeles Rams prepare for the potential return of Aaron Donald, he’s not the only superstar defensive tackle who could be added to a defense right before the season starts. Buccaneers defensive tackle Vita Vea, a two-time Pro Bowler who has averaged six sacks per season over the last four years, has requested a trade out of Tampa Bay. According to ESPN’s Ian Rapoport, Vea is unhappy with his contract and would rather go to a team willing to meet his demands. Could Vea be added to the NFC West’s arms race this year? Long-time #Bucs DT Vita Vea has requested a trade, sources say. Vea had hoped for a long-term contract extension and talks stalled. Now, he wants out. pic.twitter.com/sDl05JTYJy — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) July 27, 2026 Vea, 31, is entering the final season of a four-year, $71 million contract. A former 12th overall pick, Vea has largely lived up to his pre-draft hype and been a disruptive star in the middle of the Bucs’ defensive line, helping Tampa Bay win a Super Bowl in 2020 with Tom Brady. His age is not as much of a concern as Donald’s, but could be the reason that the Bucs are hesitant to extend him again without seeing how he holds up in 2026. It is unlikely that Vea would go to the Rams, of course. And the Seattle Seahawks have their hands full at defensive tackle with Leonard Williams and Byron Murphy II, both of whom could receive extensions soon. The 49ers could be a different story. San Francisco’s defensive tackle position is. a weakness, even after trading for Osa Odighizuwa in the offseason. Alfred Collins, CJ West, and fourth-round rookie Gracen Halton round out the group, but Collins is injured. Trading for Vea would be a very John Lynch-like move for the 49ers. This could also all be for show, and Vea could be extended by the Bucs any day. In the race to add more defensive line talent in the NFC West, Aaron Donald isn’t the only potential new face showing up this month.
