title: Ty Simpson ‘sharper, more efficient’ than Stetson Bennett on first day
summary: The most anticipated battle of Los Angeles Rams training camp will be the competition for the backup role behind Matthew Stafford. First-round pick Ty Simpson impressed those in attendance, including former Rams beat writer Vinny Bonsignore of the New York Post: There was quiet satisfaction inside the Rams building with how Simpson handled being thrown […]
full_text: Westchester, - July 26: Quarterback Ty Simpson #15 of the Los Angeles Rams during the first day of the Los Angeles Rams Rams training camp on the campus of Loyola Marymount University in Westchester on Sunday, July 26, 2026. (Photo by Keith Birmingham/MediaNews Group/Pasadena Star-News via Getty Images) | MediaNews Group via Getty Images The most anticipated battle of Los Angeles Rams training camp will be the competition for the backup role behind Matthew Stafford. First-round pick Ty Simpson impressed those in attendance, including former Rams beat writer Vinny Bonsignore of the New York Post : There was quiet satisfaction inside the Rams building with how Simpson handled being thrown into the deep end by McVay on Sunday. Splitting reps with Bennett, Simpson was the sharper, more efficient quarterback on Day One . Not perfect – he forced a sideline throw into double coverage while on the move that could have been picked – but the mistake was balanced by flashes of poise, command, mobility and a willingness to push the ball downfield. When his first reads were covered, he worked to secondary options and kept plays alive. For a rookie facing a loaded defense, it was a clean start… That’s why Simpson’s first day mattered. Not just for his throws, but for how he ran the offense We know that fourth-year quarterback Stetson Bennett was under center for most of the first-team reps . If Simpson continues to outshine Bennett, we could see the mix change in the coming weeks. It’s also important not to get ahead of ourselves. All eyes will be on the quarterback position when the national media rolls into town. Simpson will have bad days sprinkled in with the good. There will be days where Bennett is the better player. We can’t put too much stock into a single outing—especially when it’s the first day. But if Sunday was any indication, Simpson is on a path to overtaking Bennett and earn the backup role behind Stafford. Such an outcome would be a massive benefit to Los Angeles. In a year where there are probably more good players than available roster spots—which could get further crunched by Aaron Donald returning to the team—keeping only two quarterbacks would allow more depth at a position of need. LA could find it useful to carry an extra linebacker, running back, or corner—especially as they renew their commitment to special teams. I personally wasn’t expecting headlines that Simpson “shined” on the first day of camp. It’s welcome news and a possible sign of things to come. It’s going to take more than one good day in order to unseat Bennett. Stay tuned.
author: JB Scott

title: Stetson Bennett opens training camp with Rams’ 1s
summary: As expected, the Los Angeles Rams are giving starting quarterback Matthew Stafford a rest day every other day, and Sean McVay will give Stetson Bennett more opportunities than he’s ever had to feel like a starter. That was the case on Sunday, as Bennett took every rep with the 1s in the Rams’ first training […]
full_text: LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA - JULY 26: Stetson Bennett IV #13 of the Los Angeles Rams throws during training camp at Loyola Marymount University on July 26, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Ric Tapia/Getty Images) | Getty Images As expected, the Los Angeles Rams are giving starting quarterback Matthew Stafford a rest day every other day, and Sean McVay will give Stetson Bennett more opportunities than he’s ever had to feel like a starter. That was the case on Sunday, as Bennett took every rep with the 1s in the Rams’ first training camp practice of 2026. Per the Rams website, McVay opened camp with Bennett as a starter , not Ty Simpson, the rookie first-round pick who will bide his time as a third-string quarterback until the coaches see fit to make a change. Bennett leads first team offense: As noted above, today was a scheduled day off for QB1 with it being Day 1 of the Rams’ first four-day practice block (McVay on Saturday said Stafford would be off Days 1 and 3). So Sunday was a big opportunity for Bennett stepping up to lead the first-team offense, with Simpson sliding into the backup role as the leader of the second team offense. “I appreciate his competitiveness in all moments,” offensive coordinator Nate Scheelhaase said of Bennett. “And going back to last year, obviously you get to experience him in training camp, you get to experience him in preseason, and just seeing the way that he went to work, the way that guys would rally around him, he competes. And I think anybody enjoys playing with a quarterback who competes, who’s going to throw it all in there, and that’s the mentality he has. And so that’s only grown, you know, since being here, but that’s something that’s been his calling card since the jump.” Through his first three seasons in the NFL, including a tumultuous rookie year that saw him inactive for reasons that he later cited as “mental health” , Bennett has strictly been a third-string quarterback and preseason starter. Bennett’s workload in the preseason over the last two years has been far more than the average player because McVay refuses to put either Stafford or his backup into harm’s way during exhibition weeks. Bennett has had a few hero plays during that time, but also threw way too many interceptions . There was one point when Bennett had thrown seven interceptions between his most recent touchdown and his next touchdown . A quarterback who turns 29 in October, Bennett has yet to be active for an NFL game. If he wins the backup quarterback job, Bennett’s entire future could change, and it’s not the most ludicrous possibility in the world. Stafford wasn’t always backed up by experienced players like Jimmy Garoppolo and Blake Bortles, but has also had John Wolford and Bryce Perkins and Brett Rypien. Surely if the bar is Wolford, Bennett isn’t out of the running. Meanwhile, Simpson didn’t get any reps with the starters, but did work with the 2s and Stu Jackson called him “eager” to learn more: Although Simpson didn’t run with the first-team offense during the 11-on-11 drills, after every time he got taken out, he would walk over to associate coordinator/quarterbacks coach Dave Ragone for feedback. The eagerness and willingness to learn and receive feedback and criticism is good to see out of the rookie. It is perhaps more likely that the Rams would sign or trade for a veteran than to promote Simpson before Week 1, if Stetson Bennett fails to impress coaches enough to be named as Stafford’s backup. It’s only day one so a lot can happen before then. Until those decisions are made, Bennett’s going to get more opportunities in one month than he’s had in the last three years combined.

title: The Year 2 bar for Raiders offensive lineman Caleb Rogers
summary: As part of the 2025 draft class, offensive lineman Caleb Rogers found himself sitting, watching, and learning for much of his rookie campaign. Even with the team struggling mightily and competitiveness waning week-to-week — normally an opportune time for a team in the dumps to play rookies and younger players to take stock of what […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TX - DECEMBER 21: Las Vegas Raiders guard Caleb Rogers (76) waits for the snap of the ball in the first quarter during the NFL game between the Las Vegas Raiders and Houston Texans on December 21, 2025 at NRG Stadium in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Leslie Plaza Johnson/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images As part of the 2025 draft class, offensive lineman Caleb Rogers found himself sitting, watching, and learning for much of his rookie campaign. Even with the team struggling mightily and competitiveness waning week-to-week — normally an opportune time for a team in the dumps to play rookies and younger players to take stock of what they have — the third-round pick (98th overall) of the 2025 NFL Draft didn’t get an official offensive snap until Week 13. The team was 2-9 at that point and after a 31-14 thumping from AFC West foe Los Angeles Chargers, the Raiders dropped to 2-10. In between that time, however, was reported struggles in practice — with Pete Carroll’s coaching staff holding him back due what they classified as inability to absorb coaching. And when word got out that Rogers would be making the start against the Dallas Cowboys in Week 11, the Texas Tech product was instead a healthy scratch. However, from Week 14 on, the 6-foot-4 and 312-pound Rogers played all the offensive snaps in the final give games of the season, with the majority of the work at right guard. When all was said and done, the rookie graded out as a bright spot on the much-maligned Brennan Carroll-led Raiders offensive line. The Texas native proved to be an asset in pass protection while developing as a run blocker and was a paragon of discipline with zero penalties across his 284 snaps last year. Nick Emmanwori's monster day headlines the rookie performances from yesterday's action 🌊 pic.twitter.com/lCL4wrk7Hz — The 33rd Team (@The33rdTeamFB) December 8, 2025 Now, the 24-year-old heads into a 2026 season with a new head coach — Klint Kubiak — and a veteran offensive line coach — Rick Dennison — with Las Vegas cleansing itself of nepotism in the coaching staff. That alone doesn’t guarantee success of course, but the vibes have changed exponentially in the desert. Which portends good things for Rogers and the Raiders offensive line. However, much like last offseason, Rogers finds himself steeped in impressing another coaching staff and fighting for a a starting gig. With Kubiak’s desert marauders engaged in training camp with veterans slated to report this coming Tuesday, the opportunities are there. And based on his play in the final six games of the 2025 season, the Year 2 bar for Rogers is going from promising rookie to a regular starter at guard. Expect the competition on both sides of the Raiders trenches to be lively in camp and likely preseason games. For Kubiak’s offense to have any success in his inaugural season helming an NFL team, Las Vegas’ offensive line needs marked improvement. Dennison’s work with the big uglies will dictate much of the Raiders success and failures this coming season. Fortunately for both coaches, there’s talent in the offensive trenches. For much of the offseason, free agent addition Spencer Burford and incumbent Jackson Powers-Johnson took most of the early first-team repetitions at left and right guard, respectively. By all accounts and appearances heading into training camp, the two guard spots have the heaviest concentration of competition. Kolton Miller is entrenched at left tackle, nary a Raider is going to challenge prized free-agent signing Tyler Linderbaum at center, and DJ Glaze is holding down the fort at right tackle. Viewed as a one-year, $3.225 million low-risk flier and depth signing on March 17, Burford showed early his familiarity with Kyle Shanahan’s wide-zone system with the San Francisco 49ers is paying dividends in the desert as Kubiak deploys a similar system. The blocking scheme Burford experienced with Shanahan is similar to Kubiak’s in that it’s complex, relies on flawless timing, body angling, and deep understanding of running paths over raw power. Considering all that, we shouldn’t be surprised that the 6-foot-4 and 300-pound Burford has notched more first-team snaps at left guard than any other lineman. Some depth with experience in the offense and can compete with Caleb Rogers. Raiders could use the same type of signing at RT. Fred Johnson or Jawan Taylor (at the right price) would make sense. https://t.co/gGBvYiDI5v — Ted Nguyen (@FB_FilmAnalysis) March 18, 2026 Powers-Johnson, meanwhile, showcases the brute-force strength and anchor ability in his 6-foot-3 and 325-pound frame. Despite being a stockier presence compared to others, Powers-Johnson is experienced in zone concepts during his Oregon Ducks days and although the wide/outside zone is a Kubiak staple, he and Dennison showed last year with the Seattle Seahawks gap and power elements can be intermixed and deployed to put offensive linemen in the best possible position to succeed. The potential of having two people-mover-type linemen next to each other with Linderbaum and Powers-Johnson on the Raiders interior line is enticing as those are two tone-setting types. The former has put it all together mentally and physically and the latter needs to do the same to establish themselves as a reliable and consistent performer. Which brings us back to Rogers. Despite getting drafted a year later, Rogers is older at 24 years old than Powers-Johnson (drafted in the second round of the 2024 draft and is 23 years of age), but it’s the Texas Tech’s athleticism that makes him a strong fit for the zone work Kubiak and Dennison prefer. With a lightning-quick first step and fluidity in space, Rogers has the ability to move and reach targets at the second level. That agility also helps him combat pass rushers in pass protection. However, its the run blocking and ability to withstand powerful defenders that is a must-improve for Rogers. He struggled against the straight-ahead brute-force he faced as a rookie and it’ll be intriguing to see how Kubiak’s and Dennison’s scheme and teachings can either improve that or mask it somewhat with the movement of the line as a group. While he may not have the power that Powers-Johnson possesses or the institutional knowledge of the scheme Burford has, Rogers performance in 2025 tops Burford’s pass-blocking chops — he struggled with power and direct one-on-one blocking assignments in pass protection — during his four seasons with the 49ers, and he’s a much better mover than Powers-Johnson. Throwback to when #Raiders OL Caleb Rogers accidentally hung up on Pete Carroll in his draft call last year 😂 "I thought the phone call was over. I felt horrible." pic.twitter.com/exDZvTGfsM — Nick Walters (@nickwalt) April 11, 2026 That’s what makes the right for the starting guard spots all the more interesting. Rogers, Burford, and Powers-Johnson each bring something astutely unique to the table and we’ll see who comes out on top to earn the starting nod. Don’t be surprised if it comes down to the best ability any football player can showcase to a coaching staff: Availability. Both Burford and Powers-Johnson had stints on injured reserve during their respective careers and with more snaps and prolonged appearances, we’ll see how Rogers’ body holds up to the rigors of NFL life. Each player holds their destiny in their respective hands and for Rogers, improving consistency in run blocking, continuing to showcase disciple (Kubiak is a stickler for attention to detail, by the way), and proving he’s the best option as both pass protector and move blocker in the run game are all ways he can impress and lock-in a starting spot. Would not winning a starting gig be detrimental? I’m sure it’d be disappointing. But at just 24 years old and with Burford’s and Powers-Johnson’s injury history, being a ready-and-able backup wouldn’t be the end of the world.

title: Las Vegas Raiders Summer Scouting: OT Rankings
summary: I broke down the 2027 scouting classes in my early summer scouting series, and the room has a ton of potential with a long list of potential standout players. I broke down the offense and defense in articles and I suggest reading those for a broad aspect of the room. The Raiders have Kolton Miller, […]
full_text: Oct 19, 2024; Tucson, Arizona, USA; Colorado Buffalos offensive tackle Jordan Seaton (77) against the Arizona Wildcats at Arizona Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images | Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images I broke down the 2027 scouting classes in my early summer scouting series, and the room has a ton of potential with a long list of potential standout players. I broke down the offense and defense in articles and I suggest reading those for a broad aspect of the room. The Raiders have Kolton Miller, DJ Glaze, and Charles Grant at tackle, but the NFL changes quickly and with Miller pushing over 30 there’s a chance he may be a trade candidate after 2026 if Las Vegas wants to get younger. Additionally, 2026 is likely a make it or break it season for DJ Glaze, who will need to solidify himself as a real right tackle in the NFL, though at only 24 years old he should have a strong chance and may convert to G as well. Charles Grant is in store for some work in 2026 in place of injuries, or pushing out DJ Glaze, and should be a top option for the OL in 2027. These rankings are extremely early, and they will evolve over not only the summer but the next 8-10 months throughout the season, and into draft season. Some lists will feature 10, 15, 20, or more ranked prospects but I’ll include others on the list below to note. Jordan Seaton, LSU- 6’5/330, Jr Consensus first overall tackle, spent first two seasons at Colorado before transferring to LSU. True LT, 5 sacks, 44 pressures allowed in his career with a 0.5% pressure rate in 2025. Anchors extremely well, light on his feet, shows a ton of raw natural power. Seaton fires off the ball, he’s able to get into space quickly, has incredible hip flexibility, and he drives defenders through the ground. As a run blocker, Seaton is able to turn and run in space, he’ll identify second and third level targets, and knock them with his blend of raw power and size to pair with athleticism. He’ll need to improve the hand combat, and become stronger in his grip strength but the chance to be a franchise top 5-8 tackle in the NFL is real. Trevor Lauck, Iowa – 6’5/310, R-So Lauck was arguably the best lineman for Iowa last year, on a unit that saw four NFL draft picks. A LT, Lauck has some experience working at RT as well but he was a standout on the left side. He moves incredibly well, has great knee, ankle, and hip bend, and Lauck drives off the ball. His kickstep is extremely fluid, he’ll sit low and fire with his lower body to pair his strength and natural movement abilities together to drive defenders backwards. Lauck allowed just 2 hits and 5 pressures in his first season as a starter, and he’ll improve likely over the next year. I’d like to see Lauck do a bit better in the pass game sealing the outside corner, and there’s time’s hell overextend as well, but the hand combat skills pop immediately. A true athlete, Lauck may push for the first tackle ranking quickly. Melvin Siani, Texas – 6’6/302, Jr Siani is personally my favorite of the big three for Texas (Siani, Goosby, and Baker). The former Temple standout allowed 0 sacks, 3 hits, and 11 pressures in 2025 at Wake Forest, and showed the quick transition from the AAC to ACC, and now the SEC. He’s powerful, with a ton of raw natural strength, and he shows a ton of hand power, grip strength, and pure upper body abilility. The ceiling may be limited, as Siani is very refined as is, and he wins a lot with consistency, size, power, and athleticism. Siani moves well, he fires off the ball, has a ton of lower body movement skills, and in space he’s a dangerous threat to run over defenders in the run game. Siani moves well in his kickstep, he’s shown great core strength, and while he’ll need to improve giving up the outside hip to speed rushers, there’s a good shot Siani can be a franchise tackle on either side. Carter Smith, Indiana – 6’5/308, R-Sr Smith saw a nice breakout season in 2025 allowing 2 sacks, a hit, and 11 pressures for the Hoosiers, and he returned in 2026 instead of declaring for the NFL Draft. Smith has great length, he’s a fluid mover, and he’s pretty developed into his early potential at nearly 24. Smith shows a ton of raw athleticism, good strength, and he moves well. The footwork is exceptional, and very NFL ready, along with high level knowledge at offensive tackle. Smith will fire off the ball, his kickstep is good, and he shows a ton of natural understanding of the tackle position. Smith stays low, has fluid hips, he sinks well, gets to the outside, and in the run game can climb to the second level quick. He may move to guard with average length, but Smith will likely slot in as a longterm offensive line starter, but the ceiling is a little limited. Trevor Goosby, Texas – 6’7/315, R-Jr Goosby is the consensus 2nd tackle, I’m slightly lower and I almost had him even in the 7-8 range. Goosby almost declared after the 2025 season but returned and he needed to work on a few things, largely due to limited snaps. He’s a long, powerful tackle but there’s some mobility concerns with inconsistent hip flexibility, and he doesn’t move his entire body in unison at times, specifically in the lower half. Goosby does have quick feet, he can lean at times, but he’s a far better mover forward than backwards (run blocker). He shows good instincts, his hands are powerful, but he does struggle to the outside at times vs quicker rushers. There’s a huge ceiling for Goosby, but right now there’s a lot of inconsistencies, and I’d like to see him tap into his athleticism moving forward more often as a pass protector where things do struggle. Jacarrius Peak, South Carolina – 6’4/300, R-Jr Peak has longer length than expected, he’s an exceptional mover in space, fires off the ball quickly, and Peak is a freak athlete at the position as well. He’s a powerful player, uses his full body consistently, and Peak combines his power and athleticism to win consistently. Peak shows great lower body agility, sinks his hips well, and the kickstep is fluid. After transferring from NC State, where he allowed just 7 sacks and 46 pressures across the last three seasons (1219 PBLK attempts), Peak suffered a significant lower body injury playing basketball so it will be a question how much the injury affects his athleticism. Greg Johnson, Minnesota – 6’6/325, Sr Blake Frazier, Michigan – 6’6/295, Jr Frazier is someone to keep an eye on, and there’s a real world he goes inside the top 10 if he has the season many think he can. He’s an exceptional athlete, moves extremely well in his lower body, and Fraizer has natural hip/ankle flexibility. The 20 year old moves his lower body in unision, has exceptional strength in the lower half as well, with good hand strength as well. He is able to turn his hips, sink, and move off the line of scrimmage quickly, while also having a nice low kickstep to pair with elite length. A former TE, Frazier has immense upside, but the technique is very raw, he’ll need to get stronger in the upper half, improve his hand combat skills, and also learn the position more, but the sky is the limit. Fraizer played 244 PBLK snaps last year allowing 4 sacks and 17 pressures, but he has the ability to potentially develop into a similar player as Joe Alt, who was also a former TE. Lance Heard, Kentucky – 6’6/330, R-Jr PJ Williams, SMU – 6’5/315, R-Jr Anthony Donkoh, Penn State – 6’6/325, R-So Donkoh is a G/T hybrid, but I think he’ll be best at tackle in the NFL instead of kicking into guard. Donkoh is an absurd athlete, as many Penn State offensive lineman are. He spent most of 2025 working at RG, but has experience at right tackle as well in 2024, where he was better. Donkoh has a ton of natural raw athleticism, he’s shown good lower body agility, fluid hips, and a ton of movement in space and off the line of scrimmage. Donkoh pairs the lower body movement skills with good power, his grip strength is good, but he’ll need to improve the actual hand combat technique.…

title: Fernando Mendoza Big Ten Championship versus Ohio State, Part XIII of Las Vegas Raiders’ Mendoza Mania
summary: It’s time to dive into the postseason for Silver and Black Pride’s Mendoza Mania series, as we’re breaking down Fernando Mendoza’s performance in the Big Ten Championship against Ohio State. Despite a rather pedestrian stat line—15/23 (65.2 completion percentage), 222 yards, one touchdown and one interception—the Las Vegas Raiders’ new quarterback was pretty flippin’ impressive […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - DECEMBER 06: Indiana Hoosiers QB Fernando Mendoza (15) throws a pass during the Big Ten Championship football game between the Indiana Hoosiers and the Ohio State Buckeyes on December 6, 2025 at Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis, IN. (Photo by James Black/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images It’s time to dive into the postseason for Silver and Black Pride’s Mendoza Mania series , as we’re breaking down Fernando Mendoza’s performance in the Big Ten Championship against Ohio State. Despite a rather pedestrian stat line— 15/23 (65.2 completion percentage), 222 yards , one touchdown and one interception—the Las Vegas Raiders’ new quarterback was pretty flippin’ impressive on the big stage and played much better than the box score showed. Four of his incompletions were throwaways, and one came via a batted pass, according to Pro Football Focus , and the interception was on a screen where the corner jumped the route to beat the block and make the pick. On top of that, PFF credited the No. 1 pick of the 2026 NFL draft with three “ big-time throws ” and zero “turnover-worthy plays” to earn an elite 91.9 grade for the evening. That was his highest single-game grade of the 2025 season, as Mendoza’s ability to throw deep and on the run really stood out against the Buckeyes. In full disclosure, a few clips from this game were included in a previous and more general breakdown earlier in the year, which can be found via this link . To avoid repeating information, all of the plays below were not included in the previous article and vice versa. That means Mendoza’s famous deep shot to Charlie Becker that flipped the momentum of the contest isn’t included here, but a detailed breakdown of that play is in the hyperlinked article for those who are interested. Fernando Mendoza is a good linear athlete, but his lateral movement skills could use some work and can make it difficult to escape the pocket quickly pic.twitter.com/dORgSN1MCm — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) July 20, 2026 Before diving into the highlights, Mendoza’s lateral movement skills are one area of improvement for him in the NFL, and that shows up in his pocket management or mobility. He’s a good linear athlete who has the speed to pick up yards with his legs when needed, but his change of direction and agility are lacking. The latter can lead to sacks like the play above. To the quarterback’s credit, nothing is open since Ohio State’s defensive backs are doing an excellent job in man coverage with safety help over the top in the Cover 2 Man/Cover 5 look. Also, both linebackers are on the line of scrimmage and essentially playing two-on-two with the quarterback and running back. One backer covers the running back to take away the checkdown, and the other serves as a spy to take away the scramble. That gives the three-man rush enough time to get pressure, as the left defensive end beats the right tackle around the edge. Mendoza does a good job of seeing that and stepping up in the pocket, but the spy takes away the interior or linear rushing lane in the B-gap. That forces Mendoza to change directions and move laterally to get out of the pocket, exposing his lack of agility and short-area quickness to pivot and escape the pocket. Another sack against OSU, this one is more of a lack of feel for pressure. He runs himself into trouble and can't escape pic.twitter.com/Q9IftwgXcu — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) July 20, 2026 Here, we’ll take a look at another sack where the No. 1 pick’s movement skills are a factor, but his feel for pressure is the bigger issue on this play specifically. Again, nothing is open with Ohio State doing an excellent job in man coverage, on top of having one safety come off the deep over route from the slot receiver to wall off the dig route from the outside. While there is a coverage bust where the slot receiver ends up being open in the end zone since neither of the safeties stuck with him initially, that happened late in the play and the pressure was already starting to penetrate the pocket. Mendoza does show a good internal clock, as he starts to try and escape the pocket before the defensive end wins around the edge. However, instead of stepping up and taking advantage of the lane outside of the guard, he runs into pressure. That’s likely because he doesn’t have a feel for where the defensive end is. Now, Mendoza’s lateral movement skills come into play as he’s out of his element and has to be an escape artist in the pocket, leading to the sack on third down. To be fair, Arvell Reese—the fifth overall pick of April’s draft—is serving as the spy and waiting for the quarterback to scramble. So, the Heisman Trophy winner probably isn’t going to pick up the first down here anyway. But taking advantage of the open lane could at least give the offense a chance to move the chains by getting all seven yards with his legs on this play, or by cutting the distance in half to set up a potential go-for-it opportunity on fourth down. Either of those two results is better than taking a sack. On top of the toughness, I love that Fernando Mendoza comes off his 1st read and delivers a perfect throw on the run on this play #Raiders pic.twitter.com/nNaTcVBvSK — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) July 20, 2026 Now, let’s get into the fun stuff, starting with the famous first play of the Big Ten Championship where Mendoza delivers a strike on the run right before taking a huge hit. It’s a designed roll-out that Indiana ran frequently last year, where the tight end in the three-by-one formation blocks to pin the edge defender inside. But Ohio State was ready for it by having the edge defender widen right before the snap and attack the tight end instead of getting caught off-guard, leading to the pressure. On the backend of the play, the Buckeyes are in man coverage again. The outside corner takes away the go route from the outside receiver, and the slot receiver takes too long to get into his route and out of the break, especially with the pressure coming since the tight end couldn’t pin the edge defender inside. So, Mendoza comes to the backside of the read, where he finds Elijah Sarratt open on a drag route after a pair of defenders collided. While on the run and knowing that he’s about to get crushed, Mendoza hits Sarratt with a perfect ball that’s in front of the receiver and instride for a nine-yard gain. That highlights a pair of important traits from the No. 1 pick: the toughness to throw under pressure and the ability to maintain his accuracy without having a stable base. My favorite aspect of Fernando Mendoza's scrambling is how good he is at taking advantage of DBs who don't plaster to their man Results in a 3rd down conversion here #Raiders pic.twitter.com/TchmfZAhYR — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) July 20, 2026 What’s encouraging about Mendoza’s pocket management moving forward is that he can be effective at evading pressure when it isn’t coming from the blind side and is decent at making off-script plays. He has a few tricks to help with the latter, the best being that he’s really good at recognizing when defensive backs don’t plaster and come off their man on scramble drills. This time, Ohio State comes out in a five-man front and runs Tampa 2 behind it, where both edge defenders drop in coverage. With eight defenders to cover five receivers, nothing is open down the field on Indiana’s mesh concept. That being said, there is a window to hit Becker right at the sticks on the short drag route right where the middle linebacker/Tampa dropper was. But Mendoza doesn’t see it in time, and the pressure starts to come. Luckily, he bails out of the pocket in the proper direction this time and recognizes that the defense doesn’t have anyone containing the edge since both standup linebackers dropped in coverage. So, the quarterback manages to buy more time by scrambling toward the wide side of the field. Then, he sees the nickelback come downhill and leave Becker wide…

title: Keyron Crawford’s Las Vegas Raiders’ Timeline
summary: The Raiders drafted Keyron Crawford with the 67th overall pick just a few months ago. The former Arkansas State standout broke out in his sophomore season with 44 tackles, 8.5 TFL, and 5.5 sacks in just his third season playing football. Crawford has always been an exceptional athlete, he’s shown an explosive first step, quick […]
full_text: WACO, TX - AUGUST 29: Defensive End Keyron Crawford #24 of the Auburn Tigers holds up the number one sign after a sack during the college football game between Baylor Bears and Auburn Tigers on August, 29, 2025, at McLane Stadium in Waco, TX. (Photo by David Buono/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Raiders drafted Keyron Crawford with the 67th overall pick just a few months ag o. The former Arkansas State standout broke out in his sophomore season with 44 tackles, 8.5 TFL, and 5.5 sacks in just his third season playing football. Crawford has always been an exceptional athlete, he’s shown an explosive first step, quick fluid hips, and a large display of both horizontal & lateral explosiveness. The former standout basketball player, Crawford only started playing football in his senior season at Briarcrest Christian high school where he logged 78 tackles, 21 TFL, and 14 sacks. As a result, Crawford has been an exceptionally raw prospect, though he’s shown signs of development even over the last three months in the NFL. #Raiders rookie Keyron Crawford getting some work in at the Sack Summit pic.twitter.com/i3hx7wltP7 — Jesse Merrick – Silver & Black Sports Network (@JesseSBSN) July 11, 2026 Crawford transferred to Auburn, where the Raiders selected him after two seasons racking up 58 tackles, 10.5 TFL, and 5.5 sacks with a FF, 2 FR, and INT in his 24 games at Auburn. The timeline for Crawford is interesting, the Raiders are relying on him to have a runway to the NFL in terms of snap counts, but he should still see a good shot at 200-350 snaps this season in rotational situations. Crawford has a chance to become a starting 2nd pass rusher in the NFL, he’s shown good athleticism, a variety of pass rush moves, has a ton of length, and his initial movement skills are intriguing. His 2026 season should be slightly inconsistent with Crawford likely behind Maxx Crosby, Malcolm Koonce, Kwity Paye for rotational snaps and he’ll likely also be pushed by UDFA Cian Slone who’s made waves in the off-season so far. Crawford has worked throughout the off-season in minicamp & OTA’s rotating with each team on defense, but he’ll likely be in a strong rotational role seeing time in pass rush situations, third down, and late game rotations to ease out snap counts of the rest of the room. Crawford should also see time in situations as a designated drop player working into quick flats, something that he’s done at Auburn before and should add versatility to the Raiders defensive line. I love Keyron Crawford. If you're gonna bite on a speed rusher, why waste a high pick on an older player like Bailey when you can get the same kind of player in the 3rd? pic.twitter.com/bvOqbvhDV5 — Joe (@JoeA_NFL) April 19, 2026 Year two & three are likely the biggest for Crawford, 2027 can likely see one or all of those above him on the depth chart gone. You’d imagine the Raiders view him as a replacement for Malcolm Koonce should Koonce either have a breakout season and sign for 15 million or more, and/or remain an adequate third pass rusher where Crawford could take the reigns as a starter. Crawford’s goal for the 2026 season is largely working on his technique, functional strength, and applying the transition from Auburn to the NFL but athleticism has been the baseline for his career, and should remain a good path to get him onto the field quickly. Crawford may not have the production of a third rounder in 2026, but he’s a high upside player with a ton of potential, and the Raiders have shown a desire to consistently draft developmental prospects in the third round under John Spytek.

title: Silver Minings: QB Fernando Mendoza is competing, not against, Kirk Cousins
summary: The Las Vegas Raiders drafted Fernando Mendoza number one overall to become the potential franchise quarterback. His hype continues to build after he finally signed his rookie contract and is in the building for training camp. Mendoza isn’t expected to play right away, with the coaching staff not wanting to rush him onto the field. […]
full_text: HENDERSON, NEVADA - JUNE 09: (L) Kirk Cousins #8 and Fernando Mendoza #15 of the Las Vegas Raiders warmup during mandatory minicamp at the Las Vegas Raiders Headquarters/Intermountain Health Performance Center on June 09, 2026 in Henderson, Nevada. (Photo by Louis Grasse/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders drafted Fernando Mendoza number one overall to become the potential franchise quarterback. His hype continues to build after he finally signed his rookie contract and is in the building for training camp. Mendoza isn’t expected to play right away, with the coaching staff not wanting to rush him onto the field. That’s why the team signed Kirk Cousins this offseason to become the spot starter for the Silver and Black. This will allow Mendoza to learn and get accustomed to life in the NFL. Most of Raider Nation is expecting somewhat of a competition at the position. However, Mendoza was interviewed on the Upon Further Review podcast and believes they are competing with each other and not as rivals. “Being a part of the Silver and Black, we want to compete every single day and do the best that we can for the organization and best for the team so we can win games, Everybody in the quarterback room is a top-tier quarterback and it’s going to be competing with each other, not competing against each other.” This is a great mindset for Mendoza to have as it creates less pressure on himself to win the job. He can go out and sling it knowing that he was going to be coached up and allows Cousins to be a mentor without having to be fully engaged in correcting him. title: Will the Miami Dolphins overcome the odds in 2026?
summary: When the Miami Dolphins take the field on the road in Las Vegas against the Raiders in Week One, all eyes will be on new general manager Jon-Eric Sullvan’s revamped roster. Gone are plenty of high priced, aging veterans — replaced by 13 new rookies (assuming they all make the team) and several under-the-radar free […]
full_text: MIAMI GARDENS, FLORIDA - JUNE 09: Malik Willis #2 of the Miami Dolphins looks on during OTA Offseason Workouts at Baptist Health Training Complex on June 09, 2026 in Miami Gardens, Florida. (Photo by Megan Briggs/Getty Images) | Getty Images When the Miami Dolphins take the field on the road in Las Vegas against the Raiders in Week One, all eyes will be on new general manager Jon-Eric Sullvan’s revamped roster. Gone are plenty of high priced, aging veterans — replaced by 13 new rookies (assuming they all make the team) and several under-the-radar free agent signings. With all of the turnover happening in Miami Gardens, expectations from national sources are extremely low. Speaking of Las Vegas, betting experts have set the Dolphins win/loss total at just 4.5 wins for the 2026 season. Can the new-look team in aqua and orange overcome the odds and deliver 5 or more wins for their loyal fanbase this year? Count Bleacher Report’s Brad Gagnon as someone who isn’t a believer in Miami this season. Earlier on Monday, he released an article talking about all 32 teams in the National Football League and whether or not they can beat their Las Vegas predictions this season. He has the Dolphins winning four or less games in 2026. Here’s what he had to say about Miami’s chances: “Last year, the Dolphins won seven games with the fourth-easiest schedule in the NFL. This year, as they climb deeper into a rebuild, they face the second-toughest sked in the league. Maybe they’ll have better injury luck after leading the AFC in adjusted games lost in 2025, and maybe Malik Willis and a coaching staff will energize the franchise, but that’s a lot of change. And the support for Willis doesn’t inspire a lot of confidence as the post-Tyreek Hill/Jaylen Waddle era kicks off in South Florida. For now, this profiles as one of the weakest rosters in the league, and the road back to contention looks steep.” It will certainly be an interesting year for our South Florida squad. Even if the win total isn’t a high one, they can still show they’re headed in the right direction by playing tough, smart football and getting better as the season rolls on. How many wins do you think the Dolphins will have in 2026? Do you see them winning more or less than the 4.5 total Las Vegas has set for Miami? Let me know in the comments below or on Twitter/X at @MBrave13 . Fins up!

Photo by Peter Joneleit/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Miami Dolphins have had the soft opening to their 2026 training camp, with the rookies reporting to the team’s training facility last week. While the rest of the team is set to descend on Miami Gardens this week, the excitement for fans as training camp begins is growing. Last week, we wanted to tap into some of that excitement, asking which Dolphins early-round drafted rookie you are most excited to see in camp. The Dolphins might not be expected to contend this year, with FanDuel Sportsbook’s latest betting odds having Miami as the AFC team the least likely to make the playoffs this year (+1500 – double the odds of the next closest team, the New York Jets), but that does not mean there are not exciting things to watch this year. Miami has started a rebuild period, moving on from the Mike McDaniel era and transitioning into the vision of new head coach Jeff Hafley. A necessary part of that transition is the move from veterans to younger players who will grow into the system. And Miami made a deliberate move to younger players, especially when you consider their 13 drafted rookies and 12 undrafted free agent signings. But, which first-, second-, or third-round selection most excites you for this summer? Linebacker Jacob Rodriguez dominated the vote, coming in just a little under a majority. The second-round pick received a larger share of the responses than first-round picks guard Kaydn Proctor and cornerback Chris Johnson combined. Third round wide receiver Caleb Douglas was fourth with nine percent of the vote, followed by third-round tight end Will Kacmarek with three percent, and and third-round wide receiver Chris Bell rounded out the group with two percent of the vote. Rodriguez, coming to the Dolphins out of Texas Tech, finished fifth in the 2025 Heieman Trophy vote and won the Chuck Bednarik, Butkus, Lombardi, and Bronko Nagurski awards. He brings with him playmaker expectations and an ability to join a legacy of success at the linebacker position for the Dolphins from Texas Tech products – including Hall of Fame linebacker Zach Thomas and current starter and All-Pro Jordyn Brooks. Are you excited to see Rodriguez this summer? What are your expectations for him? Should we be watching a different rookie when the Dolphins get on the practice field? title: How the Vikings’ Offensive Scheme May Evolve This Season
summary: As the Minnesota Vikings get ready for the start of training camp, one thing the Vikings’ offensive coaching staff is likely preparing for is continuing the installation of the offense. That carries added importance this season if the Vikings have a new starting quarterback, particularly in the passing game, but the run game is also […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - SEPTEMBER 15: Head coach Kevin O'Connell of the Minnesota Vikings and head coach Kyle Shanahan of the San Francisco 49ers meet before the game at U.S. Bank Stadium on September 15, 2024 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. The Vikings beat the 49ers 23-17. (Photo by Alika Jenner/Getty Images) | Getty Images As the Minnesota Vikings get ready for the start of training camp, one thing the Vikings’ offensive coaching staff is likely preparing for is continuing the installation of the offense. That carries added importance this season if the Vikings have a new starting quarterback, particularly in the passing game, but the run game is also likely to get a bit of a makeover with the addition of assistant head coach Frank Smith, who is focusing on the run game. Kevin O’Connell is an offshoot of the McVay branch of the Shanahan coaching tree while Frank Smith worked under Mike McDaniel in Miami, who is an offshoot of the Kyle Shanahan branch. McDaniel specialized in the run game working under Kyle Shanahan and Frank Smith will bring a lot of those concepts to Minnesota. I won’t go into the Shanahan coaching tree history, which you can get it here , but there is a lot of overlap between various offshoots, even as each of them evolve too. Wide Zone Mixed with Power A core feature of the Shanahan offense is the wide zone run scheme. When you see all the offensive linemen take a drop or bucket step and then all block horizontally in the same direction, that is zone blocking. In wide zone, the running back aims for the butt of the tight end or if there is no tight end on the play side, then the outside leg of the tackle. The back then reads the defensive end and makes his cut after 3-5 steps. If he moves inside, the back bounces the run outside, if he pursues outside, the back bends it back inside, if the hole is open, he bangs through. Below is a classic outside zone play, called on 1st and 10. Vikings wide zone run- just how it's drawn up pic.twitter.com/r7GXn0SQVR — Warren Ludford (@wludford) July 19, 2026 This isn’t new for the Vikings or Kevin O’Connell’s scheme. It’s been a staple for years. In fact, it’s not all that different than ‘super power left’ power sweeps we used to run in pee-wee football back in the 1970s. And if you watch the play, it didn’t fool the Bengals defense. The defensive formation was toward the play side, countering the double tight-end set, the linebackers flow toward the run immediately, there is even a backside defensive back blitzing to try and get to Mason behind the line of scrimmage. The play was successful because it was well blocked and Mason didn’t hesitate, but the play design itself didn’t do much to tilt the outcome in the Vikings’ favor. The Frank Smith Factor Here is a variation of outside zone that the Dolphins ran last season under Frank Smith, the new Vikings de facto run game coordinator: On 3rd and 3, the Dolphins initially show five-wide with an empty backfield and a shotgun formation- strongly suggesting a pass play. However, De’Von Achane at the bottom of the screen, motions back to the backfield: Following Achane’s motion to the backfield, the Colts have the linebackers shifted toward the 3-wide receiver side and the safety is cheating that way too on the far hash. The Colts are running a 5-man defensive front and the strong safety is covering the tight end at the bottom of the formation. Here’s how the play unfolded: Miami Dolphins outside zone run with eye candy pic.twitter.com/z6T6V1x1yo — Warren Ludford (@wludford) July 26, 2026 The Colts’ secondary was primarily concerned about the 3-wide group right, while based on Achane’s position, it seemed like the front seven were expecting either pass or an inside run. The play side edge defender’s first step was backward- perhaps looking to work down the line in run defense- and was easily taken out by the tight end. That left the playside tackle to take out the strong safety, which was a mismatch. The playside guard had a more difficult block on the 4i defensive tackle but got just enough of him to allow Achane to break an attempt at an arm tackle. The linebacker blitzed- whether that was the play call or because he was expecting an inside run or a pass isn’t clear, but Achane’s position just behind the quarterback is a tell that the play is a run. But the Colts’ defense wasn’t expecting the handoff behind the quarterback for an outside zone run and paid for it by allowing an explosive 26-yard run. The Vikings run a variety of non-standard outside zone runs and have for years, but the level of deception here is more advanced. It caused the Colts’ defense to cheat a bit away from the play and a split-second hesitation in a key edge defender that provided an advantage for the Dolphins offense. And beyond outside zone runs, Frank Smith worked with Mike McDaniel installing some outside-the-box run designs that really challenge defense’s ability to read the play. Here is an example the Dolphins ran last season: First and ten for the Dolphins in the first quarter up 6-3 over the Chargers just past mid-field. The Dolphins are in shotgun and 22 personnel- two running backs and two tight ends- with wide receiver Jaylen Waddle in the backfield to the quarterback’s left. Running back De’Von Achane is at quarterback depth to his right, with the other running back positioned further right in the backfield outside the inline tight end while the other tight end, Darren Waller, is lined up as a receiver at the top of the picture. The initial formation and personnel package is something most defenses never see all season, if ever. The Chargers’ defense counters with a 4-3 personnel look (with strong safety Derwin James in a linebacker role) with the line strength matching the offensive formation strength. The secondary shows a Cover-2 look. Overall, a base defense look that the Dolphins might anticipate with this personnel package. Now see how the play unfolded: An outside the box play design from Mike McDaniel/Frank Smith last year in Miami leads to an uncommon result. pic.twitter.com/kEpx2SlXKQ — Warren Ludford (@wludford) July 27, 2026 The beauty of this play- and its successful execution- is both the play design and the attention to detail. A few examples: De’Von Achane lines up at quarterback depth in the backfield, rather than just behind. Normally a ‘tell’ for a run play from shotgun is when the running back lines up a step or so deeper than the quarterback. Lining up at equal depth can sometimes indicate a blocking assignment or receiving route or possibly a toss to that side- none of which is the right read in this case. The pre-snap motion of the running back, Darren Waller blocking the defensive back, Jayden Waddle looking back for a pass, and Tua Tagovailoa looking at Waddle while he hands the ball off to Achane, all contribute to the idea of the play being a screen pass to Waddle. That works to have the linebackers and safety take a couple steps toward the direction of the motion and in the case of the safety makes him just a step late to make the tackle (although his line was a bit off too). The center and right guard pulling and taking out Derwin James and the cornerback while the left guard got in front of the nose tackle and the tight end pinched the edge rusher were all well executed blocking assignments that got Achane to the second level and beyond. These are the type of run plays the Vikings may incorporate into their offense this season with Frank Smith coming over from Miami. Just a little more detail, a little more nuances, and some fresh thinking built into the play design to help give the Vikings’ offense an advantage. More Fullback? Another aspect of the acquisition of Frank Smith as the de facto run game coordinator is fullback use. The Dolphins had Alec Ingold at fullback and he averaged around 400 snaps a season over his four years in Miami under Mike McDaniel- closer to 350 his last two years and around 425 his first two years.…

title: Vikings Signing LB/S Jamal Adams
summary: On the eve of training camp officially getting underway in Eagan, the Minnesota Vikings have made a signing that can best be labeled as. . .interesting. The Minnesota Vikings are signing longtime safety/linebacker Jamal Adams. The source for this is longtime safety/linebacker Jamal Adams. Adams comes with a significant pedigree, as he garnered First-Team All-Pro […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - DECEMBER 7: Jamal Adams #33 of the Las Vegas Raiders stands on the sidelines during the national anthem prior to an NFL football game against the Denver Broncos at Allegiant Stadium on December 07, 2025 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images On the eve of training camp officially getting underway in Eagan, the Minnesota Vikings have made a signing that can best be labeled as. . .interesting. The Minnesota Vikings are signing longtime safety/linebacker Jamal Adams. The source for this is longtime safety/linebacker Jamal Adams. Year 10. #skol — Jamal Adams (@Prez) July 28, 2026 Adams comes with a significant pedigree, as he garnered First-Team All-Pro honors in 2019 and Second-Team All-Pro honors in 2018 and 2020. He was drafted by the New York Jets with the sixth overall pick in the 2017 NFL Draft and played for them until 2019, when he was traded for two first-round picks (among other compensation) to the. . .well, would you look at that. . .the Seattle Seahawks. Nolan Teasley was a part of the Seattle front office when that trade was made, so there’s your connection if you’re into looking for such things. Adams signed a big contract extension with the Seahawks ahead of the 2021 season, a four-year, $72 million deal that made him the highest-paid safety in NFL history at the time. Unfortunately, he didn’t really live up to the deal, as in 2022 he suffered a torn labrum in Week 1 that caused him to miss the entire season. Adams only appeared in nine games in 2023 with five starts, and was released by the Seahawks in March of 2024. In 2024, Adams made stops in both Tennessee and Detroit. With the Titans, he played in only three games before being placed on injured reserve and requesting his release. He played in just two games with the Lions and was released in January. Adams then spent the 2025 season with the Las Vegas Raiders, reuniting with his former coach from Seattle, Pete Carroll. He also switched positions from safety to linebacker. He avoided the injury bug, playing in all seventeen games, only starting four. He had 45 tackles, one sack, and one forced fumble. I’ve gotta tell you, folks. . .I’m not sure how Adams fits into the Vikings defense as things stand right now. I mean, I’m sure if anyone can figure out a role for someone like Adams, it’s Brian Flores and his mad scientist tendencies, but we’ll have to see what, if anything, Adams has left in the tank going into this season. What do you make of the signing of Jamal Adams, ladies and gentlemen? Give us your thoughts and impressions in the comments section.

We asked you, the readers of the best Minnesota Vikings fan site on the internet, how many receiving yards star wide receiver Justin Jefferson would have this season after a rough 2025 season. Not surprisingly, it seems that a lot of you are expecting a solid bounce-back year from #18. In a close race, the top spot in our poll for this week went to those who feel that Justin Jefferson is going to find his way to somewhere between 1,400 and 1,599 yards this coming season. That’s how 34% of our respondents voted in our poll. Just behind them, at 33%, was the group who think that Jefferson will get somewhere between 1,200 and 1,399 yards. There were 19% of you who believe that Jefferson will really explode and will go over the 1,600-yard mark once again, while 9% feel that he’ll be somewhere between 1,000 and 1,199 yards. He’s got a long way to go to catch Carter for the franchise lead in that category. . .Carter had 12,383 receiving yards as a member of the Vikings while Jefferson currently has 8,480. Moss had 9,316 yards in his two tours of duty with the Vikings. . .yes, the second one counts, even though we’ve largely tried to forget about it. title: Bradyn Swinson’s offseason overhaul has him ready to seize opportunity
summary: Bradyn Swinson’s rookie season was an eye-opening experience. The fifth-round pick acknowledged he did not take things seriously enough, which led to him being cut at the end of training camp. After re-signing with the Patriots practice squad, he signed to the active roster in November but played in just three games — logging 27 […]
full_text: Jul 23, 2025; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots defensive end Bradyn Swinson (43) walks to the practice field for training camp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | Eric Canha-Imagn Images Bradyn Swinson’s rookie season was an eye-opening experience. The fifth-round pick acknowledged he did not take things seriously enough, which led to him being cut at the end of training camp. After re-signing with the Patriots practice squad, he signed to the active roster in November but played in just three games — logging 27 defensive snaps — before being inactive throughout the playoffs. That led Swinson to attack the offseason with the goal of making a Year 2 jump, which began with changing his diet after conversations with head coach Mike Vrabel and team nutritionist Ted Harper. “I lost a ton of weight,” Swinson said. “Really just understanding the business side of everything, just losing weight, staying on my diet, and just focusing on the stuff that they want me to get better at.” Gone are the days of Swinson snacking and eating fast food, Fruit Roll-Ups, Gushers and other candy. Instead, Swinson embraced a healthier diet with more vegetables, even surprising himself by eating plantains. “I never thought I’d eat plantains,” he joked. “You got to sacrifice if you want to be great in this league.” After playing at around 270 pounds as a rookie, Swinson reported to training camp at 255 pounds. So far, he has noticed the difference. “I’m a lot stronger, and I like looking in the mirror now,” he said. “It’s good to look in the mirror when you got a couple of abs right there. But everything is going well. Just my overall speed of the game and just understanding the game and the overall power that I have behind myself now. We don’t have pads on now, but I’m looking forward to that.” In his final season at LSU, Swinson was one of the most productive pass rushers in college football, recording 60 pressures and 8.5 sacks. The talent has always been there for the 24-year-old. Now, the opportunity may be there as well in a Patriots edge group searching for someone to emerge alongside veteran Dre’Mont Jones. Swinson, who has already earned praise from the coaching staff throughout the offseason for his work, believes he is ready to capitalize on his opportunity. “Being ready for when the opportunity arises,” Swinson said. “Just always being prepared. It doesn’t matter who’s there, and who’s not. It’s more about what you’re going to do. I’m already focused on what I need to do. We got a great group of guys, a lot of guys that are hungry. I’m hungry, as well.”

title: Patriots 2026 scouting report for TE Mitch Van Vooren
summary: The New England Patriots’ tight end group remains a work in progress, even with team captain Hunter Henry a quality player firmly entrenched atop the depth chart. Behind him and third-round draft pick Eli Raridon, however, there are serious questions about the depth — especially after Julian Hill was lost for the year with injury. […]
full_text: Jul 25, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots tight end Mitch Van Vooren (46) reaches for the ball at training camp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | Eric Canha-Imagn Images The New England Patriots’ tight end group remains a work in progress, even with team captain Hunter Henry a quality player firmly entrenched atop the depth chart. Behind him and third-round draft pick Eli Raridon, however, there are serious questions about the depth — especially after Julian Hill was lost for the year with injury. In order to increase their chances of finding viable answers, the Patriots brought in a pair of depth pieces before training camp. One, Jeremiah Franklin, we already looked at in our Patriots scouting report series . Now, it’s time for the other. Hard facts Name: Mitch Van Vooren Position: Tight end Jersey number: 46 Opening day age: 25 (1/13/2001) Measurements : 6’4 1/2”, 255 lbs, 8 3/8” hand size, 33 1/8” arm length, 81” wingspan, N/A Relative Athletic Score Experience NFL: Seattle Seahawks (2025), Cleveland Browns (2025), New England Patriots (2026-) | College: Marquette (2019-22), St. Norbert (2023-24) Van Mooren lettered in football, track and basketball at Peshtigo, WI, High School and went on to join Marquette as a hurdler. He spent four seasons with the Golden Eagles, setting a school record in the 400-meter hurdles and being voted to the All-Big East Outdoor team (2022). He then moved to St. Norbert College as a graduate student, and promptly earned first-team All American honors (2023). During his first year at the school, he also revived his football career. He caught 32 passes for 535 yards and three touchdowns in his first season, followed by a 33-catch, 510-yard, 10-touchdown season during a 2024 season that saw him focus exclusively on football. He was named first-ream All-NACC in 2024 and was an honorable-mention in 2023. Despite his success in Division III, Van Vooren was not drafted in 2025. Via stints in Seattle and Cleveland, he found his way to New England during the 2026 offseason. He has yet to appear in a non-preseason NFL game. Scouting report Strengths: Van Vooren combines decent size with a mouth-watering athletic skillset. He has the straight-line speed to get behind defenders down the seam or on go routes down the sideline, and the build let alone the leaping ability — he is a former hurdler, after all — to be competitive in jump-ball and contested-catch situations. Aiding him in that regard is his length; his long arms allow him to make catches out side his natural frame. He also has shown a good feel for tempo and good concentration on back-shoulder throws. In addition, Van Vooren also is alignment-flexible and offers ability to move around the formation both as a receiver and a blocker. In general, he is a feisty blocker who plays with active hands at the point of attack. Weaknesses: Even though he has the athleticism needed to compete at the NFL level, Van Vooren is as a whole still very raw. That is not a surprise given that his only significant football experience since high school has come in the form of 22 games against Division III opposition. His route running lacks nuance, his route tree is underdeveloped, and he has not yet shown the technical repeatability to shake free from man coverage; he won mostly through superior athleticism in college — something he can not count on against the pros. 2025 review Stats : N/A Season recap: Van Vooren did not hear his name called in the 2025 NFL Draft, and also was not treated as a hot commodity during rookie free agency. He did get an invitation to the Browns’ rookie minicamp but ended up not receiving a contract offer. It took until early June before he signed his first pro deal, joining the Seahawks on a stint that ultimately was short-lived: he was released again after just nine days. Van Vooren remained unsigned into training camp, and until the Browns came knocking again. Cleveland signed him this time around, and kept him on its roster until late August. In between, he appeared in three preseason games and played 13 offensive snaps plus seven more on special teams without registering any statistics. Following his release from the Browns, Van Vooren was not picked up by another NFL team and spent the 2025 season as a free agent. 2026 preview Position: F-tight end | Ability: Camp body/Practice squad candidate | Contract: Signed through 2026 (2027 ERFA) What will be his role? Van Vooren’s athleticism was his best attribute in college, and he was used accordingly at St. Norbert. The Patriots will likely also try to make use of it this summer, potentially employing him as a rotational flex tight end capable of filling multiple spots in the lineup. What is his growth potential? Bringing only limited football experience to New England, Van Vooren remains a raw player even at age 25 who has yet to perform up to his athletic abilities in the NFL. Will he ever do so? That’s the big question, but with some more time in a pro-level program he could find himself competing for a role as a backup inline/H-back-type player. Does he have positional versatility? Theoretically, yes, even though it remains to be seen just how much the Patriots will actually lean into it in 2026. He has, however, had reps as an in-line blocker, slot receiver, split out wide and a backfield option. In addition, the Brown used him on their kickoff return, punt return and punt coverage units during last year’s preseason. What is his salary cap situation? Van Vooren signed a one-year minimum deal to join the Patriots. It consists entirely of a non-guaranteed $885,000 base salary that a) simultaneously functions as his cap number, and b) does not qualify him for Top 51 status. How safe is his roster spot? Even though he has some skill, Van Vooren’s outlook appears to be quite bleak. Not only is he an underdeveloped player, he also joined the team a few days before training camp. While the Patriots do have an opening behind Hunter Henry and Eli Raridon, other tight ends on the team’s roster are in better position to fill it. Summary: For Van Vooren, training camp will not primarily be about pushing for a roster spot but for proving himself worthy of further development on the practice squad. If he can show some promise in practice and preseason, he could have a shot. If not, he will remain a camp body. What do you think about Mitch Van Vooren heading into the 2026 season? Will he make it out of camp? Or will his Patriots tenure be over quickly? Please head down to the comment section to share your thoughts.

title: A.J. Brown getting increasingly comfortable in Patriots offense
summary: It’s been just under two months since the New England Patriots acquired star wide receiver A.J. Brown via trade with the Philadelphia Eagles. Now, just three days into training camp, Brown is settling into New England’s offense, he told the media on Monday. “I’m still getting comfortable every day,” Brown said after the Patriots’ walkthrough […]
full_text: Jun 9, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots wide receiver A.J. Brown (1) runs after the catch at minicamp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | Eric Canha-Imagn Images It’s been just under two months since the New England Patriots acquired star wide receiver A.J. Brown via trade with the Philadelphia Eagles. Now, just three days into training camp, Brown is settling into New England’s offense, he told the media on Monday. “I’m still getting comfortable every day,” Brown said after the Patriots’ walkthrough practice. “I’m in a pretty good spot. I want to say I’m like 90% [with the playbook]. It’s really just about going out and executing and getting on the same page with Drake each and every day. But I’m really comfortable.” New England parted ways with its 2028 first-round selection to acquire Brown at the start of June, effectively pairing Drake Maye with an elite receiver following his second-place finish in the 2025 NFL MVP race. Brown has amassed 56 touchdowns through the air during his seven-year career. He is now entering an offense that struggled in red-zone touchdown efficiency, ranking 20th in the league last season. The 29-year-old and Maye’s chemistry will play a crucial role in the offense reaching its highest potential in 2026. It’s also something the duo is continuing to work on, as the receiver called his new quarterback a “true professional.” “Non-stop communication,” Brown said about what goes into creating that bond. “I’m just hearing what he thinks, and he listens to me. It’s constant communication.” Their development with each other didn’t stop after mandatory minicamp in June either, with Maye hosting his wide receivers on a workout trip to his home turf in North Carolina. “It was really helpful,” Brown said of the trip. “We spent three days down there. It was pouring rain, and we were still out there.” On Saturday, Maye targeted Brown on the first team-period play of training camp, saying he saw his receiver matched up with standout cornerback Christian Gonzalez and wanted to start camp off with a “bang.” However, Brown attempted to secure the pass by reaching out with one hand, which he said Mike Vrabel ”ripped” him during the first meeting. He agreed with his head coach that he should have caught the ball. “Just being on the same page — communication,” Brown said of what tweaks he and Maye have to make. “Maybe an angle here. I may need to go higher or something small like that. The details are very small in this league, and you have to execute … You know how the game goes.” Despite the incompletion, Vrabel took note of Brown’s effort in learning what is a new offense for him ahead of practice. “There is a lot there to unpack as a receiver, especially if you want to move around and you do not want to just line up in one spot,” Vrabel said. “So, A.J. worked really hard with Todd [Downing] and his position coach, and they will continue to do that … I think he will have plenty of time through training camp and everything that we are going to do to make sure that he is where he needs to be.” For the other wide receivers this offseason, the Ole Miss product has been a valuable resource. DeMario Douglas in particular mentioned he’s learned tips he can apply to his route running and understanding of the defense in front of him, with Brown’s “different” perspective. “Great leadership,” Douglas said about what he’s seen from Brown. “He doesn’t say much, but if you watch what he does, it’s very glorifying. It helps — like lead by example. Don’t get me wrong, he does say stuff in the [receiver] room that us younger guys definitely need to know … But just to see what he says and does, it’s amazing.”

title: Will Campbell headlines Patriots’ 2026 offseason award winners
summary: After a run to Super Bowl 60, it was a shorter offseason for the New England Patriots. That did not stop players from attacking their offseason work before and after they returned to the facility in the spring. For their efforts throughout organized team activities and mandatory minicamp, Mike Vrabel announced four players as the […]
full_text: Foxborough, MA - July 25: New England Patriots offensive tackle Will Campbell signs autographs at training camp on July 25, 2026. (Photo by John Tlumacki/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images After a run to Super Bowl 60, it was a shorter offseason for the New England Patriots. That did not stop players from attacking their offseason work before and after they returned to the facility in the spring. For their efforts throughout organized team activities and mandatory minicamp, Mike Vrabel announced four players as the team’s offseason award winners: offensive tackle Will Campbell, center Jared Wilson, wide receiver Kyle Williams, and outside linebacker Elijah Ponder. “It was a good showing by the second-year group,” Vrabel said during a press conference ahead of Monday’s walkthrough . “So, that is really good to see from a second-year group. We had a lot of really good efforts in there, and I thought guys made strides, but it was good to see those guys from year one to year two be able to help us establish something in the offseason.” Last year’s first-round pick, Campbell spent the early parts of the offseason rehabbing the knee injury that cost him four games down the stretch last season. Now healthy, the 22-year-old has impressed veteran teammates with the way he attacked the offseason. “Just the mindset, the ability to keep working after a good year,” Morgan Moses said. “The acknowledgement and knowing that there’s always room for improvement. And I think there’s also the veteran presence in there… the mindset of just coming in every day and getting better. “So setting that tempo and seeing how he’s eager to learn and eager to get better and take steps. I talked to him all through the offseason and things that he was doing and getting together with Lane Johnson and those guys. I try to tell them, man, anytime you can get veteran input from what you want to be and where you want to go, that’s high quality.” Campbell was joined by fellow offensive lineman Jared Wilson, who transitioned back to his natural center position this offseason, while Kyle Williams earned recognition as the speedster bulked up over the course of the spring. On defense, former undrafted free agent Elijah Ponder was honored as he continues to trend upwards along the edge. “Came in, didn’t say a whole lot. He’s not a boisterous person by nature. I think he just continued to get better,” Vrabel said of Ponder’s rookie season. “His confidence probably improved. He earned a role on special teams and then continued to earn a role on defense. He just kept getting better.”

full_text: Jun 2, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots quarterback Tommy DeVito (16) hands the ball off to running back Lan Larison (34) during the team's OTA at Gillette Stadium. Instead of a regular practice, they held a walkthrough on the fields behind Gillette Stadium. To recap the session, please click here . Standout of the day N/A: Due to the walkthrough nature of Monday’s session, no player was in a position to truly stand out among peers. That is why we are leaving this section empty. The pace should be picked up again on Tuesday, though, which means that we will be on the lookout again for a standout performer. Other performances of note RB Lan Larison: From the outside looking in, walkthroughs are less about player performance and more about how those players are used. With that in mind, Larison stands out: as has been the case the first two days of camp, he once again repped as the third running back behind Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson. The introduction of full pads has the potential to change the picture, but right now the sophomore looks like the clear frontrunner for the RB3 job. WR Kyle Williams and WR Efton Chism III: The top of the Patriots’ wide receiver depth chart seems relatively set. A.J. Brown, Romeo Doubs, DeMario Douglas, Mack Hollins and Kayshon Boutte — the latter with a potential asterisk given that he remains a trade candidate — will be the top wideouts. The next and potentially final spot, meanwhile, looks like the subject of a competition between two sophomores: former third-round draft pick Kyle Williams and former undrafted rookie Efton Chism. The two rotated in an out of the top-level offense on Monday in a competition that very well could go either way. TE Tanner Arkin: Like Lan Larison, Arkin was already listed among yesterday’s performances of note . And like his teammate, he too appears to be in a good position to earn a depth spot on the roster. Arkin, after all, continued to see meaningful reps with the first-team offense on Monday. With fellow blocking tight end Julian Hill out for the year, he very well could be on the inside track to earn the role — at least if the first few practices including today’s walkthrough are concerned. The Patriots will hold their fourth practice of training camp on Monday. Gates will open at 9:15 p.m. ET with the session set to start approximately an hour later.
