title: Steelers training camp: Defensive position battles, top storylines to follow
summary: Last week, Ryan and Ryland gave you the top storylines to follow on the offense as the Steelers prepare to start training camp. With Wednesday marking the first practice open to the public, Read & React return to give you all the things you should be on the lookout for on the opposite side of […]
full_text: Jun 9, 2026; Pittsburgh, PA, USA; Pittsburgh Steelers linebacker Nick Herbig (51) participates in drills during Minicamp at UPMC Rooney Sports Complex. Mandatory Credit: Charles LeClaire-Imagn Images | Charles LeClaire-Imagn Images Last week, Ryan and Ryland gave you the top storylines to follow on the offense as the Steelers prepare to start training camp. With Wednesday marking the first practice open to the public, Read & React return to give you all the things you should be on the lookout for on the opposite side of the ball. Patrick Graham’s influence RP : Of all the changes the Steelers made this offseason, the naming of Patrick Graham as defensive coordinator may be the hardest to pre-evaluate with any sense of certainty. Graham comes to Pittsburgh with a seemingly positive reputation among NFL circles, though it is difficult to point to any particularly stellar defenses on his resume. Rather, he is a coach who has been credited with making the most out of some rosters that look truly awful on paper. Graham has worked under several respected defensive minds during his NFL journey. For seven seasons, starting in 2009, Graham worked his way up the coaching ranks in New England, learning from Bill Belichick. Following that, a two-year stop with the Giants had Graham paired with Steve Spagnuolo. A one-year stop in 2018 had him working under Mike McCarthy and defensive coordinator Mike Pettine. In 2019, Graham took his first defensive coordinator job with first-year head coach Brian Flores. Graham then spent two seasons as the Giants defensive coordinator and assistant head coach before joining the Raiders as coordinator in 2022. With such a varied CV and a wealth of coaching philosophy inspirations, it’s no wonder that Graham has thus far been a bit of a chameleon. He’s known for adapting his defenses to the players at his disposal, which makes pinning down a signature concept or scheme with his defenses difficult. Head coach Mike McCarthy insisted during his introductory presser that much of the Steelers’ defensive philosophies will remain the same, which I interpret to mean that the Steelers “base” defense will remain in a 3-4 alignment. However, with the 2025 Steelers running sub-packages at a 61% rate, according to Sharp Football Analysis , I’m not exactly sure how important that will be to the bottom line. Looking at some basic stats also makes it hard to paint a picture of Graham’s potential and impact, given the rosters he was handed. As I mentioned previously, his three prior defensive coordinator jobs have been the Raiders, the Ben McAdoo-led Giants, and the first year of the Brian Flores Dolphins — you know, when Flores alleges Miami owner Stephen Ross offered him a $100,000 bonus for every loss. I won’t list out every defensive roster Graham has overseen, but a quick Wikipedia or Ourlads search of those teams will show you what I’m talking about. Stat Seasons with a top-10 ranking Seasons with a bottom-10 ranking PPG 2 5 Total YPG 0 2 Passing YPG 0 2 Rushing YPG 1 2 It could be argued that this year’s Steeler defense is the best collection of talent Graham has ever had to work with as a coordinator. Whether Graham’s playcalling and scheming proves to be a ceiling raiser, merely provides a relatively high floor, or something else entirely will be one of the top storylines to follow this season. Can Steelers’ pass rush return to elite form? RB : The Steelers’ outside linebacker room is still considered very good and perhaps the biggest strength of the team, but it’s fair to say it doesn’t look quite as formidable as it has in past seasons. In fact, not a single member of the black and gold logged a double-digit sack season in 2025, with Alex Highsmith coming the closest with 9.5. Nick Herbig finished second with 7.5, while T.J. Watt surprisingly came in at third with just seven. It’ll be interesting to see how Watt’s game evolves as he plays deeper into his 30s. He obviously still has gas in the tank, but isn’t as twitchy of a speed rusher as he was in his prime. With a fresh start of sorts under a new coaching staff in 2026, there’s hope he’ll be able to unlock more of his game with a greater emphasis on power and moving around the formation. Meanwhile, Herbig is an ascending talent who got a big payday from the Steelers in June, showing the team sees him as a long-term starting piece moving forward. His increasing development and usage will be something to watch. Highsmith, who I’d argue was the team’s best all-around outside linebacker last year, isn’t as intriguing from a storyline perspective, but it will be interesting to see how coordinator Patrick Graham decides to split snaps between him, Watt and Herbig. Don’t forget about second-year outside linebacker Jack Sawyer, either. He’s still the clear No. 4 option in the room, but made some plays as a rookie, and could make a leap in 2026. The interior pass rush is a bit of a story as well. While Keeanu Benton recorded a career-best 5.5 sacks in 2025, Cam Heyward recorded his lowest total in a full season since 2012 with 3.5. How will the Steelers best push the pocket from the inside in 2026? A new look secondary RP : Of the eight defensive backs that were on the Steelers’ initial 53-man roster in 2025, only four remain on the roster. This change is especially clear at safety, where DeShon Elliott — who played in only five games due to injuries in 2025— is the lone safety remaining from that group. Gone too are Kyle Dugger and Jabril Peppers, who were both added in-season but not retained for 2026. Meanwhile, three cornerbacks return: budding star Joey Porter Jr., Jalen Ramsey, and the versatile Brandin Echols. A fourth corner, Asante Samuel Jr., is also back after joining the team last November and agreeing to a one-year contract this offseason. While Porter had a great individual season a year ago, the rest of the unit was in disarray. The Steelers allowed the fourth-most passing yards per game (243.9), yards after catch (2,224), and were tied for the fourth-highest average yards of separation per target (3.7). They also tied for the eighth-most passing touchdowns allowed (30), which is crazy to consider when you account for their top corner (Porter Jr.) surrendering zero touchdowns all season. Opposing offenses often could tell what looks the Steelers were about to run during the pre-snap, and they picked the defense apart accordingly. It comes as little surprise then that the front office has completely revamped the defensive backfield. Cornerback Jamel Dean was the team’s prized free agent acquisition, and the 29-year-old is coming off his best season as a pro. Likewise, safety Jaquan Brisker, a Penn State product, is expected to provide a massive upgrade at safety. He signed a one-year, prove-it deal after a bounce-back season in 2025. Brisker is an electric athlete and a hard hitter, but missed all but five games in 2024 while dealing with concussion symptoms. The Steelers added additional depth pieces — which Ryland will address in a section below — but the hope is that those two major additions will bring out the best of the returning players. Ideally, Dean will complete a smothering duo with Porter Jr., Elliott can remain healthy and form a feisty tandem with Brisker, and that will allow Ramsey to play more nickel and be moved around the backfield strategically by Graham. Will it all work as smoothly as intended? That’s something I hope we can catch glimpses of this summer. Will the run defense be better? RB : This isn’t as much of a storyline as it was coming into last season, but the Steelers run defense still has its warts depending on what stats you’re looking at. In terms of raw totals, Pittsburgh’s 2025 run defense was respectable, although certainly inconsistent, finishing with the 13th-fewest yards allowed per game with a 113.1-yard average. Next Gen Stats also shows they had decent results with 1.16 yards before contact per carry (11th), and the team also finished…

McIntosh was not immediately replaced, so the Seahawks will enter Tuesday with an open roster spot. It’s an unfortunate situation for the national champion from Georgia, who injured his knee during 2023 training camp and barely played as a rookie. In 2024, McIntosh played in every game but predominantly on special teams. When he did get involved in the offense, rushed for 172 yards on 31 carries and caught three passes for 22 yards in limited playing time. He also was part of Seattle’s kick return rotation. With the Seahawks drafting Jadarian Price in the first round and signing Emanuel Wilson in free agency, it was always going to be difficult for McIntosh to make the roster this season. George Holani, who lost out to McIntosh for a roster spot in 2024, was able to secure a spot after McIntosh’s injury and has the inside track to have an increased role in the offense. Factor in the eventual return of Zach Charbonnet from his own ACL tear , and there just wasn’t much of a realistic path for McIntosh to make the 53-man roster.

summary: The retirement of a Seattle Seahawks legend and current Washington Commanders linebacker finally arrived on Monday with the announcement that… special teamer Nick Bellore was hanging up the cleats. What, did you think I was referring to someone else? No, the one-time fan favorite and do-it-all man from Central Michigan called it a career and […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WA - DECEMBER 5: Russell Wilson #3, Bobby Wagner #54 and Nick Bellore #44 of the Seattle Seahawks head to midfield for the coin toss before the game against the San Francisco 49ers at Lumen Field on December 5, 2021 in Seattle, Washington. The Seahawks defeated the 49ers 30-23. (Photo by Michael Zagaris/San Francisco 49ers/Getty Images) | Getty Images The retirement of a Seattle Seahawks legend and current Washington Commanders linebacker finally arrived on Monday with the announcement that… special teamer Nick Bellore was hanging up the cleats. What, did you think I was referring to someone else? No, the one-time fan favorite and do-it-all man from Central Michigan called it a career and was added to the reserve/retired list by the Commanders . If Bellore unretires, the Commanders still hold his contractual rights. Bellore spent five seasons with the Seahawks, the longest tenure of the journeyman’s career, serving as a linebacker and fullback during his time under Pete Carroll. A two-time Pro Bowler (2020 and 2023), Bellore recorded 65 of his career 280 tackles in Seattle while forcing one fumble and recovering two. He also grabbed his lone career interception during his time with the San Francisco 49ers against the Seahawks, picking off then-Seahawks backup Trevone Boykin in garbage time of a 37-18 Seahawks’ win. During his time on offense, Bellore caught two touchdowns across 15 seasons in the NFL. One of which came with the Seahawks in an underwhelming 27-13 loss to the Arizona Cardinals in 2019. While Bellore was a favorite of those who enjoyed gritty special teams play, he endeared himself to Seahawks fans primarily off the field. Between his interestingly photoshopped tweets, taking comedic jabs at teammates over Twitter or his short-lived “Between Two Bellores” parody series on the Seahawks’ YouTube channel, Bellore was putting in overtime to make sure fans of the era remembered his name. I make the rules bud. #ProBowlVote @qdiggs6 @NBELLORE54 https://t.co/TnKYPLIqyu pic.twitter.com/cncLgWDETE — Nick Bellore (@NBELLORE54) December 16, 2021 Bellore was released by the Seahawks in 2024 and found a new home in Washington, where he continued to make an impact on special teams for Dan Quinn’s team. In March of last year, Bellore signed a two-year extension. However, he’s called it a career after 15 years in the league, leaving him more than enough time to pick up his passion for comedy.

title: What can the Seahawks ‘D’ for a Super Bowl encore?
summary: History used to be kinder to dynasties. Steelers, Niners, Ming. You know, the big three. Now it kneecaps them, with notable exceptions. It’s widely known that Tom Brady, Patrick Mahomes and John Elway are the only quarterbacks to lead their team to Super Bowl repeats in the salary cap era. Of course, you’ll rightly tell […]
full_text: Leonard Williams of the Seattle Seahawks holds up the Vince Lombardi Trophy during a Super Bowl LX trophy celebration at Lumen Field in Seattle, Washington, on February 11, 2026. (Photo by Jason Redmond / AFP via Getty Images) | AFP via Getty Images History used to be kinder to dynasties. Steelers, Niners, Ming. You know, the big three. Now it kneecaps them, with notable exceptions. It’s widely known that Tom Brady, Patrick Mahomes and John Elway are the only quarterbacks to lead their team to Super Bowl repeats in the salary cap era. Of course, you’ll rightly tell me Brady and Mahomes are no Sam Darnold. And Rob Gronkowski or Travis Kelce aren’t even in the same discussion as AJ Barner. Silly to talk about those old men when it’s a young man’s league. Plus, Seattle is armed with Jaxon Smith-Njigba, the reigning Defensive AND Offensive Player of the Year, a cleated malevolent sprite who breaks ankles for breakfast and swallows souls for Sunday dinner. Ah, but to frame the Seattle Seahawks’ repeat chances through their offensive playmakers is both unjust and inaccurate. While Mahomes gets the endorsements, Brady gets to play owner in Vegas and Darnold is throwing out first pitches at ball games , the truth remains, defense wins championships, same as always. Same. As. Always. Which is better news for the Dark Side anyway. So in honor of the type of defense the 2025 Seahawks played, four D-related reasons they can repeat are listed below; in honor of how the National Football League actually works, three D-related reasons they cannot repeat will follow. Quick apology which is fake: I’m calling them Dreasons. Dreason 1: Defense wins Lombardis Longtime fans will easily recall the 2000 Ravens, the 2002 Buccaneers, the 2013 Seahawks, the 2015 Broncos, and other examples from decades of defensive determinism. However, the Brady and Mahomes examples are also arguments for defense. The Patriots won consecutive titles before Tom was in anyone’s top QB tier because defensive guru Bill Belichick assembled a unit that led the league in scoring defense for 2003 and came in second a year later. The Chiefs’ last title came because defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo developed enough Shanahan counter-moves and spooked Brock Purdy in crunch time. Man, that guy would’ve made such a great Seattle DC when we desperately needed one. Minus a raw milk asteroid hitting the V-Mac midseason, the Seahawks defense will again stake a claim to be the league’s best. Ernest Jones, Julian Love, Leonard Williams, and Devon Witherspoon shepherded by Mike Macdonald in his third year — those are the dudes I want leading the charge for a repeat that would put Seattle in anyone’s discussion of the NFL’s most storied franchises. I want them angry that people are picking the Rams, and keeping their teammates sharp. DeMarcus Lawrence, Derick Hall, Byron Murphy, Jarran Reed and Uchenna Nwosu along the defensive line all at once? Sorry to say, your offensive play is probably wrecked. Nick Emmanwori being everything everywhere all at once, teleporting from the defensive backfield to the line of scrimmage because he can, sauntering from sideline to sideline, salivating with malice? God have mercy. Growing role players like Josh Jobe, Drake Thomas and Ty Okada coming into their own, now with valuable experience and a taste for winning? You can try and pick on them out of necessity, but they are not weak links. Y’all, if we’re throwing the Seahawks another parade in February, it’ll be because of those 14 men, their capable understudies, and their head coach, about whom no amount of superlatives will do. Which brings up — Dreason 2: Depth While it may sometimes feel to opponents like Seattle has 14 defenders on the field at once, I checked, and the rulebook says 11 at most, and no touching the receivers, ever. Still, you get my drift — while other squads struggle to fill the 53-man with 53 men who can actually hold their own on the field, the Seahawks have more starting-level players than starting spots. And that’s not even counting the incoming rookie class, which figures to hold one or more immediate pleasant surprises (Bud Clark, Julian Neal, please pick up an action green courtesy phone). I’m not the spirit of John Clayton, RIP. I can’t recite the entire roster of all 32 teams, plus practice squads. So apply the traditional grain of salt to this assertion — Seattle has the deepest team in all of football. The depth argument even extends to a place we haven’t taken it recently: the offensive line. Yes, the offensive line, yes of the Seahawks, you’re thinking of the same Seahawks as me, don’t close the tab yet. Did you know? Seattle returns all five starters from the unit that allowed the fifth-fewest sacks. Did you know? If I had a quarter for every time an ex-lineman came on the local radio or TV broadcast to say that continuity is everything to a line, I’d be happily stuck in the 80s arcade all day. So much Galaga. Don’t look now, but the Hawks have cohesion, competency, experience, talent. As a result, they also suddenly have (drum roll) legitimate depth. They don’t have to start guys like Bryce Cabeldue and Josh Jones in a pinch, but could. Backup center Olu Oluwatimi has 13 starts, just in case. No need to plug in youngsters Beau Stephens and Mason Richman right away; they can learn behind the scenes first. That’s a real OL, people. I would not be surprised to hear this offensive line praised for securing multiple wins in 2026. Dreason 3: Duration of windows We can laugh at the 2022 Rams all we want for missing the playoffs with a 5-12 record one year after hoisting the trophy. No, really, we can. There is no laughing police on Field Gulls until you drop an lol in the chat. But usually, teams defending their title don’t crater immediately. This is how the 59 winners before our Seahawks fared a season later: Missed playoffs: 17 times Lost in Wild Card round: 6 times Lost in Divisional Round: 13 times Lost Conference Championship game: 7 times Lost Super Bowl: 7 times. (Yeah, we know.) Won Super Bowl: 9 times. Which is a lot, but again, only three times under the cap rules. NFL teams are more likely to win multiple playoff games coming off a title than they are to miss the playoffs. If you reorganize the results into three roughly equal groups it’s more apparent: Missed playoffs entirely: 17 times Eliminated before conference championship game: 19 times Got to conference championship game or Super Bowl: 23 times With one of the youngest rosters in the NFL and a 38-year old head coach who already wears a ring, the window is wide open for 2026, according to history, which is more predictive than your neighborhood football blogger. Dreason 4: DNA For a solid quarter century now, the Seahawks are a franchise that doesn’t suffer mediocrity. They don’t let it get in the water, they don’t let it get in their veins, they don’t let it get in their heads. Because once it makes a home in your facility, your uniform, your brand, the stench of repeated losing is exceedingly hard to wash off. Jacson Bevens mentioned this all the time and I can’t get it out of my mind, nor refute it, even if I wanted to. Losing isn’t in Seattle’s football DNA. They win the division more than any of their rivals. They fired a coach after one season and took a big swing to bring in the man who’d soon start filling the trophy case. They’ve finished last once in the NFC West. Wanna know how they responded the next three seasons? 1. Back to playoffs, 2. Ten wins with new coach, 3. Super Bowl title. Cowabunga. Imagine the Jets, Browns, Cardinals, Lions (it’s true), Bears, Commanders, Dolphins, Jaguars, Titans or Raiders trying to emulate that paragraph. I’ll save you the time: they haven’t and they can’t. An occasional conference title game appearance is their ceiling, as demonstrated by… them. Need more proof? I gotchu. Nobody from the 2005 Seahawks remained on the 2014 team that reached its own Super Bowl, and nobody from…

title: John Lynch underlines ‘heightened focus’ on area where 49ers struggled in 2025
summary: Despite the injuries with which they had to deal at quarterback and at the offensive skill positions in 2025, the 49ers still had one of the most efficient offenses in football. Indeed, the Niners finished sixth in EPA per play and third in success rate on offense rate last season, though they did so while […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CA - JUNE 03: Brock Purdy #13 of the San Francisco 49ers throws the ball during a team OTA practice at SAP Performance Facility on June 3, 2026 in Santa Clara, CA. (Photo by Matthew Huang/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Despite the injuries with which they had to deal at quarterback and at the offensive skill positions in 2025, the 49ers still had one of the most efficient offenses in football. Indeed, the Niners finished sixth in EPA per play and third in success rate on offense rate last season, though they did so while struggling in one key area that has flown under the radar. Despite their strong performance in the metrics that are key measures of offensive efficiency, the 49ers did not have an explosive offensive in 2025. To the contrary, the 49ers ranked 21st in explosive play rate last season. Per Sumer Sports, the 49ers had 80 explosive plays — defined as a pass play of 20 yards or a rush of at least 12 yards — from a total of 1,055 total plays, giving them an explosive play rate of just 7.58%. San Francisco focused heavily on offense this offseason and, as the 49ers opened training camp on Saturday, GM John Lynch made it clear that they are concentrating heavily on significantly improving the number of explosives. Asked about the issue at a press conference, Lynch said: “We’ve always been an explosive team and probably fell off there a little. And so, in your personnel you go attack that. [WR] Mike Evans has been a tremendously explosive player. But I think the bigger approach has been collectively because explosives come in a lot of different shapes and sizes. They come in the run game and we fell off there. The explosives weren’t there as much and so that’s all 11 on the field. That’s your entire team and that’s what you emphasize. I think we spend a lot of time emphasizing that. We did address our personnel. I love what we were able to get accomplished this offseason. And now we’ve got to go to work and you’ve got to earn everything in this league. Explosives are no different. And they are an important part of football, limiting them on defense and going out there and being an incredibly explosive team on offense and on special teams. We always focus on that, but there has been a heightened focus on that.” A huge part of the 49ers boosting their number of explosives will be the health of quarterback Brock Purdy. If Purdy can stay on the field for a full 17-game regular season, then the 49ers should have much more joy in creating explosives than they did in a 2025 campaign that saw Mac Jones fill in for eight games. Having Mike Evans, a ball-dominant X whose Hall of Fame career has seen him establish a track record of making big plays downfield, should considerably aid the 49ers in terms of producing more pass game explosives. A healthy Ricky Pearsall would also help in a substantial way, considering his rapport with Purdy and the flashes he has displayed as a big-play weapon at all three levels, while the 49ers will be hoping free agent signing Christian Kirk and top draft pick De’Zhaun Stribling can have an impact with their ability to stretch the field and operate inside and out. The situation in improving as an explosive run team is perhaps less straightforward. The 49ers only had 29 explosive runs last season, with their rate of 6.03% ranking 26th in the league, way behind the rate of 11.05% set by the Baltimore Ravens, who led the league. Much will depend on the level of explosion Christian McCaffrey has in his legs after a 2025 season in which he averaged 3.9 yards per carry, his worst performance in that area since 2020, and had only three rushes of 20 yards or more. Kaelon Black or Jordan James emerging as a reliable backup to take some of the strain off McCaffrey would aid his cause, but history says the chances of either consistently eating into his career are slim. There will also be an onus on the offensive line after McCaffrey averaged just 2.3 yards before contact last season, below the league average of 2.5. That number reflected a need for the 49ers to do a better job of opening running lanes for the future Hall of Famer and, as such, the makeup of an O-Line that still has question-marks on the interior figures to have a significant bearing on San Francisco’s success in becoming a more explosive football team in 2026. San Francisco has made several moves with a view to becoming more explosive this season. However, fittingly for the 49ers, it is likely to be health and a longtime problem area that determine whether they pay off.

title: Nick Bosa heaps praise on rookie pass rusher, believes he’ll be an early contributor
summary: The San Francisco 49ers are back at training camp, with the first practice happening this past Sunday. It was an eventful non-padded practice, with several of San Francisco’s stars on the field, including Fred Warner and Nick Bosa, who missed much of last season due to injury. Bosa, who tore his ACL early in the […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - MAY 28: Romello Height #94 of the San Francisco 49ers works out during a team OTA practice at SAP Performance Facility on May 28, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers are back at training camp, with the first practice happening this past Sunday. It was an eventful non-padded practice, with several of San Francisco’s stars on the field, including Fred Warner and Nick Bosa, who missed much of last season due to injury. Bosa, who tore his ACL early in the season, was not among the group of players placed on the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list and was out in uniform for the first day of camp. It’s been a different type of offseason than usual for Bosa, as the veteran elected to rehab at the facility rather than do his usual offseason training at his home in Florida. That has kept him in the building for every stage of the offseason, and he’s gotten to rehab with his teammates, in particular Mykel Williams, who is also recovering from a torn ACL. Being in the building has also given Bosa a first glance at his new teammates on the defensive line. The 49ers added veteran Osa Odighizuwa to the defensive tackle mix via a trade with the Dallas Cowboys, giving the team some much-needed pass rush at the position. They also added rookies Romello Height (edge rusher) and Gracen Halton (defensive tackle) to a young group that still includes 2025 rookies Mykel Williams, C.J. West, and Alfred Collins. Height, who played at Texas Tech in 2025, was the team’s third-round pick and was considered one of the more accomplished pass rushers entering the draft. A six-year college player, he was one of the older prospects in the draft, but he showed quickness, good get-off, and strong production in his final season at Texas Tech, where he earned First Team All-Big 12 honors. This offseason, he’s the player who’s caught Bosa’s eye. “For rookie-wise, I’ve never seen a guy come in and get the scheme as quickly and seamlessly as he has,” Bosa said about Height. “Even when vets come in who haven’t played in this scheme, he’s gotten it quicker than I did. Just the way he picked it up, it just seems like second nature to him, and he’s super explosive. He’s got a bag of tricks in pass rush that you can tell he’s been coached well. And he’s a little older, so that might be a part of it for a rookie, but I think he’s going to contribute pretty quick.” The 49ers need pass rush badly after their unit ranked 32nd in the NFL last season in sacks. Granted, Bosa’s return and the addition of Odighizuwa should certainly benefit that unit, but it’s clear the 49ers envisioned a pass-rush role for Height when drafting him in the third round this offseason. With Bryce Huff’s sudden retirement, Height has a clearer path to earn snaps this season and will compete to climb the depth chart in camp. It’s a good sign that he’s already drawing praise from his teammates ahead of the season.

title: 49ers Training Camp Day 1 Notes: There will be a battle at safety for the 2nd year in a row
summary: Day one of training camp for the San Francisco 49ers got underway on Sunday afternoon. Aside from the four members beginning camp on PUP, the 49ers were relatively healthy heading into camp, with only Nate Hobbs missing the session in a bit of a surprise. Let’s get the in-session injuries out of the way, as […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - JANUARY 11: Ji'ayir Brown #27 of the San Francisco 49ers warms up prior to the NFC Wild Card playoff game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field on January 11, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images Day one of training camp for the San Francisco 49ers got underway on Sunday afternoon. Aside from the four members beginning camp on PUP, the 49ers were relatively healthy heading into camp, with only Nate Hobbs missing the session in a bit of a surprise. Let’s get the in-session injuries out of the way, as OT Vederian Lowe and WR Christian Kirk left the first practice with what are being described as “not major” injuries. Let’s review some of the news from day one from the people in attendance: Brock Purdy and Mike Evans’ rapport is displayed on day one When Evans signed with San Francisco for less money than what the open market offered, the main sticking point was playing in a Kyle Shanahan offense with Brock Purdy. One of the highlights of the practice was Purdy connecting with Evans on a long gain with CB Deommodore Lenoir in coverage. Evans and Purdy’s skill sets blend very well, and you can expect more long gains during the season. As the anchor of the receiving group, Evans needs to hit the ground running in Week 1 in Australia. The first-day performance, coupled with the praise from teammates and being “unguardable, only pushes the hype for the 49ers offense in 2026 into overdrive. Sparking a new connection 👏 pic.twitter.com/gGy11Q6xD2 — San Francisco 49ers (@49ers) July 26, 2026 LG Connor Colby is up first with the left guard spot open This isn’t exactly a surprise. The 49ers likely are giving the player they brought in last season, and who was pushed into duty in 2025, the first look at the spot, and OL coach and acting head coach Chris Foerster confirmed the thought process in his press conference after the session. Foerster also added that veteran Robert Jones will get his reps, but on Sunday it was all Colby. The placement of the second-year lineman is of note, but there can’t be an evaluation of the trenches without pads. Still, the 49ers want Colby to get the first crack during the install period of camp. Something to monitor during camp as the spot does need to be filled. ESPN’s Nick Wagoner explained in his notes and observations: “In terms of some positional battles, a few things stood out: Connor Colby is getting the first crack at left guard. He and Robert Jones are the top contenders, but it was all Colby on Sunday. Foerster said that is earned by his incumbent status, but nothing will be solidified until pads come on and evaluations can take place.” The safety position sees three players fighting for two positions Ji’Ayir Brown, Marques Sigle, and Malik Mustapha were the three safeties seen the most during team periods. Sigle and Mustapha rotated at the same spot, while Brown stayed in his spot. It’s safe to say all three will be in rotation, and two of the 49ers’ draft picks are preferred as the permanent starters by the staff. Sigle notched an interception tossed by Mac Jones, and Mustapha had a PBU on an intended pass to Ricky Pearsall. One has to wonder if Raheem Morris wants two free safety types as opposed to a free and strong safety.

Foerster spoke about Lowe, who suffered some type of ankle injury: “We’ll […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ - DECEMBER 28: Vederian Lowe #59 of the New England Patriots during the game against the New York Jets on December 28, 2025 at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Rich Graessle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Chris Foerster spoke for Kyle Shanahan on Sunday for the San Francisco 49ers. Foerster was mum about injuries. Two free agents the 49ers signed this past offseason, Vederian Lowe and Christian Kirk, didn’t make it through practice. Foerster didn’t say anything about Kirk. Foerster spoke about Lowe, who suffered some type of ankle injury: “We’ll see. It’s his ankle. We’ll see exactly what it is. With all the injuries, I know Kyle [Shanahan] goes through the report. I’m not doing that. We’ll see. Hopefully, he’s not that bad.” Rookie Enrique Cruz Jr. filled in for Lowe. Foerster had positive things to say about Cruz Jr.: “Yeah, Enrique’s been a real plus. Everybody in the building’s pleased with him. People come up out of nowhere from all over the building and say, ‘Gosh, that Enrique’s doing a really nice job.’ He’s really professional, really working on it. He has a learning curve, like all the young guys do. He’s got a long way to go, but he’s done all the right things to this point.” Cruz Jr. wasn’t the only player who didn’t make it through practice. Newly signed wideout Christian Kirk walked off with the trainers midway through practice. Unfortunately for Kirk, injuries are nothing new for him. He dealt with hamstring injuries that caused him to miss the first couple of games of the 2025 season, before later re-aggravating those. With Jacksonville in 2024, Kirk had groin and core muscle injuries. We’ll see if the injury ends up keeping Kirk out for an extended time, but there is no guarantee that he makes the roster. He’s on a one-year deal. The 49ers would eat $2.78 million by releasing Kirk, but, as the saying goes, you cannot help the club from the tub. Foerster did have glowing reviews for a couple of the other receivers. Here’s what he said about Mike Evans: “Man, I love having him out there. The guy’s obviously he’s a real pro. His skillset and the things he does well are going to add so much to our football team. We saw a play today in the red zone in OTAs. There’s just so many places where Mike’s going to help our football team and I’m very excited to have him.” The red zone will be the No. 1 place where Evans’ presence will be felt. Brock Purdy’s margin for error is sky-high when targeting Evans. Foerster also spoke highly about rookie De’Zhaun Stribling: “He’s awesome, man. He’s phenomenal. He’s everything that I think we thought he would be and more when he came out. Just mature, strong, fast, physical, understands the game, lines up the formations, very professional about things. He’s been so good and everything we thought he could be. It’s really nice to see.” The team isn’t wearing any pads yet, but it shouldn’t take long for Stribling’s presence to be felt. Kyle’s update, 10:21 a.m. PT: Matt Maiocco tweeted that Vederian Lowe has a high-ankle sprain and will miss extended time. Wide receiver Christian Kirk officially sustained a calf strain. Rookie defensive tackle Gracen Halton has a knee bone bruise, while defensive lineman Andrew Farmer has a back injury. Neither player will practice today.

title: How 49ers veterans are stepping up in Kyle Shanahan’s absence
summary: Over the weekend, the San Francisco 49ers community was hit with unexpected news, as ESPN reported that head coach Kyle Shanahan had been in a serious car accident that left him with several injuries, including a broken nose and a concussion. As a result, Shanahan would be limited throughout training camp, with assistant head coach […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CA - JUNE 03: Trent Williams #71 of the San Francisco 49ers speaks with the media after a team OTA practice at SAP Performance Facility on June 3, 2026 in Santa Clara, CA. (Photo by Matthew Huang/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Over the weekend, the San Francisco 49ers community was hit with unexpected news, as ESPN reported that head coach Kyle Shanahan had been in a serious car accident that left him with several injuries, including a broken nose and a concussion. As a result, Shanahan would be limited throughout training camp, with assistant head coach Chris Foerster stepping into an interim role for the time being. Now, Shanahan has been around the building, general manager John Lynch shared, and was present at the start of training camp on Sunday. But he will be limited until the symptoms of his concussion resolve, with a current expectation that he should be on the sidelines for San Francisco’s Week 1 contest against the Los Angeles Rams in Australia. Speaking to the media after San Francisco’s first practice, Foerster shared that it would be a collective effort to spell Shanahan, with the entire coaching staff helping out in various ways. In addition, Lynch noted how San Francisco’s strong core of veteran leaders is stepping up in Shanahan’s absence as well. “Yes, absolutely [it’s valuable to have that veteran leadership],” Lynch said. “I was with Fred [Warner] the other day. We went over to a local firehouse, and we hung out with those guys. And, you know, Fred got back to Kyle right away, and his message was, ‘We got this, Coach. We got this. Trust us.’ “And so absolutely, the Trent Williams, the Kyle Juszczyks, the Fred Warners, Christian McCaffreys, Brock Purdys. I mean, we’ve got tremendous leadership.” Williams reiterated that statement, sharing that there isn’t any pressure on Shanahan as he recovers. “We got a lot of vets,” Williams said when asked about leadership. He really can be on autopilot. We got that locker room.” While Shanahan has arguably been the most important person in the 49ers franchise since his arrival in 2017, he’s constructed a strong setup of players and coaches that can really help run things smoothly in a situation like this. On the player side, San Francisco has several trusted veterans who have been leaders on the team for years. Fred Warner is back and healthy at training camp with his usual energy. Trent Williams is back for his 16th NFL season and seventh with the 49ers. Kyle Juszczcyk is entering his 10th season with the 49ers. Christian McCaffrey is heading into Year 5 with the team. And Brock Purdy has been a proclaimed leader in San Francisco since his rookie season. On the coaching side, there’s a ton of familiarity and continuity, starting with Chris Foerster, who has 34 years of coaching experience, has been with Shanahan at multiple stops, and has been with the 49ers since 2019, where he’s received multiple promotions. Raheem Morris is a former head coach who is well respected on the defensive side of the ball. Klay Kubiak has steadily grown into San Francisco’s offensive coordinator role on offense. Additionally, former Indianapolis Colts head coach Matt Eberflus is on staff. Longtime staffers Kris Kocurek, Bobby Turner, Johnny Holland, and even K.J. Wright all hold down their respective position groups. This 49ers organization is a well-oiled machine that should be able to pick up Shanahan as he recovers, and it’s a good sign that the veterans are stepping up heading into training camp.

title: 49ers news: It sounds like Nick Martin will get the first shot at SAM linebacker
summary: This morning you’ll read about some training camp updates from some of the San Francisco 49ers beat. And good old Mike Florio’s thoughts on Kyle Shanahan’s accident. User KeepThemGuessing shared his thoughts in The Feed about John Lynch’s press conference from this past weekend. 2026 San Francisco 49ers training camp: Latest intel, updates More observations […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - NOVEMBER 24: Nick Martin #45 of the San Francisco 49ers gets set during the first half of an NFL football game against the Carolina Panthers at Levi's Stadium on November 24, 2025 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images This morning you’ll read about some training camp updates from some of the San Francisco 49ers beat. And good old Mike Florio’s thoughts on Kyle Shanahan’s accident. User KeepThemGuessing shared his thoughts in The Feed about John Lynch’s press conference from this past weekend. 2026 San Francisco 49ers training camp: Latest intel, updates More observations from the day: Defensive back Nate Hobbs was the only player on the active roster not participating at the beginning of practice. Hobbs dealt with knee issues last season. Offensive tackle Vederian Lowe and wide receiver Christian Kirk were hobbled a bit during the session. It was a strong day for QB Brock Purdy , who went 10-of-12 in team drills with the highlight coming on a deep ball down the left sideline to WR Mike Evans for a big gain against CB Deommodore Lenoir . Conversely, we saw a couple of interceptions for backup QB Mac Jones , including one thrown right to S Marques Sigle . LB Nick Martin appears to be getting the first crack at the Sam linebacker spot, though the Niners have multiple options to work through there. The same is true of Connor Colby at left guard. He took all the reps with the starters Sunday, though Chris Foerster said Robert Jones will also compete there. 49ers first impressions: Shanahan arrives, Purdy and Evans connect, and Bosa returns “Nick Bosa looks better than he did before he got hurt last year,” 49ers left tackle Trent Williams said. “I see him every day. I can’t tell he had an injury and came back from anything. Most people with an injury that catastrophic, you can see it with something, like with atrophy in the leg.” Bosa looks like a player who can singlehandedly rectify one of the 49ers’ most glaring weaknesses from last season: the pass rush. The team finished last in the NFL with just 20 sacks. Their struggles came after the 49ers actually sealed two early-season wins, including one over the Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks, with their pass rush. 49ers wanted to keep Shanahan accident quiet, and some in the media complied Others who cover the 49ers knew about it, too. Before the news was released, Tim Kawakami of the San Francisco Standard dropped a hint: “I think there’s going to be some news later this morning.” Kawakami later admitted that he was aware of the situation, but that he didn’t report it because he “ knew about 15% of the details .” Still, he apparently knew 100 percent of the fact that there was an accident. Not every detail related to the story needed to be reported, especially when plenty of the basic information about the collision was available from public sources. News regarding events that entail the involvement of the police and/or other first responders rarely gets held. It’s public information. (For example, news regarding Tony Romo’s recent arrest was shared as soon as Fox News 6 in Wisconsin obtained the public arrest detention report.) In this situation, the conduits for publicly-available information to the general public either were asleep at the switch or made a deliberate choice not to perform one of the core functions of journalism. Day 1 of 49ers training camp shows glimpse of change on LB depth chart Big changes appear to be coming for the San Francisco 49ers linebacking corps. At least that’s what Day 1 of training camp taught us. The Sacramento Bee’s Chris Biderman reported second-year linebacker Nick Martin was running with the first-team defense as the Sam linebacker alongside veterans Fred Warner and Dre Greenlaw. This could be an indicator of some of the changes coming from defensive coordinator Raheem Morris. Warner will take his usual Mike LB spot, while Greenlaw slots back in as the Will LB where he spent his first six NFL seasons in San Francisco. The third LB wasn’t used as frequently in past iterations of the 49ers’ defense and the prototypical player at that spot was bigger than Martin’s 6-foot, 220-pound frame. 49ers training camp report: Kyle Shanahan on hand for Day 1 after car accident Offensive play of the day Quarterback Brock Purdy and veteran wide receiver Mike Evans figure to get quite familiar with each other through training camp and heading into the regular season. Those two gave an early preview of what might be expected this year, as they hooked up on a couple of pass completions. The top play was a deep pass down the left sideline in which Evans was matched against cornerback Deommodore Lenoir. Safety Marques Sigle was a split-second late, as Evans made the reception. Defensive play of the day Linebackers Garret Wallow and Jalen Graham teamed up for the most-notable defensive play of the day for an interception of backup quarterback Mac Jones. Jones looked to fit a throw into Jordan Watkins over the middle, but Wallow made a leaping deflection of the pass. The ball was deflected again before hitting the ground, and Graham finally gathered it in and returned it back the other way. Competition to watch Connor Colby appears to be in the lead in the competition for the starting job at left guard. Now, all he has to do is give the 49ers no reason to try anyone else in that spot. Colby and veteran pickup Robert Jones separated themselves during the offseason program, Foerster said. Colby, who started six games for the 49ers last season, is playing with a lot more confidence and decisiveness, Williams said.

title: Mike Borgonzi keeps relying on familiarity to bolster Titans’ CB depth
summary: Tennessee Titans general manager Mike Borgonzi totally revamped the cornerback room this offseason. It was necessary after he gutted the position by trading Jarvis Brownlee and Roger McCreary, and cut L’Jarius Sneed. As soon as free agency began, Borgonzi signed Alontae Taylor, Cor’Dale Flott, and Joshua Williams to be the Titans’ top three new boundary […]
full_text: Photo of the new Titans helmets set up during a pre NFL draft press conference held at the Titans practice facility Thursday, April 16, 2026. | Alan Poizner/For The Tennessean / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images Tennessee Titans general manager Mike Borgonzi totally revamped the cornerback room this offseason . It was necessary after he gutted the position by trading Jarvis Brownlee and Roger McCreary, and cut L’Jarius Sneed. As soon as free agency began, Borgonzi signed Alontae Taylor, Cor’Dale Flott, and Joshua Williams to be the Titans’ top three new boundary corners. Now, a fourth addition has arrived. The Titans agreed to terms with cornerback Nazeeh Johnson before training camp opened. Johnson marks the second former Kansas City Chiefs cornerback to sign with the Titans this offseason, joining Williams. It seems that Borgonzi is very content to rely on familiarity to remake the Titans’ depth at cornerback. He didn’t know Flott and Taylor from Kansas City, but still signed them to very lucrative contracts to be the new starters. But when it came to supporting Flott and Taylor, he felt comfortable calling on Williams, and now Johnson. Borgonzi was with the Chiefs when they drafted both Williams and Johnson. That certainly isn’t a coincidence. He’s also signed defensive end Malik Herring and punter Tommy Townsend this offseason, two other players he spent time with in KC. Essentially every free agent the Titans signed this offseason had ties to Borgonzi or the new coaching staff. Daniel Bellinger, Flott, Austin Schlottmann, and Wan’Dale Robinson have connections to Brian Daboll. John Franklin-Myers, Jacob Martin, Solomon Thomas, Tony Adams, and Jordan Elliott are among those with connections to Robert Saleh. Williams is essentially guaranteed to be the Titans’ primary backup cornerback on the outside behind Flott and Taylor. Johnson probably isn’t assured a 53-man roster spot, but he has a decent chance to compete for the fifth cornerback role with Micah Robinson, Keydrain Calligan, and a bunch of undrafted free agent rookies. Johnson will arrive at training camp with designs on making the 53-man roster.

title: The Titans signed an offensive tackle, but he doesn’t solve their problem
summary: The Tennessee Titans officially start training camp this week. The veterans report on Tuesday. The first practice session occurs Wednesday, and Saturday’s session is the first open practice. Before reporting, the Titans placed offensive tackle JC Latham and safety Amani Hooker on the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list. It caused an immediate chain-reaction in […]
full_text: Nov 30, 2025; Nashville, Tennessee, USA; Tennessee Titans offensive tackle JC Latham (55) attempts to slow down Jacksonville Jaguars defensive end Josh Hines-Allen (41) during the first half at Nissan Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Steve Roberts-Imagn Images | Steve Roberts-Imagn Images The Tennessee Titans officially start training camp this week . The veterans report on Tuesday. The first practice session occurs Wednesday, and Saturday’s session is the first open practice. Before reporting, the Titans placed offensive tackle JC Latham and safety Amani Hooker on the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list. It caused an immediate chain-reaction in a fanbase that is concerned about Latham having another inconsistent season. They also made a pair of roster moves. The Titans signed offensive tackle Zachary Thomas and waived tackle Ryan Hayes. Hayes was with the Titans during minicamp and OTAs. He’s now been replaced with Thomas, who does not solve their true roster issue. Thomas was a sixth-round pick during the 2022 NFL Draft out of San Diego State. He’s already been a journeyman, spending time with six different NFL teams already. Thomas has appeared in 17 career games, last playing meaningful snaps in 2024 with the Patriots and Texans. Thomas played roughly 100 snaps as a reserve in 2024. Pro Football Focus credited him with allowing two sacks and four pressures. Thomas has not proven to be an NFL-caliber offensive tackle. Nothing about the move indicates the Titans think Thomas is anything more than a camp body, but the point is the roster still desperately needs a swing tackle. Having Latham land on the PUP only exasperates the issue. The Titans cannot possibly have faith in sophomore undrafted free agent Brandon Crenshaw-Dickson being the No. 3 tackle this season. Perhaps the Titans feel veteran Austin Deculus is their swing tackle. Deculus played extremely poorly in a similar role with the Los Angeles Chargers last season. Based on his history, the Titans shouldn’t trust Deculus to not sink the offense if he has to play meaningful snaps. The Titans signed an offensive tackle, but they still badly need one.

full_text: The Commanders have so much new in place as the full squad reports to training camp on Tuesday . New offensive and defensive coordinators. An overhauled defensive front and linebacker corps. There are new rushers and receivers. There’s some new player leadership, with authoritative voices helping captain the roster. This group looks younger, faster and more talented than a 2025 crew that regressed into a 5-12 shell of its former self . Injuries severely depleted a Commanders team that reached the NFC title game the year before , which was one of a few factors that sent them tumbling down. While this year’s group seems better than the 2025 assembly, Washington remains in a tough division with uncertainty at some important spots. Some have the Commanders returning to the NFC playoffs as a wild-card team. Others have them missing the postseason but improving by three or four wins. Would you consider that a successful season? Is that determined by improvement in key areas, the development of Adam Peters’ draft picks or other factors examined by the eye test? Or is it all about the overall record? Let’s just keep this discussion post simple: How do you define success for Washington’s 2026 campaign? What’s good enough? What would put Peters and head coach Dan Quinn on the hot seat? Let us know in the comments below.

full_text: The Commanders have placed linebacker and core special teams player Nick Bellore on the reserve-retired list, the team announced on Monday afternoon. Bellore played 15 NFL seasons, including the last two in Washington. He played 32 games during that span, with 33 tackles and one for a loss. The two-time Pro Bowler also played for the Jets, 49ers, Lions and Seahawks. This is the corresponding move with the signing of veteran cornerback Rasul Douglas. This represents the corresponding move to the CB Rasul Douglas signing. Maguranyanga. Bellore made a career out of excellent special teams play, and his absence will be felt in the kicking game during the 2026 campaign. title: Expect to see more one-on-ones in Commanders training camp
summary: ESPN Commanders’ reporter John Keim spoke on his recent podcast about the upcoming training camp which begins for Washington this Wednesday. One thing he mentioned that caught my attention is how he expects to see more one-on-one matchups during camp this year – something they surprisingly deviated from last year under head coach Dan Quinn. […]
full_text: ESPN Commanders’ reporter John Keim spoke on his recent podcast about the upcoming training camp which begins for Washington this Wednesday. One thing he mentioned that caught my attention is how he expects to see more one-on-one matchups during camp this year – something they surprisingly deviated from last year under head coach Dan Quinn. John went on to talk a bit about how Quinn absolutely loves competition, and how the decision to not see as many one-on-ones at last year’s camp was a bit of a surprise. There was an interesting dynamic last year, as Washington had an older roster compared to this season. Could that have been a reason why Washington shied away from this so very important part of camp? We may never know the answer to the question above, however both Peters and Quinn are scheduled to speak to the media later on Tuesday at 6 p.m. ET, so maybe this topic gets brought up by our journalists. The importance of one-on-ones Competition breeds excellence. This is not just for football, but essentially every facet of life. Iron sharpens iron As an athlete growing up, one-on-ones were part of my life. At the early age of 8, my father would have my best friend (who lived across the street from me growing up in Martinsburg, WV) and I out in the back yard in pads doing nutcrackers prior to the midget football season starting. In high school, we’d carve out time to compete in what we called the “box of war”, which was a position-specific live one-on-one open-field tackling drill against our teammates. We’d also do Oklahoma’s, 7v7 and O-line-D-line 1v1s. In college back in the late 90’s-early 2000’s, restrictions were much different than they are now. More live action was allowed and our coaches made sure they took full advantage of this teaching time to do one-on-ones. Today, collegiate practices are much different, only allowing a certain amount of “contact” per week. I always joke with my son that he has it easy in college compared to what I did, but there is still plenty of one-on-one exposure these athletes get. From a pure coaching perspective, I always valued one-on-ones with my athletes. It was my measuring stick from practice to practice, week to week and even year to year. Without this competition, there was truly no way to judge where my athletes stood or how much progress they were making. I would carve out time into my weekly INDY periods to have my players do specific 1v1 drills. We would run passing skelly at minimum twice a week, and I would often end my practices with some one-on-ones. Everything we’d work on during any specific practice would be reinforced through one-on-ones. We’d often have our film crew tape these as they were incredible teaching moments. In an NFL training camp, one-on-ones are the measuring stick that coaches can hold their players to. Some examples below are intriguing matchups I’d be interested in seeing this camp for Washington. OL vs. DL Laremy Tunsil vs. Odafe Oweh Josh Conerly vs. K’Lavon Chaisson Sam Cosmi vs. Daron Payne Brandon Coleman vs. Johnny Newton Nick Allegretti vs. Tim Settle Chris Paul vs. Javon Kinlaw *These battles can tell us a LOT; especially: If a D-lineman gets stoned initially, what secondary moves does he have. Can an interior o-lineman anchor against a powerful bull-rush? Can a quick guy like Newton win with just his first step? Do our offensive tackles have correct hand-placement (this is BIG)? Do our interior offensive linemen have patience and not lunge or over-extend? LB vs. TE/RB (out of the backfield) in coverage Sonny Styles vs. Chig Okonkwo Leo Chenal vs. Ben Sinnott Frankie Luvu vs. John Bates Jordan Magee vs. Colson Yankoff Sonny Styles vs. Rachaad White Leo Chenal vs. Bill Croskey-Merritt * Here, I’m looking at a few different things: Can the LBs flip their hips and run vertically with a TE? Can the LBs be on their toes and not get caught flat-footed by a RB on a choice-route? Can the LBs open up and run with a RB on a wheel? I expect an athletic TE to beat a LB – can they do that consistently? S vs. TE Nick Cross vs. Chig Okonkwo Quan Martin vs. Ben Sinnott Tyler Owens vs. Chig Okonkwo/Ben Sinnott Jeremy Reaves vs. John Bates *Here is what I’d be looking to see: Can Cross stay with Chig in off-coverage? Does Owens have the hip fluidity to stay with a shifty TE? Can Martin be physical when the ball arrives? TE play-strength – using their body against a smaller defender. Although a lot of zone may be played on the backend this year, 1v1s with wide receivers against corners can tell the coaches a lot. WR vs. CB Terry McLaurin vs. Trey Amos Antonio Williams vs. Mike Sainristil Luke McCaffrey vs. Amik Robertson Treylon Burks vs. Darius Rush Dyami Brown vs. Rasul Douglas *Here is what I’d be looking for: Does Terry still have that extra gear? Mikey vs. Williams – the short-area-quickness matchup? Can Burks win with play-strength against a young, big, physical CB? How aggressive is Robertson within the cushion? Can Douglas cover deep speed? I am very excited to see more one-on-one matchups this summer during training camp. I also expect to see this in some of our joint practices . All the above are just examples (there will certainly be many more) of what I hope becomes a very competitive 2026 camp and help to prepare our team for a very intense start to the 2026 season.

title: Commanders part ways with TEs coach Ben Steele after DWI arrest
summary: The Washington Commanders are set to open training camp this week, but they will be doing it without new tight ends coach Ben Steele. Per Virginia court records, Steele was arrested for suspicion of driving while […]
full_text: The Washington Commanders are set to open training camp this week, but they will be doing it without new tight ends coach Ben Steele. The team announced Monday morning that it was parting ways with Steele, and wouldn’t comment further on the situation. Per Virginia court records , Steele was arrested for suspicion of driving while intoxicated on June 7, and he faces an additional charges for refusing the field blood/breath test, obstruction/resisting arrest without force and changing course without a signal. More details on the arrest from The Athletic’s Nicki Jhabvala : According to the arrest affidavit, a Loudoun County Sheriff’s deputy observed Steele in the area of Route 28 and Route 7 around 3:50 a.m. with his right signal on, drifting left and weaving within his lane. The officer clocked Steele at speeds between 25 and 30 mph on Gloucester Parkway, where the posted speed limit is 45 mph. Once stopped, the officer noticed that Steele appeared intoxicated with “glassy/red eyes, slurred speech, confused speech” and had a “strong and distinct odor of an alcoholic beverage.” The officer advised Steele to get out of his vehicle several times, according to the affidavit, but Steele repeatedly refused, asking why he needed to step out. The officer then physically entered the car to remove Steele, who pulled back against the officer during his attempt. Steele refused to provide a breath test on the scene, according to the affidavit, but he later submitted to a blood test that revealed a 0.214 percent blood alcohol content, records show. Per The Athletic’s Nicki Jhabvala, Steele was dismissed for violating team policy. Steele was the Cardinals tight ends coach for the last three seasons before joining Washington’s staff in 2026. The Commanders previous TEs coach was David Raih, but he was promoted to offensive pass game coordinator when David Blough got the promotion to OC. He is considered a future offensive coordinator himself, but could help with the group until Washington hires another coach. There is no assistant TEs coach on staff. Per NBC4’s JP Finlay, Steele did not coach during the team’s mandatory minicamp, with offensive assistant Wes Welker coaching the tight ends. He was also not available for the team’s media availability on June 10th, Head coach Dan Quinn will speak with the media on Tuesday and could announce Steele’s replacement at that time. We are parting ways with tight ends coach Ben Steele. title: Breaking Down Sonny Styles, Commanders’ high-upside linebacker corps
summary: Following the massive overhaul general manager Adam Peters has done to Washington’s front seven, the Commanders’ linebacker unit has a chance to be special. The group boasted high football intelligence with Bobby Wagner’s leadership the past two seasons, but lacked athleticism and dynamic playmaking ability. Wagner played 99% of the team’s defensive snaps; he never […]
full_text: Following the massive overhaul general manager Adam Peters has done to Washington’s front seven, the Commanders’ linebacker unit has a chance to be special. The group boasted high football intelligence with Bobby Wagner’s leadership the past two seasons, but lacked athleticism and dynamic playmaking ability. Wagner played 99% of the team’s defensive snaps; he never got off the field, and at times, depending on the matchup, he struggled covering or running in space. This unit easily has become Washington’s highest-ceiling position group in 2026, and that potential starts and ends with their athleticism, versatility, and schematic flexibility. Washington made it a priority to upgrade the second level of its defense this offseason, pairing first-round pick Sonny Styles with the free agent addition Leo Chenal . Styles is the most important player in this unit’s ascension. His ability to impact the game in multiple ways makes him one of the most intriguing defensive rookies in the NFL. Whether he’s rushing the passer, dropping into coverage, defending the slot, penetrating the line of scrimmage, or flowing sideline to sideline against the run, Styles has the skill set to stay on the field in virtually every situation. The question with Styles, when you discuss this projection, is how quickly he adjusts to the speed of the NFL. If the transition time is quick and effortless, Washington’s defense could unlock a level of flexibility it has not had in years. Chenal, who spent his first four seasons in Kansas City behind an established linebacker corps, now has an opportunity to earn a significant role in Washington and cement himself as something bigger than just a depth piece. His profile undoubtedly complements Styles and gives the Commanders two linebackers capable of wreaking havoc on the first two levels of the defense. With Styles and Chenal being expected to play large roles in Daronte Jones’s defense, the biggest unknowns of the position group are the two returning linebackers, Frankie Luvu and Jordan Magee . Stylistically, both are exactly what Jones could use in his defensive scheme. Luvu’s ability to create pressure as a blitzer and disrupt plays as a penetrating linebacker is a weapon that Jones needs. Despite entering the final year of his contract , Luvu, if utilized correctly by Jones this year, could reestablish himself as one of the league’s dynamic linebackers as he was in 2024. While on paper things could work out in Luvu’s favor, it will still be interesting to know if Washington would be entertaining calls on the vet LB as they get closer to the regular season. Magee was Washington’s most explosive linebacker on the team the last two seasons, but the biggest hindrance for him was his ability to stay on the field. In 2024, injuries kept him off the field, and in 2025, while healthy and seeing more defensive snaps, he was overshadowed by Wagner and Luvu. The best news for Magee heading into his third season is that Jones doesn’t owe loyalty to anyone in front of him on the depth chart. The competition is the most important separator moving forward, and his athletic traits make a difference on the field. But Magee’s athletic ability alone won’t keep him on the field. There are still questions surrounding the interior defensive line, and that group will ultimately help determine just how dominant the linebackers can become. But if Washington’s front can consistently occupy blockers, this linebacker corps has the speed, range, and versatility to dictate as many matchups as they want. I break down in detail on YouTube why this is the position group that could change everything for Washington.
